title: Geopolitical Risks and International Business
text:
Foreword
Every multinational now says that geopolitics matters to it. Far fewer can say how much, through which channel, or what they would do differently if the number changed. The gap is not one of attention — boards discuss sanctions, export controls, wars and elections every quarter — but of measurement. Geopolitical risk reaches a firm through its market access, its inputs, its finance, its people and its data, and each of those channels can be counted. Most firms do not count them.
This book is the lecture notes of a twelve-session graduate course that tries to close that gap. Its method is simple and a little stubborn: every big idea is read, then rebuilt from its data. A landmark article or book — Caldara and Iacoviello’s geopolitical risk index, Baldwin’s Great Convergence, Kuziemko and Werker on the price of a Security Council seat, the Global Sanctions Data Base — is paired with a practice round in which the data are collected at source and its central figure is replicated in Tableau. A famous chart is a set of decisions: which countries, which years, which deflator, which coding rule. You only see the decisions when you make them yourself.
Each chapter ends on the same question: what does this figure not license a multinational to conclude? That is the habit the course is built to leave behind.

title: Geopolitical Risks and International Business
text:
The twelve chapters




Chapter
Question




1
What is geopolitical risk?
Before we can manage geopolitical risk, what exactly are we counting?


2
The international economic order
Who wrote the rules multinationals play by — and what happens to the rules when the writers’ share of the world shrinks?


3
Anarchy and the balance of the major powers
In a system with no government above states, who sets the terms of trade — and how would a multinational know that the balance is shifting?


4
Trade, conflict and geoeconomic fragmentation
If states trade more with friends than with rivals, how does a multinational find out which side each of its markets is on — and how fast the lines are hardening?


5
International institutions
When a multinational relies on an international institution to finance, insure or protect its business, is it relying on a rule — or on the states that buy and sell influence inside it?


6
Private authority, standards and global regulation
Most of the rules that govern a multinational’s daily operations were not written by a government. Who wrote them, with whose power — and does trade spread them up or down?


7
Measuring risk: content analysis, coding, big data and composite indices
Every geopolitical risk score a multinational buys or builds is a chain of choices: which texts, which words, which coder, which weights. Can you see the chain — and defend each link?


8
Cyber geopolitics and digital threats
Is cyberspace a new battlefield for great powers — or a new way for old rivals to hurt each other, with multinationals as collateral?


9
The redefinition of economic diplomacy
When states compete for markets, investment and technology, is the multinational the object of diplomacy, its instrument — or a diplomat in its own right?


10
Economic sanctions
Sanctions have become the instrument of first resort. Are they an efficient mechanism for regulating geopolitical risk — or a source of it?


11
Space geopolitics
Satellites now carry the position, timing, connectivity and imagery a multinational runs on. When orbit is crowded, contested and dominated by one operator, who holds the risk — and what can the firm do about it?


12
Team presentations
Can you make a board act on your assessment — and say what would change your mind?

title: 1  What Is Geopolitical Risk? Counting the Threat Before the War
text:
1.1 A question about counting
Every risk function in every multinational firm already has a view about geopolitics. It sits in the annual report, in the paragraph on principal risks; it sits in the treasury’s hedging policy, in the procurement team’s list of single-source suppliers, in the country manager’s sense of which visas will be hard to renew next year. What it rarely has is a number — and when it does, the number usually comes from somewhere else, built by someone else, for a purpose the firm never examined.
This course begins with a deliberately narrow question: before a firm can manage geopolitical risk, what exactly is it counting? The question sounds pedantic. It is not. A board that is told “geopolitical risk is at its highest level in forty years” has been told something precise about a particular index, constructed from particular newspapers, normalised to a particular base period. Whether that statement should change a capital-expenditure plan in Monterrey or a supplier contract in Penang depends entirely on what was counted, and the person presenting the slide often does not know.
The answer this chapter builds towards is that geopolitical risk is not one thing to be measured but a family of things, each visible to some instruments and invisible to others. We start with the oldest distinction in the subject, between risk and uncertainty; separate three kinds of risk that are routinely confused; sort the instruments that try to measure them into six families; and then take one instrument apart in detail — the Geopolitical Risk index of Caldara and Iacoviello (2022), the big work of this session and the target of its replication. The chapter closes on what that index cannot tell a firm, because a measure whose limits you cannot state is a measure you should not use.

section: 1.2 Risk, uncertainty, and the ground in between
text:
1.2 Risk, uncertainty, and the ground in between
The modern vocabulary starts in 1921, with an economist trying to explain where profit comes from.

From the archive · Knight, 1921
Frank Knight’s Risk, Uncertainty and Profit began as a doctoral dissertation at Cornell and was published in 1921. Its problem was a theoretical embarrassment: in a perfectly competitive economy with full information, competition should drive profit to zero, yet profit plainly exists. Knight’s answer was that some of what businessmen face can be reduced to known odds and therefore insured, pooled or priced into costs — and some cannot.
The first he called risk: a situation in which the distribution of outcomes is known, either a priori, as with dice, or statistically, from the experience of many similar cases, as with fire insurance. The second he called uncertainty: a situation that is unique enough that no such distribution can be formed, and in which the decision-maker must act on judgement. Risk, being insurable, becomes a cost like any other. Uncertainty cannot be shifted to an insurer, and it is the bearing of uncertainty — the entrepreneur’s willingness to commit resources on a judgement no one can verify in advance — that profit rewards (Knight 1921).
A century later, the distinction is quoted more often than it is read, and usually as a binary. Knight’s own treatment was more graded: what matters is whether instances can be grouped into classes homogeneous enough to support an estimate. That is precisely the question a geopolitical risk analyst faces every morning.


Risk (in Knight’s sense) — a situation in which the probabilities of outcomes can be estimated, from theory or from the experience of sufficiently similar cases, so that the exposure can be priced, pooled or insured.


Uncertainty (Knightian uncertainty) — a situation in which no reliable probability distribution over outcomes can be formed, because the case is too unlike any class of past cases. It cannot be insured away; it can only be judged.

Geopolitics lives in the ground between the two. A shipping insurer pricing piracy off the Horn of Africa is close to Knightian risk: there are thousands of transits, hundreds of incidents, and a market for war-risk premiums that updates as the incidents accumulate. A board asking whether a particular strait will be blockaded within five years is close to Knightian uncertainty: there have been blockades, but never this one, by this state, against this coalition, with these weapons. Wars recur, coups recur, sanctions recur — the categories are populated — but each instance is unlike the last in ways that matter for the estimate.
The honest description of this course is that it is an attempt to move questions from the second category towards the first, and to be candid about how far they move. Every index you will replicate is a device for grouping unlike events into classes so that something can be counted. Grouping is never neutral. When the Geopolitical Risk index counts an article about a nuclear test and an article about a terrorist bombing as two instances of the same thing, it has made a modelling choice about what is homogeneous. When the Correlates of War project averages steel output and population into one number for “power” (Session 03), it has made another. The skill the course tries to teach is not to avoid these choices — no measurement is possible without them — but to see them, state them, and ask what they do to the conclusion.
There is a practical corollary for the firm. Knightian risk can be transferred: political-risk insurance, war-risk cover on cargo, credit insurance on export receivables are all markets for it. Knightian uncertainty cannot be transferred, only managed — by flexibility, by diversification, by keeping options open, by being willing to pay for the ability to change one’s mind. Much of the strategic response to geopolitical change that firms now describe as “resilience” is, in Knight’s terms, an admission that the relevant exposures are uncertain rather than risky, and that the premium has to be paid in redundancy because there is no one to pay it to.

section: 1.3 Three kinds of risk, and the layer that comes from outside
text:
1.3 Three kinds of risk, and the layer that comes from outside
The second distinction is between three phrases that firms, consultancies and journalists use almost interchangeably: political risk, country risk and geopolitical risk. They answer different questions, attach to different units of analysis, and call for different instruments.

Political risk — the possibility that the government of a host country changes the rules applying to a foreign firm in a way that reduces the value of its investment: expropriation, forced renegotiation, discriminatory taxation, licence withdrawal, restrictions on repatriation. Its natural unit is the firm in a host country.


Country risk — the possibility that a country as a whole fails to pay, convert or transfer: sovereign default, capital controls, currency inconvertibility, a banking crisis. Its natural unit is the country, and its natural user is the lender.


Geopolitical risk — the possibility that relations between states and other political actors move against the firm: war, terrorism, sanctions, export controls, the formation of blocs, state-sponsored cyber operations. Its natural unit is the international system or a pair of states, and it frequently originates outside any country in which the firm operates.

Political risk is the oldest of the three in the international business literature, and its archetypes are dramatic. When Mexico nationalised the assets of foreign oil companies in 1938, or Iran nationalised the Anglo-Iranian Oil Company in 1951, the threat came from the host government and fell on identifiable foreign firms. The scholarly literature that grew up in the 1960s and 1970s, as decolonisation multiplied the number of host governments and expropriations became frequent, was preoccupied with this kind of event. Its classic synthesis is Kobrin (1979), who reviewed a decade and a half of work and complained that “political risk” was used to mean too many things — sometimes the political event itself, sometimes the instability of a regime, sometimes the consequences for a firm’s operations — and that the literature rarely connected the first to the last.
Kobrin’s lasting contribution was to insist that risk is a property of the relationship between an environment and a particular firm, not of the environment alone. Political instability in a country matters to a foreign investor only through specific contingencies that affect specific operations; a coup that changes nothing about the mining code may be irrelevant to the mining company, while a quiet amendment to a tax treaty may be decisive. From this followed the distinction between macro risk, which affects all foreign firms in a country, and micro risk, which falls on a sector, an industry or a single firm. Expropriation of every foreign asset after a revolution is macro; a windfall tax on telecommunications operators is micro.
Country risk grew from a different root — the bank lending of the 1970s to developing-country governments, and the debt crisis that followed in the 1980s. Its question is whether a country, as an economic and financial unit, will service its obligations and let money move. Its instruments are sovereign ratings, debt-sustainability analysis and the spreads on sovereign bonds and credit default swaps. It cares less about what the government will do to a particular investor than about whether the treasury will have the dollars.
Geopolitical risk adds a third layer that neither of the earlier traditions was designed to see: risk that originates outside the host country. A Canadian firm operating in Vietnam can be hurt by a decision taken in Washington about Chinese inputs, by a decision in Beijing about rare-earth exports, by a decision in Brussels about which payment systems may be used for which counterparties, or by a naval incident in a sea lane neither Canada nor Vietnam controls. The host government may be perfectly stable and perfectly friendly; the threat travels through the firm’s suppliers, customers, banks and networks.
The three are not mutually exclusive, and the clearest way to see that is a single case. Take a Canadian bank with a subsidiary in Moscow in February 2022. It faces political risk when the host state restricts the ability of foreign firms to sell their assets and leave. It faces country risk when capital controls trap the subsidiary’s earnings and the rouble’s convertibility is suspended for foreigners. And it faces geopolitical risk in its purest form when its own government, acting with its allies, forbids transactions on which the subsidiary depends. All three arrive in the same quarter; they arrive through different channels; and they call for different responses — a write-down, a liquidity plan, a compliance review. A risk function that has only one of the three words in its vocabulary will see one-third of the problem.

text:
1.4 Six ways of counting
If geopolitical risk is a family of phenomena, it is measured by a family of instruments, and the instruments disagree. It helps to sort them by what they count, because what an indicator counts determines what it cannot see.










Family
What it counts
Examples in this course
Strength
Blind spot




Event-based
things that happened, coded from reports
cyber incidents (S08), sanctions episodes (S10)
concrete, datable
only what was reported and coded


Text-based
how much the press or firms talk about a risk
GPR (today), EPU, firm-level risk (S07)
timely, long, high-frequency
measures attention, not exposure


Expert-based
scores assigned by analysts or surveys
governance indicators, commercial ratings
reaches latent concepts
opaque, sticky, perception-driven


Structural
slow-moving features of the system
material capabilities (S03), trade dependence (S04, S11)
explains why

Market-based
prices that embed risk
sovereign CDS spreads, implied volatility
forward-looking, daily
mixes risk with risk appetite


Firm-level

earnings-call text (S07), disclosed exposures
speaks to the decision
self-reported, listed firms only



Event-based indicators record occurrences — a war began, a sanction was imposed, an intrusion was attributed — coded by researchers from reports. They are concrete, but they see only what was reported and coded, and they are backward-looking: a threat never carried out leaves no event. Text-based indicators count words. The Geopolitical Risk index is one; the Economic Policy Uncertainty index of Baker, Bloom, and Davis (2016) is its older sibling; the firm-level political-risk measure of Hassan et al. (2019) applies the idea to earnings calls. Text is abundant, long and timely, but it measures attention: how much the writers thought a subject worth discussing, which is related to, but not the same as, how much risk any particular reader faces.
Expert-based indicators ask people to score what cannot be observed directly — the rule of law, the likelihood of political violence. The Worldwide Governance Indicators aggregate many such sources (Kaufmann, Kraay, and Mastruzzi 2011). They reach latent concepts, at the price of opacity, stickiness and shared perceptions. Structural indicators — the distribution of capabilities, the concentration of a country’s imports — explain why a situation is fragile but rarely when the fragility will matter, which is the question a firm is usually paid to answer. Market-based indicators are prices, bets placed by people with money at stake; but a price combines the quantity of risk with the appetite for bearing it, and a spread can widen because danger rose or because investors grew more fearful of the same danger. Firm-level indicators record what the people who allocate capital say worries them; they are also self-reported, shaped by liability and investor relations, and available almost only for listed firms.
No family is enough on its own. The team project in this course requires a risk assessment that triangulates across at least three, and the reason is not that more is better. It is that the families fail in different ways, so their disagreements carry information. When the text is calm and the market is not, someone may be pricing something the press has not yet seen. When the structure is fragile and the events are quiet, risk is accumulating rather than absent. When the experts are alarmed and the firms are not, either the exposure is concentrated in a few firms or the experts are behind. A single index can only tell you its own story; three indices that quarrel force you to say which one you believe, and why.

section: 1.5 How a newspaper archive becomes an index
text:
1.5 How a newspaper archive becomes an index
The rest of the chapter takes one text-based instrument apart. Dario Caldara and Matteo Iacoviello, economists at the Federal Reserve Board, published the Geopolitical Risk index in the American Economic Review in 2022, after circulating it for several years as a working paper. It has become the default series for anyone — central bank, investment bank, consultancy or doctoral student — who needs a number for geopolitical risk. That ubiquity is the reason to understand its construction exactly.

1.5.1 The definition
The authors begin with a definition, and it is worth copying word for word, as the pre-session asked you to do. Geopolitical risk is “the threat, realization, and escalation of adverse events associated with wars, terrorism, and any tensions among states and political actors that affect the peaceful course of international relations” (Caldara and Iacoviello 2022).
Read it for what is in and what is out. In are threats as well as realisations — the index is meant to rise when war becomes more likely, not only when it starts. In are non-state actors: “political actors”, not only states, which is how terrorism enters. In are tensions short of war. Out are domestic politics, elections, regulation and economic policy, which belong to other indices. The definition is therefore closer to the third row of the typology above than to the first two: it is about relations between actors, not about what a host government does to a firm.

Geopolitical Risk (GPR) index — a monthly text-based index, constructed by Caldara and Iacoviello (2022), equal to the share of articles in a fixed set of major newspapers that discuss adverse geopolitical events and threats, rescaled so that its average over a base period equals 100.



1.5.2 Four steps
The construction has four steps, and each is a decision that could have been taken differently.
The corpus. The recent index, from 1985, is built from the electronic archives of ten leading newspapers published in the United States, the United Kingdom and Canada. The historical index, from 1900, uses three American newspapers whose archives reach that far back. Already the scope is clear: this is the anglophone press of three allied countries, and the historical series is the American press alone.
The dictionary. An article counts as a GPR article if it contains words from one of eight categories: war threats, peace threats, military build-ups, nuclear threats, terror threats, the beginning of war, the escalation of war, and terror acts. In most categories, the search requires a combination — a word for the threat and a word that anchors the article to geopolitics — so that an article about a “price war” or a “threat” to a football team’s league position does not qualify. Designing such a dictionary is a trade-off between precision (only relevant articles) and recall (all relevant articles), and it is the step on which most of the paper’s validation effort is spent.
The share. For each month, the number of GPR articles is divided by the total number of articles published. The division matters more than it looks. Newspapers grow and shrink; their archives are digitised unevenly; the number of articles a newspaper publishes in a month changes for reasons that have nothing to do with geopolitics. A raw count would rise whenever the archive grew. The share does not care how large the newspaper is, only what fraction of its attention went to war and terror.
The normalisation. Finally the share is rescaled so that its average over 1985–2019 equals 100. The historical index is normalised to its own average over 1900–2019. A reading of 300 therefore means that, in that month, the share of articles discussing geopolitical threats and acts was three times its average over the base period. It does not mean that risk was three times higher in any sense a probability could express; it means that attention was.

The misconception to drop now. A high GPR reading does not mean that risk is high for your firm. It means that the anglophone press was writing a great deal about geopolitical tension that month. The second statement is what the index measures; the first is an inference that requires everything else in this course.



1.5.3 Threats and acts
The eight categories are split into two groups. The first five — war threats, peace threats, military build-ups, nuclear threats, terror threats — form the GPR Threats sub-index. The last three — the beginning of war, the escalation of war, terror acts — form GPR Acts. The split is the most useful thing in the paper for a firm, because the two need not move together. Threats can build for months before anything happens, and they can subside without anything happening at all. Acts can arrive with almost no prior threat, as a terrorist attack usually does.
The authors report that threats, and not only realised acts, depress economic activity. For a firm, that finding has a blunt implication: you do not need the war to pay its cost. If what moves investment is the threat, then the cost is borne in the months of tension, by firms that delay, hedge and wait, whether or not the feared event ever occurs.

From the archive · The Cuban missile crisis, 1962
In mid-October 1962, photographs taken by American U-2 reconnaissance aircraft showed Soviet medium-range ballistic missile sites under construction in Cuba. On 22 October President Kennedy announced the discovery in a televised address and a naval “quarantine” of the island. For the next six days the two nuclear powers negotiated in public and in private while ships approached the quarantine line. On 28 October Khrushchev announced that the missiles would be dismantled and returned to the Soviet Union; the United States pledged not to invade Cuba and, privately, agreed to withdraw its own Jupiter missiles from Turkey.
No war began. No shot was exchanged between the principal forces. In the categories of the GPR dictionary, the crisis is almost entirely threats: nuclear threats, military build-ups, war threats. It is also one of the episodes at which the historical index spikes, which is why the practice round asks you to annotate it alongside the two World Wars and Korea.
The episode makes two points at once. First, it is a case in which the index is doing exactly what its definition promises — registering the threat of adverse events, not only their realisation. Second, it is a case in which the risk was arguably greatest at a moment, not over a month: the crisis lasted thirteen days. A monthly index records it as one high observation. A firm deciding whether to load a ship that week needed a finer clock.



1.5.4 Country-specific indices
For several dozen countries, the authors also publish country-specific series: the same search, restricted to articles that also mention the country. In the monthly file these are the GPRC_ columns, one per country identified by its three-letter ISO code. They are not normalised to 100; they are the percentage of articles that both discuss geopolitical risk and mention the country. They measure, in other words, how much the anglophone press associates a given country with geopolitical tension. That is useful, and it is also a very particular thing: a country can be the source of tension, its victim, its mediator or merely its location, and the count does not distinguish them.

title: 1  What Is Geopolitical Risk? Counting the Threat Before the War
text:
1.6 Does it measure something real?
A text-based index is a hypothesis about the world: that the frequency of certain words in certain newspapers tracks a phenomenon of interest. The paper tests the hypothesis in three ways, and reading them is the best training this course offers in how to evaluate an index you did not build.
The first is narrative. The index should spike when, on any reasonable reading of history, the world’s geopolitical tension spiked: at the outbreak of the two World Wars, the Korean War, the Cuban missile crisis, the Gulf War, the attacks of 11 September 2001, the invasion of Iraq in 2003, the Russian invasion of Ukraine in 2022. It does. This is a necessary test and a weak one: any index that failed it would be discarded, but many indices would pass it, including some that measure something other than what is claimed.
The second is audit. The authors drew samples of articles flagged by the dictionary and had them read by people, to estimate how often the algorithm counted an article that a human would not consider to be about geopolitical risk, and how often it missed one that a human would. A text measure whose false-positive rate is unknown is a measure whose movements cannot be interpreted; the audit is what licenses the claim that the counted articles are, for the most part, about what they are supposed to be about.
The third is economic content. If the index measures something real, it should be related to economic outcomes in the ways theory predicts. The paper finds that higher geopolitical risk predicts lower investment and employment, and that the effect is stronger in industries more exposed to geopolitical risk. That is the bridge to the firm, and the subject of the next section.
None of the three tests establishes that the index measures risk in Knight’s sense — a probability of adverse outcomes. What they establish is that it measures attention to geopolitical adversity, that this attention is concentrated in the right months, that the counted articles are mostly about the right things, and that the attention is associated with economic decisions. That is a considerable achievement. It is also a narrower one than the word “risk” in the name suggests, and the gap between the two is where the misuse of the index lives.

title: 1  What Is Geopolitical Risk? Counting the Threat Before the War
text:
1.7 Why waiting has value
Why should a firm’s investment fall when the newspapers write about war, if the war has not yet begun and may never begin? The answer comes from the theory of irreversible investment under uncertainty, and it is one of the few results in economics that every manager already knows intuitively.

The real-options channel — when an investment is costly to reverse and its payoff depends on information that will arrive later, the opportunity to wait has value; an increase in uncertainty raises that value and so leads firms to postpone investment, hiring and entry, even if expected returns are unchanged.

Bernanke (1983) made the argument for cyclical investment: a firm choosing between investing now and waiting for news gives up some return by waiting, but avoids the possibility of having sunk capital into a project that the news would have shown to be a mistake. Because the investment is irreversible — a plant cannot be un-built at its cost — the bad outcomes weigh more heavily in the decision than the good ones, and more uncertainty about the bad outcomes makes waiting more attractive. Dixit and Pindyck (1994) gave the idea its general treatment, borrowing the mathematics of financial options: an unexercised investment opportunity is like a call option, and exercising it early destroys the option’s time value.
Bloom (2009) turned the theory into a macroeconomic prediction and tested it: a spike in uncertainty should produce a rapid drop in hiring and investment as firms pause, followed by a rebound as the uncertainty resolves and pent-up decisions are taken. The pause-and-rebound pattern is the fingerprint of the real-options channel, and it is what distinguishes uncertainty effects from a simple loss of confidence about the level of future demand. Political uncertainty has been shown to work the same way: Julio and Yook (2012) find that corporate investment falls in the period before national elections, when the identity of the next government is unknown, and recovers after it.
Geopolitical risk is a natural candidate for the same mechanism, and it fits the threat-versus-act distinction exactly. A threat raises uncertainty about future states of the world without yet changing the present one; it is the purest form of the shock the real-options model describes. Caldara and Iacoviello’s finding that threats depress investment is, read this way, an application of Bernanke’s 1983 argument to a new source of uncertainty.
The firm-level implication is concrete. The decisions most exposed to geopolitical threats are those that are large, lumpy and hard to reverse: a greenfield plant, an acquisition, a long-term supply contract with take-or-pay terms, a decision to localise production for one market. The decisions least exposed are those that can be scaled up and down: inventory, temporary staff, contract manufacturing. A firm that wants to keep investing through a period of geopolitical tension is, in effect, paying to convert the first kind of decision into the second — leasing rather than building, dual-sourcing rather than committing, staging an investment in tranches with exit points. That conversion has a cost, and the measure of what the firm is willing to pay for it is a measure of how much it believes the tension is uncertainty rather than noise.
The classroom question that closes the lecture is this: in March 2022, with the GPR index several times its long-run average, you run a Canadian fertiliser exporter. What do you do differently this month? “Monitor the situation” is not an answer. A real answer names a decision — hedge the currency, delay the warehouse in Europe, reroute shipments, sign longer contracts with customers who have lost a Russian or Belarusian supplier — and names the threshold that would trigger it. The index can be an input to that threshold. It cannot be the threshold, because it says nothing about the exporter in particular.

section: 1.8 From the system to the profit and loss account
text:
1.8 From the system to the profit and loss account
The real-options channel explains why aggregate investment responds to geopolitical risk. A firm needs something more specific: the routes by which a change in relations between states reaches its costs, revenues and assets. This course uses five, and they return in every session.









Channel
How it reaches the firm
An example
Where it returns




Market access
tariffs, quotas, bloc-based trade diversion, procurement bans
a market closes to firms from a rival bloc
Session 04


Inputs
a critical input or service controlled by a foreign state or a single provider
a critical service from one satellite operator
Session 11


Finance and payments
sanctions on banks, asset freezes, exclusion from payment networks
a correspondent bank exits a jurisdiction
Session 10


Assets and people
conflict, expropriation, evacuation, detention
staff evacuated, a plant abandoned
Sessions 03, 05


Data and operations
state-sponsored cyber operations, data-localisation demands
operations halted by an intrusion
Session 08



The channels matter because the same geopolitical event reaches different firms through different channels, and therefore with different magnitudes and different timing. A war in a grain-exporting region reaches a food processor through inputs, a shipping line through assets and people and the insurance market, a bank through finance and payments, and a software firm through data and operations when the conflict spills into cyberspace. A global index records one event. A firm’s exposure is a vector, and the index is a scalar.
The channels also tell you which data to look for. Market-access exposure is visible in the geographic breakdown of revenue that most listed firms publish. Input exposure is visible, if at all, in the supply-chain maps that firms are increasingly asked to produce by regulators and customers. Financial exposure sits in the treasury: which banks, which currencies, which payment routes. Asset exposure sits in the fixed-asset register and the list of staff posted abroad. Data exposure sits with the chief information security officer. A geopolitical risk assessment that does not ask each of these offices a question is a geopolitical risk assessment written from the newspaper.

title: 1  What Is Geopolitical Risk? Counting the Threat Before the War
text:
1.9 What the index cannot see
The practice round ends every week with “the catch”: one sentence saying what the figure you have just rebuilt does not license a multinational to conclude. This session supplies the template, and the GPR index supplies at least four limits.
The first is that it measures attention in the anglophone press. The newspapers are American, British and Canadian. Their editors decide what is news for their readers, and their readers are not in Abidjan or Shenzhen. A violent dispute that dominates the regional press of West Africa can leave the index untouched; a crisis involving the United States can dominate it. The index is therefore partly a measure of what is geopolitically salient from the perspective of three allied countries — which is a legitimate thing to measure, and which is not the same as the risk faced by a subsidiary elsewhere.
The second is that it is global. One number per month for the whole world cannot distinguish a risk that falls on the Baltic from one that falls on the Taiwan Strait, and for most firms that distinction is the whole question. The country indices help, but only for the countries the newspapers write about often enough to produce a stable series, and only in the sense of “mentioned together with tension”.
The third is that attention fades while risk persists. Newspapers cover change. A frozen conflict — an unresolved territorial dispute, a ceasefire line, a sanctions regime in its tenth year — can be a constant and material risk for firms operating near it while generating ever fewer articles. On the index, a persistent risk looks like a declining one. This is the most important limit for a firm, because firms often hold assets for longer than editors hold attention.
The fourth is that the index is not a forecast. It rises with events and with threats as they are reported. It does not tell you what the next event will be, or when. Its predictive content for investment arises because firms respond to the same reported threats; that is a statement about behaviour, not about the probability of war.
A fifth, which the lecture invites you to supply, can be drawn from the construction itself. The denominator is all articles: if newspapers devote their space to an election or a pandemic, the geopolitical share can fall with no change in geopolitics. Each such limit is a reason to triangulate.

title: 1  What Is Geopolitical Risk? Counting the Threat Before the War
text:
1.10 How a concept becomes data
The practice round follows a sequence that recurs in every session. A concept — geopolitical risk, defined in words — becomes an operational definition: the eight categories of the dictionary, the ten newspapers, the share, the base period. The operational definition becomes a dataset: a spreadsheet, published by the authors, with one row per month and columns for the recent index, its threats and acts components, the historical index and the country series. The dataset becomes a figure. And the figure becomes an argument, the moment someone puts it on a slide in front of a board.
Every link in that chain is a place where meaning can be lost. Between concept and operational definition, everything the dictionary does not capture is dropped. Between operational definition and dataset, the series is revised — the index is updated monthly and the authors refine it, so the values you download need not equal the values printed in the paper. Between dataset and figure, choices of frequency, smoothing and axis change what the eye sees: the same series averaged by year loses most of its spikes, because a geopolitical shock is a monthly phenomenon and a yearly average buries it. And between figure and argument, the slide’s title replaces the paper’s caveats.
That is why every practice round in this course has the same rule: the deliverable documents at least one place where the data disagreed with the paper. The disagreement is not a failure of the replication. It is evidence that you looked.

section: 1.11 A short review of the literature
text:
1.11 A short review of the literature

The distinction between measurable risk and unmeasurable uncertainty is due to Knight (1921), and it remains the vocabulary of the field even where the measurement it describes has moved on. In international business, political risk became a subject in its own right in the 1960s and 1970s, when expropriations were frequent; Kobrin (1979) is the synthesis that defined it as a property of the firm–environment relationship rather than of the environment alone, and that distinguished macro from micro risk. Later work moved from case-based assessment to measurement: Henisz (2000) built an index of political constraints on policy change from the structure of political institutions, and Jensen (2003) showed that democratic regimes attract more foreign direct investment, consistent with their greater credibility towards investors. The expert-based tradition is summarised in the methodology of the Worldwide Governance Indicators (Kaufmann, Kraay, and Mastruzzi 2011). Bremmer and Keat (2009) wrote the practitioner’s case for treating political knowledge as an investment input.
The economics of why uncertainty matters for investment runs from Bernanke (1983) through the real-options synthesis of Dixit and Pindyck (1994) to the empirical work of Bloom (2009), who showed that uncertainty shocks produce a sharp fall and rebound in activity. Julio and Yook (2012) documented the same mechanism for political uncertainty around elections.
The measurement of uncertainty from text is the most recent strand. Baker, Bloom, and Davis (2016) built the Economic Policy Uncertainty index by counting newspaper articles that combine terms for the economy, policy and uncertainty, and validated it by human audit — the template Caldara and Iacoviello (2022) followed for geopolitical risk, adding the split between threats and acts, a historical series to 1900, and country-specific indices. Hassan et al. (2019) moved the method from newspapers to the firm, measuring each company’s political risk from the transcripts of its own earnings calls — the measure Session 07 replicates.
The through-line is a shift of the unit of analysis: from the host country, to the system, and back to the firm. The indices have become better at counting what is said. Whether what is said is what a firm is exposed to remains the open question.

title: 1  What Is Geopolitical Risk? Counting the Threat Before the War
text:
1.12 Into the practice round
The practice round rebuilds the paper’s central figure: the monthly GPR index since 1985 with its spikes labelled, then its historical counterpart since 1900, then the threats and acts sub-indices on one axis. The steps are in the brief that follows. What this chapter adds is the question to hold while you build.
When you place a reference line at 100, remember that it is the base-period average of a share of newspaper articles, and that the two series you plot are normalised to different base periods. When you annotate the spikes, check the months yourself rather than trusting any list, and ask which episodes were mainly threats and which mainly acts. When you compare your figure with the paper’s, expect differences — the series is revised — and record one. And when you change the monthly view to a yearly average, watch which spikes disappear, because that is a demonstration, on your own screen, that a measurement choice can erase the phenomenon the index was built to see.
Then write the catch. Not a criticism of Caldara and Iacoviello, whose index does what it says, but a sentence about a firm: what this figure does not license a multinational to conclude. The strongest answers will name a channel and a place — a supplier, a subsidiary, a payment route — that a global count of anglophone newspaper articles cannot see. That sentence is the first entry in the risk register your team will build for its multinational over the term, and the next eleven sessions are, in a sense, a sequence of instruments designed to see what this one misses.

title: 2  The International Economic Order: Who Wrote the Rules, and What Happens When Their Share Shrinks
text:
2.1 The rules a firm does not notice
A multinational firm lives inside a set of rules it rarely thinks about. When a Canadian manufacturer ships components to a plant in Mexico, assembles them, and sells the result in Germany, it assumes a great deal: that the tariff it pays in Germany is the same as its competitors pay; that a dispute over that tariff will be settled by procedure rather than by retaliation; that the dollars it earns can be converted and moved; that the patent on the component will be respected in the country where it is assembled. None of these assumptions is a law of nature. Each was written, by particular states, at particular moments, in their own interest, and each is held in place by something — power, shared interest, or institutions with momentum of their own.
This chapter is about that set of rules: the international economic order. Its question is the one the session poses. Who wrote the rules multinationals play by, and what happens to the rules when the writers’ share of the world shrinks? The answer has three parts. The first is historical: how the post-1945 order was built, in layers, by the United States and its allies. The second is economic, and comes from the session’s big work, Richard Baldwin’s The Great Convergence: how a fall in the cost of moving ideas after about 1990 moved industry and income from the countries that wrote the rules to a handful that did not. The third is political: why that convergence produced a backlash, and what the backlash means for a firm whose supply chain was built on the old assumptions.

title: 2  The International Economic Order: Who Wrote the Rules, and What Happens When Their Share Shrinks
text:
2.2 What an order is
The word “order” is used loosely, so it is worth fixing.

International order — a set of rules, institutions and shared expectations governing relations between states, sustained by some distribution of power among them.


International economic order — the part of the international order that governs trade, money and investment: tariff commitments and their exceptions, exchange-rate and capital-account arrangements, the treatment of foreign investors and their property, and the procedures by which disputes about all of these are settled.

Three questions describe any economic order, and they are worth keeping in view for the rest of the course. Who wrote the rules? — which states designed the institutions, and in whose interest. What do the rules say? — how open they are to trade, to capital and to investment, and how disputes are resolved. What holds them in place? — whether it is the power of a dominant state, a common interest among many, or the inertia of institutions that are costly to abandon. The first question is about history, the second about law, and the third about politics. A firm’s exposure to geopolitical risk is largely a matter of the third: rules that are held in place by one state’s power are as durable as that power and that state’s willingness to use it.
The third question has a classic answer in political economy, and a classic rejoinder. Kindleberger (1973), writing about the Great Depression, argued that the interwar collapse of trade and finance happened because no state was both able and willing to stabilise the system — Britain was able no longer, and the United States was not yet willing. An open world economy, on this view, needs a stabiliser: a state that keeps its market open in a slump, lends counter-cyclically, and acts as lender of last resort. Krasner (1976) generalised the point into what became known as hegemonic stability theory: openness is most likely when a single state is economically dominant, because the dominant state gains most from openness and has the means to enforce it. The rejoinder came from Keohane (1984), whose After Hegemony argued that institutions, once established, can sustain cooperation even as the hegemon that created them declines, because they reduce the costs of making and monitoring agreements and states have reasons to keep them. Whether the post-1945 order outlives the relative decline of its authors is the empirical test of that debate, and it is being run now.

Hegemonic stability — the proposition that an open international economy is most likely to be created and maintained when a single dominant state has both the capacity and the interest to supply its rules and absorb the costs of enforcing them.

title: 2  The International Economic Order: Who Wrote the Rules, and What Happens When Their Share Shrinks
section: 2.3 The post-1945 order, in four layers
text:
2.3 The post-1945 order, in four layers
The order that multinationals take for granted was assembled in layers over half a century. It is easier to understand as a stack than as a single design.

From the archive · Bretton Woods, 1944
In July 1944, while the war in Europe and the Pacific was still being fought, delegates of forty-four allied nations met at the Mount Washington Hotel in Bretton Woods, New Hampshire. The two dominant figures were John Maynard Keynes for the United Kingdom and Harry Dexter White for the United States Treasury, and the conference largely ratified a compromise their governments had negotiated in advance. The British wanted a system that would protect a debtor country’s freedom to pursue full employment; the Americans, who would be the world’s creditor, wanted a system in which their money would not be used to finance others’ deficits indefinitely.
The conference created the International Monetary Fund, to oversee a system of fixed but adjustable exchange rates and to lend to countries facing temporary balance-of-payments difficulties, and the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development, the core of what became the World Bank. Currencies were pegged to the dollar; the dollar was convertible into gold at a fixed price for foreign official holders. Capital controls were not merely tolerated but expected: the founders had watched short-term capital flows destabilise the interwar economy and did not intend to repeat the experience (Eichengreen 2019).
What is striking, read from the twenty-first century, is how much of the design reflected the balance of power in the room. The United States held most of the world’s monetary gold and was the only major economy undamaged by the war. The institution’s voting shares, its headquarters in Washington, and the central role of the dollar all followed. The rules were multilateral in form and American in their foundations — which is the observation that every later debate about the order starts from.

The second layer was trade. The planned International Trade Organization, which was to have stood beside the Fund and the Bank, was never established: its charter was negotiated but not ratified by the United States. What survived was a provisional agreement, the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade of 1947, which turned out to be one of the most durable provisional arrangements in history. The GATT rested on two principles. Most-favoured-nation treatment required each member to extend to all members any tariff concession it gave to one; national treatment required that imported goods, once across the border, be treated no worse than domestic ones. On that basis, successive negotiating rounds cut tariffs on manufactured goods among the industrial countries.
The third layer is not an institution but a bargain, and the political scientist John Ruggie gave it its name.

Embedded liberalism — the post-war compromise in which states committed to multilateral openness in trade while retaining the domestic policy autonomy — macroeconomic management, social insurance, capital controls — needed to make that openness politically sustainable at home (Ruggie 1982).

Ruggie’s point was that the post-war order was not the liberalism of the nineteenth century restored. It was liberalism embedded in a domestic social settlement: governments would open their markets, but they would also cushion their citizens from the dislocations openness caused, and they would keep the instruments to do so. Free trade was managed; capital was controlled; full employment was a government responsibility. The bargain held for roughly a quarter of a century, and its unravelling is the background to most of what follows.
The fourth layer is the neoliberal turn and the creation of the World Trade Organization. The monetary pillar of Bretton Woods broke first.

From the archive · The end of gold convertibility, 1971
On 15 August 1971, President Nixon announced that the United States would suspend the convertibility of the dollar into gold for foreign official holders, and imposed a temporary surcharge on imports. The announcement was made without consulting the other members of the IMF. A realignment of exchange rates negotiated at the Smithsonian Institution in December 1971 tried to restore a system of pegs; by 1973 the major currencies were floating against one another, and they have floated since (Eichengreen 2019).
The episode is usually told as the end of Bretton Woods, and in its monetary design it was. But it is more instructive as a demonstration of the third question — what holds the rules in place. The system had depended on the United States’ willingness to subordinate its own policy to the gold parity. When that willingness ended, the rule ended, unilaterally, on a Sunday evening. The institutions survived: the IMF found new roles, and the dollar remained the centre of the system, now without the anchor. The order changed form without collapsing, which is the pattern to look for whenever someone announces the end of an order.

Through the 1980s and 1990s, capital controls in the industrial countries were dismantled, and many developing countries followed. In trade, the Uruguay Round of negotiations, launched in 1986, ended with the creation of the World Trade Organization in 1995. The WTO differed from the GATT in two ways that matter for firms. Its rules reached far beyond tariffs on goods — into services, into intellectual property through the TRIPS agreement, into investment measures through TRIMs — so that the order began to govern not only what crossed borders but what happened behind them. And it had a binding dispute-settlement mechanism, with an Appellate Body, so that rulings could no longer be blocked by the losing party. China joined in 2001, after fifteen years of negotiation, on terms that bound it to many of these rules.
How should the result be characterised? Ikenberry (2011) argues that the American-led order was easy to join and hard to overturn: open, rule-based, and institutionalised enough that rising states would gain more by joining it than by challenging it. On this reading, the order is not merely an expression of American power but a set of institutions that bind the hegemon too, and that therefore give others a reason to accept it. Session 03 sets the realist reply beside this view: that institutions reflect the distribution of power and will be revised when it shifts.

title: 2  The International Economic Order: Who Wrote the Rules, and What Happens When Their Share Shrinks
section: 2.4 Firms as authors as well as subjects
text:
2.4 Firms as authors as well as subjects
It would be a mistake to read the order as something states wrote and firms merely obeyed. At several points, firms were among its authors, and the layers that matter most to multinationals today are the ones in which their influence was greatest.
The clearest case is intellectual property. Before the Uruguay Round, patents, copyrights and trademarks were governed by conventions administered outside the trade regime, with weak enforcement and wide latitude for national policy; many developing countries did not grant patents on pharmaceuticals at all. The TRIPS agreement changed that, by making minimum standards of intellectual-property protection a condition of WTO membership, enforceable through the dispute-settlement mechanism. Sell (2003) traces how this happened: a small coalition of chief executives from American pharmaceutical, software and entertainment firms organised in the 1980s, defined the problem as one of trade rather than of intellectual property, persuaded the United States government to adopt their framing, and worked with counterparts in Europe and Japan to build a joint position. Twelve corporations, in her account, effectively drafted the core of a public international law. The episode is the strongest evidence that the post-1945 order was not only American in its foundations but, in some of its later layers, corporate.
A second case is the protection of foreign investment, which the GATT and the WTO largely left aside. Here the instrument was the bilateral investment treaty. The first was signed between West Germany and Pakistan in 1959; the Convention establishing the International Centre for Settlement of Investment Disputes, under World Bank auspices, followed in 1965; and in the 1990s the number of such treaties multiplied. Their distinctive feature is that they allow a foreign investor to bring a claim directly against a host state before an international tribunal, without needing its own government to take up the case. For a multinational, this is the layer of the order that most directly answers Kobrin’s political risk (Session 01): it is the legal response to expropriation and discriminatory treatment. It is also the layer that has attracted the most political contestation in the 2010s, from governments that came to see investor-state arbitration as a constraint on regulation — Rodrik’s trilemma, applied to a single clause.
The point for this course is twofold. First, the rules a firm relies on are not all of a piece: some are multilateral (tariff bindings), some are bilateral (investment treaties), some are private or semi-private (standards, the subject of Session 06). They are held in place by different things and they will fail in different ways. Second, if firms helped write some of the rules, they have a stake — and sometimes a voice — in how they are rewritten. A firm’s government affairs function is, in this sense, part of its risk function: the influence a firm exercises over the rules is one of the few geopolitical exposures it can partly manage from the inside.

title: 2  The International Economic Order: Who Wrote the Rules, and What Happens When Their Share Shrinks
text:
2.5 Three costs, three unbundlings
Baldwin’s book offers a different way into the same history, one that starts not from institutions but from costs. Globalisation, he argues, has been shaped by three successive constraints: the cost of moving goods, the cost of moving ideas, and the cost of moving people (Baldwin 2016). Each time one of these costs fell sharply, it “unbundled” something that geography had previously held together.

Unbundling — in Baldwin’s account, the separation, made possible by a fall in a particular cost of distance, of activities that had previously had to take place in the same location: first production from consumption, then the stages of production from one another.


2.5.1 The first unbundling: goods move, ideas stay
From the nineteenth century, steam ships and railways made it cheap to move goods. Production no longer had to happen near consumption: a factory in Manchester could clothe customers in India. But the cost of moving ideas remained high, because coordinating complex production still required people to be close to one another. So industry clustered — in Britain, western Europe, North America, later Japan — where know-how could circulate cheaply within a local area. The result was the great divergence: the industrialising North pulled away from the rest of the world in income, because the knowledge that made factories productive stayed where it was invented. Trade grew, but it was trade in finished goods between nations, and the comparative advantage that governed it was a national property.


2.5.2 The second unbundling: ideas move, inside the firm
From about 1990, information and communication technology made it cheap to move ideas — to coordinate complex activities at a distance. The factory itself could now be unbundled. Stages of production that had to sit together in one place could be dispersed across countries, each stage located where its costs were lowest, and coordinated from headquarters by telecommunications and computers. A firm could combine its own technology, management and marketing with low-wage labour in a nearby developing country — for the United States, Mexico; for Germany, Poland and central Europe; for Japan, the rest of East Asia.
The crucial move in Baldwin’s argument is what travelled with the stages of production. When a Japanese firm moved assembly to Thailand, it did not move only the assembly. It moved the know-how to perform it: the process engineering, the quality systems, the managerial practice. Know-how that had been confined within national borders now flowed across them — but inside the firm’s own production network, under its control. This is why the second unbundling produced convergence rather than divergence. A handful of developing economies, those that joined the supply chains of northern firms, industrialised at a speed previously unknown, because they did not have to invent the know-how; they had it brought to them.

Global value chain — the international fragmentation of a production process into stages located in different countries and coordinated, usually by a lead firm, so that what crosses borders is increasingly intermediate goods, services and know-how rather than finished products.

Baldwin’s empirical picture of the shift emphasises its regional character. Supply-chain trade, Baldwin and Lopez-Gonzalez (2015) show, is organised around a few hubs — “Factory North America”, “Factory Europe”, “Factory Asia” — each pairing high-technology headquarter economies with lower-wage neighbours. The second unbundling was less a globalisation than a set of regionalisations, linked by the headquarters economies.


2.5.3 The third unbundling: people, virtually
The third constraint is the cost of moving people, and specifically of face-to-face interaction. Baldwin’s prospective third unbundling would come from telepresence and telerobotics: technologies that let a worker in one country perform services in another without travelling. If it arrives at scale, competition would reach occupations rather than sectors, and services would be traded as tasks, the way manufacturing stages are now. It is a forecast rather than a finding, and it is the least developed part of the argument.


2.5.4 The multinational as the vehicle
For this course, the key point of the book is a single sentence’s worth of argument: in the second unbundling, the multinational firm is the vehicle of convergence. The convergence of incomes between the old industrial economies and the new ones did not happen through anonymous markets in finished goods. It happened through supply chains that multinational firms built, owned or controlled, along which they moved technology and organisational capability.
That is why geopolitics now reaches firms so directly. If know-how, jobs and capabilities travel along supply chains, then supply chains are where states will intervene when they decide that the movement of know-how threatens their security. The export controls of the 2020s on advanced semiconductors and the equipment to make them are attempts to stop exactly the flow the second unbundling made cheap. The firm’s supply chain has become a geopolitical object, not because firms chose to make it one, but because it carries what states care about.

title: 2  The International Economic Order: Who Wrote the Rules, and What Happens When Their Share Shrinks
section: 2.6 The target figure, and what it measures
text:
2.6 The target figure, and what it measures
Baldwin’s evidence for the convergence is a picture: the share of the G7 — Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the United Kingdom and the United States — in world income, which rose for over a century and then fell sharply from around 1990. The share lost by the G7 was gained mostly by a small group of developing economies, which he calls the “Industrialising Six”: China, Korea, India, Poland, Indonesia and Thailand. That figure is the session’s replication target.
The replication uses the World Bank’s World Development Indicators, and building it forces three decisions, each of which matters for interpretation.
The first is that the G7 is not in the data. The World Bank publishes the world total and many aggregates — income groups, regions, the euro area — but no G7. You must construct it by summing the seven members, and you must do so by their ISO codes rather than their names, because names change between releases and between datasets and codes are designed not to. The G7 is a political grouping, and any measure of it is a construction by the analyst.
The second is the unit of account. The target figure uses GDP in current US dollars at market exchange rates. That is the natural measure if the question is purchasing power on world markets — what an economy’s output can buy abroad, how large it looks to an exporter selling in dollars. But it means that the share moves with the dollar. When the dollar strengthens, every other economy shrinks in dollar terms and the US share rises, without any change in what anyone produces. Part of any year-to-year movement in the series is the exchange rate.

Purchasing-power parity (PPP) — a conversion of national output into a common unit using the relative prices of a common basket of goods and services rather than market exchange rates, so that an economy’s output is valued at what it would cost in a reference country.

The alternative is GDP at purchasing-power parity. Because many goods and services — especially non-traded services — are cheaper in lower-income economies, converting their output at market exchange rates understates its real volume. At PPP, the economies of China and India are much larger relative to the G7 than they are at market rates, and the G7’s share is correspondingly smaller. The World Development Indicators’ PPP series begins in 1990, so the comparison covers only the convergence period.
Which measure is right depends on the decision, which is the point the lecture puts to the room. If a board is deciding where the purchasing power for its exported product sits — how many dollars or euros a market can pay — market exchange rates are the relevant measure. If it is deciding where real production capacity and local markets for locally made goods are, PPP is closer. A firm that shows its board only one of the two has made a strategic choice without stating it. Measurement choices are strategy choices.
The third decision is about who is in the denominator. The world total is a World Bank aggregate that includes economies for which data are sparse or estimated, particularly in the early decades. Some members of the Industrialising Six lack values for parts of the 1970s and 1980s. A stacked chart of shares — G7, I6, rest of the world — will therefore show the “rest of the world” absorbing whatever is missing from the I6, which is an artefact of the data, not a fact about the world. The practice round asks you to find it and record it.

title: 2  The International Economic Order: Who Wrote the Rules, and What Happens When Their Share Shrinks
text:
2.7 From convergence to backlash
The convergence was, by most measures of global welfare, a remarkable success: incomes in the economies that joined supply chains rose at a pace without historical precedent, within a single generation. It was also politically destabilising in the countries whose share was shrinking, and the most useful framework for understanding why comes from Dani Rodrik.

Rodrik’s trilemma — the proposition that a country can have at most two of three things: deep economic integration with the world economy, national sovereignty in policy-making, and democratic politics (Rodrik 2011).

The logic is that deep integration requires harmonised rules — on products, on investment, on capital flows — and those rules constrain what national governments can do. If the nation-state keeps its sovereignty and pursues deep integration, democratic choice must be constrained: governments adopt whatever policies markets reward, a condition Rodrik describes with Thomas Friedman’s phrase, the “golden straitjacket”. If integration and democracy are both kept, the rules must be made democratically above the state — a global federalism no one has built. If sovereignty and democracy are kept, integration must be shallow: the Bretton Woods compromise, with managed openness and room for national policy.
The trilemma is a reading of the history in the previous sections. Embedded liberalism was the third option: shallow integration that left room for democracy and sovereignty. The neoliberal turn and the WTO pushed towards deep integration — Rodrik calls it hyperglobalisation — and, for a while, the countries concerned accepted the straitjacket. The backlash of the 2010s and 2020s — Brexit, the tariff wars that began in 2018, the return of industrial policy, export controls, investment screening, “de-risking” — can be read as a sequence of choices of sovereignty and democracy over deep integration.
The economics behind the politics became clearer with evidence on the distribution of the gains. Autor, Dorn, and Hanson (2013) showed that US local labour markets more exposed to rising Chinese import competition after 2000 suffered larger falls in manufacturing employment and wages, and higher take-up of public transfers, with effects that persisted. Trade theory had always predicted losers as well as winners; what the “China shock” literature showed was that the losers were geographically concentrated, that adjustment was slow, and that the compensation the embedded-liberal bargain had promised did not reach them. A bargain that is not honoured stops being a bargain.

2.7.1 Slowbalisation
The phenomenon that the press calls slowbalisation is visible in a single series: world trade as a percentage of world GDP. It rose steeply from the early 1990s to 2008, fell in the financial crisis, and has broadly flattened since. Whether the flattening is a retreat from globalisation or a change in its form is contested. A retreat would show up as firms reshoring and supply chains shortening. A change of form would show up as trade in goods stagnating while trade in services and cross-border data flows — much of which is poorly measured in trade statistics — continue to grow. The practice round’s extend step asks you to plot the series and judge it; the honest answer is that the series alone cannot settle the question, because its denominator, GDP, has shifted towards services, which are traded less, in exactly the period in question.


2.7.2 The dispute mechanism
One institutional fact belongs in every firm’s risk register. The WTO’s Appellate Body has been unable to hear appeals since December 2019, when the terms of its members expired and the United States blocked the appointment of replacements. A panel ruling can now be appealed “into the void”, where no body exists to hear it, and so never become binding. The dispute-settlement mechanism that distinguished the WTO from the GATT therefore functions only partially. For a firm, that means that a discriminatory measure by a trading partner is now more likely to be resolved by bilateral bargaining, retaliation or negotiation between governments than by a legal ruling — that is, by power rather than by procedure.

title: 2  The International Economic Order: Who Wrote the Rules, and What Happens When Their Share Shrinks
text:
2.8 Interdependence as an instrument
The first two parts of this chapter describe an order designed to make interdependence safe. The third must add that interdependence was never only an economic fact. Albert Hirschman, writing in 1945 about Nazi Germany’s trade with south-eastern Europe, showed that trade relations could be structured deliberately to create dependence: by trading with small partners for whom the trade was a large share of their total, a great power could make the threat of interrupting it a source of political influence (Hirschman 1945). The gains from trade, in his account, were also the measure of the power the trade conferred — the cost a partner would bear if it stopped.
Farrell and Newman (2019) brought the argument into the age of networks. The infrastructure of globalisation — financial messaging, dollar clearing, internet backbones, cloud platforms — is not flat; it has hubs, and the hubs sit disproportionately in a few jurisdictions. States that control the hubs can use them for surveillance, observing what flows through, and for exclusion, cutting adversaries off. Interdependence, on this reading, has been “weaponised”: the very networks that the economic order built become instruments of coercion. Sessions 08, 10 and 11 develop the argument for cyber, sanctions and space. Its relevance here is that the order’s openness and its vulnerability are the same thing seen from two sides.
For a multinational, the practical form of weaponised interdependence is jurisdictional reach. A firm that clears payments in dollars, stores data with a provider headquartered in one country, or uses components containing technology controlled by another, has placed part of its operations under that country’s law, wherever the firm itself is incorporated and wherever the transaction takes place. The order built after 1945 made it cheap and natural to route business through American banks, American platforms and American technology; the same routing now carries American regulatory authority with it, and other states — China, the European Union — have begun to build their own instruments of reach in response. A firm’s exposure to the rules of the international economic order is therefore not only a matter of where it sells and produces. It is also a matter of which networks it runs through, and whose law travels along them. That is a question few firms asked when the networks were built, because the order was designed to make it unnecessary.

title: 2  The International Economic Order: Who Wrote the Rules, and What Happens When Their Share Shrinks
section: 2.9 What it means for the multinational
text:
2.9 What it means for the multinational
The history and the economics lead to four implications that a firm’s strategy team can act on.
Your market is no longer where the rules are written. For most of the post-war period, the largest markets and the rule-makers were the same countries. The convergence separated them. A European firm now earns a growing share of its revenue in markets whose governments did not design the WTO, did not participate in Bretton Woods, and do not feel bound by the spirit — as distinct from the letter — of rules they joined late. The firm’s legal environment and its commercial environment have come apart.
Your supply chain is a geopolitical object. If the second unbundling moved know-how along supply chains, then supply chains are where governments now intervene to stop it: export controls, outbound investment screening, restrictions on technology transfer, requirements to locate certain stages of production in trusted jurisdictions. The question for the firm is no longer only where a stage is cheapest, but where it is permitted, and by whom.
Multilateral protection is weaker. With the Appellate Body unable to hear appeals, the guarantee that a trading partner’s discriminatory measure could be challenged and removed through procedure has weakened. Firms that relied implicitly on that guarantee — exporters into markets with a history of trade remedies, for example — face disputes settled more often by negotiation and retaliation. The firm’s government’s bargaining power has become part of the firm’s risk profile.
Measurement choices are strategy choices. At market exchange rates, the G7 still looks large; at PPP, it looks much smaller. Which figure a board sees will shape where it builds, where it sells, and how it assesses the bargaining position of the governments it deals with. A risk analyst’s first duty is to show both and say which question each answers.
Mapped onto the five channels of this course, the order’s transformation runs mainly through market access — the tariffs, trade remedies and bloc-based diversion of Session 04 — and through inputs, where the know-how and components that the second unbundling dispersed are now subject to control. But it reaches finance and payments too, because the dollar-centred monetary system that survived 1971 is the platform on which financial sanctions operate.

title: 2  The International Economic Order: Who Wrote the Rules, and What Happens When Their Share Shrinks
section: 2.10 What the figure does not license
text:
2.10 What the figure does not license
The target figure is a powerful image, and its power is a reason for care. It does not license four conclusions that boards and commentators routinely draw from it.
A falling G7 share is relative. The G7 economies kept growing in absolute terms through the whole period; the denominator grew faster. A falling share does not mean the G7 market shrank, and a firm selling into the G7 did not lose customers because the line went down.
At current US dollars, the share moves with the dollar. Part of any year-to-year change is the exchange rate, not production. A strong dollar flatters the United States and with it the G7, and a reading in any single year can say as much about currency markets as about convergence.
Convergence is concentrated. Most of the gain went to a handful of economies, and above all to China. “The South” did not converge; specific economies that joined specific supply chains did. A firm that reads the figure as a story about emerging markets in general will over-invest in the markets that did not participate.
It shows income, not rule-making power. Whether a shrinking share of world GDP means a shrinking ability to set the rules is a question about the relation between economic size and political influence — the subject of Session 03. Hegemonic stability theory predicts that it does; institutionalists predict that rules can outlast the share. The chart cannot settle the dispute, because it does not measure the thing in dispute.

title: 2  The International Economic Order: Who Wrote the Rules, and What Happens When Their Share Shrinks
section: 2.11 A short review of the literature
text:
2.11 A short review of the literature

The political economy of the post-war order begins with the hegemonic-stability debate. Kindleberger (1973) attributed the interwar collapse to the absence of a stabilising power; Krasner (1976) generalised the argument to the structure of trade; Keohane (1984) replied that institutions can sustain cooperation after hegemony. Ruggie (1982) named the domestic bargain — embedded liberalism — on which post-war openness rested, and Ikenberry (2011) reinterpreted the American-led order as liberal, institutional and self-binding, and therefore “easy to join and hard to overturn”. The monetary history, from Bretton Woods through the end of gold convertibility, is told by Eichengreen (2019).
The economics of the new globalisation is organised by Baldwin (2016) around falling costs of moving goods, ideas and people, with the multinational’s supply chain as the conduit for the second unbundling; Baldwin and Lopez-Gonzalez (2015) map the regional structure of supply-chain trade. The distributional consequences in the rich countries are documented most influentially by Autor, Dorn, and Hanson (2013), and their political consequences are read through Rodrik (2011)’s trilemma of integration, sovereignty and democracy.
A third strand treats economic interdependence as a source of power rather than only of gains. Hirschman (1945) showed how asymmetric trade could be designed to create political dependence; Farrell and Newman (2019) extended the argument to the networked infrastructure of finance and communications, introducing “weaponised interdependence” — the strand that Sessions 08, 10 and 11 follow.
The through-line is that every account of the order answers the same question — what holds the rules in place — and that the answers differ chiefly in how much weight they give to the distribution of power. The great convergence is the event that puts that weight to the test.
