title: 2  The International Economic Order: Who Wrote the Rules, and What Happens When Their Share Shrinks
text:
2.12 Into the practice round
The practice round rebuilds Baldwin’s figure from the World Bank’s data: the G7’s share of world GDP in current dollars, from 1970 to the latest year, followed by a stacked picture of who gained. The steps are in the brief that follows. What this chapter adds is a set of questions to carry into it.
When you construct the G7, remember that you are building a political aggregate that the statistics do not contain, and that you build it by code rather than by name. When you find the peak and the latest value, ask how much of the movement between any two years is the dollar. When you switch to PPP, notice that the series starts in 1990 — just as the convergence begins — and ask which board decision each line informs. When the Industrialising Six have missing values in the early decades, record what that does to the “rest of the world”, because that is your first place where the data disagree with the book. And when you plot world trade as a share of GDP, ask whether the flattening after 2008 is a retreat or a change of form, and what evidence would tell the two apart.
Then write the catch, about your team’s firm rather than about Baldwin. A falling G7 share does not tell a multinational that its G7 customers are poorer, that the emerging markets in general are richer, or that the rules it relies on have already changed. It tells it that the economies that wrote the rules now produce a smaller share of the world’s income than when they wrote them — and that whether the rules follow the income is the question the next session takes up.

title: 2  The International Economic Order: Who Wrote the Rules, and What Happens When Their Share Shrinks
text:
2.13 In the practice

The target. Baldwin (2016): the G7 share of world GDP, rising for a century and falling sharply after about 1990. You rebuild it from 1970 with World Bank data, then ask what changes when the dollars change.



2.13.1 0 · Form your team — 10 min
Teams of three or four, for the rest of the term. Agree on one multinational from your shortlists and register it on ZoneCours (first come, first served). Write the team name and firm at the top of your provenance log.



2.13.2 1 · Collect — 10 min
If you did the pre-session, your DataBank extract is in data/raw/. If not, build it now — ../data/README.md. One extract per team is enough; everyone builds their own workbook from it.
Copy templates/provenance-log.csv into data/ and fill one line per file. For WDI, the version is the “Last Updated” date DataBank shows for the database.



2.13.3 2 · Prepare — 20 min

Connect → Microsoft Excel → your extract. Drag the data sheet to the canvas.
If there are notes rows at the bottom (“Data from database…”, “Last Updated…”), tick Use Data Interpreter, or filter them out later. Write which you did.
Pivot the years. Click the first year column, shift-click the last → right-click → Pivot. Two new columns appear.
Rename Pivot Field Names → Year, Pivot Field Values → Value.
Year is text like 1990 [YR1990]. Create a calculated field from the data source pane: Year (n) = INT(LEFT([Year], 4)). (If your extract has plain 1990, just change the type to Number (whole).)
Value is text — DataBank writes missing data as ... Change its type to Number (decimal); the dots become nulls. Check the null count: is it plausible?
Look at Country Code and Series Code (in the Route B CSV the second is Indicator Code, the years are plain 1990, and missing values are blank). From now on you filter on codes, never on names.




2.13.4 3 · Replicate — 25 min

2.13.4.1 Sheet 1 · “The G7 share of world GDP”

Filters: Series Code = NY.GDP.MKTP.CD only.
Create two calculated fields:
G7 GDP     = IF [Country Code] IN ("CAN","FRA","DEU","ITA","JPN","GBR","USA") THEN [Value] END
World GDP  = IF [Country Code] = "WLD" THEN [Value] END
And the share:
G7 share   = SUM([G7 GDP]) / SUM([World GDP])
Format it as a percentage (right-click → Default Properties → Number Format).
Year (n) → Columns as a continuous dimension (green); G7 share → Rows.
Annotate the peak year and the latest year with their values. Title the sheet with the finding, not the variable. Caption: World Bank, WDI, NY.GDP.MKTP.CD, last updated …, accessed ….



2.13.4.2 Sheet 2 · “Who gained?” — a stacked area of world shares

Two more calculated fields:
I6 GDP              = IF [Country Code] IN ("CHN","KOR","IND","POL","IDN","THA") THEN [Value] END
Rest of world GDP   = SUM([World GDP]) - SUM([G7 GDP]) - SUM([I6 GDP])
Year (n) → Columns. Drag G7 GDP, I6 GDP and Rest of world GDP onto Rows as Measure Values (drop the second and third onto the first axis).
Marks → Area. Measure Names → Colour.
Right-click Measure Values → Quick Table Calculation → Percent of Total. Then Edit Table Calculation → Compute Using → Measure Names, so that the three shares sum to 100% within each year — not across years. Check one year by hand against Sheet 1.





2.13.5 4 · Compare and break — 15 min

Compare. Put Sheet 1 beside Baldwin’s figure. Where does the curve peak in yours? How far has it fallen by Baldwin’s last year, and by the latest year? Write down one difference and its most likely cause (dollars, years, data revision).
Missing data. Which I6 members have no GDP value in the 1970s or 1980s? What does that do to the I6 and “rest of world” areas in those years? This is your “the data disagreed” entry.
Break — change the dollars. Duplicate Sheet 1 and switch the filter to NY.GDP.MKTP.PP.CD. The PPP series starts in 1990. How much smaller is the G7 at PPP? Which board decision would you use each line for?
Extend — slowbalisation. New sheet: NE.TRD.GNFS.ZS for WLD — world trade in % of GDP (an index, so check the aggregation: there is one value per year; AVG or SUM give the same only because you filtered to one country — say so). Annotate 2008. Is the line after 2008 a retreat?




2.13.6 5 · The catch — 10 min
One slide (a dashboard exported as an image):








Original
Ours
The catch




Baldwin’s G7 share figure
Your Sheet 1, plus the PPP line
One sentence: what this figure does not license your team’s multinational to conclude



A member drawn at random presents in two minutes.



2.13.7 Hand in
On ZoneCours before leaving, one per team: the .twbx (File → Export Packaged Workbook), the provenance log, and the slide. Formative: commented, not marked; counts towards participation.
The one rule: your log records at least one place where the data disagreed with the book.



2.13.8 What loses credit

Filtering on country names (“Korea, Rep.” will bite you in Session 04)
A percent of total that sums to 100% across years instead of within each year
A share chart in current dollars with no mention of exchange rates
A catch about Baldwin’s book rather than about what your firm may conclude

title: 3  Anarchy and the Balance of Power: Who Sets the Terms When No One Governs
text:
3.1 A system with no government
The previous chapter described the international economic order as a set of rules, written by particular states and held in place by something. This chapter asks what that something is when it is not law. Inside a country, a contract is enforced by courts, and the courts are backed by a state that holds a monopoly of legitimate force. Between countries there is no such state. There is no world government that can make a rule binding, enforce a contract between two governments, or guarantee that a state which disarms will not be invaded. That absence is the starting point of the realist tradition in international relations, and it is the reason this course cannot treat geopolitics as a branch of regulation.
The session’s question follows directly. In a system with no government above states, who sets the terms of trade — and how would a multinational know that the balance is shifting? The realist answer to the first half is blunt: the terms are set, in the end, by those who hold the capabilities others need, and they are revised when the distribution of capabilities changes. The second half is a measurement problem, and it is the subject of the practice round, which rebuilds the long-run distribution of material capabilities among the major powers and asks when, and on what measure, China overtook the United States.
The chapter proceeds in five steps. It defines anarchy and what follows from it; sets out the two main realist theories of how states respond, defensive and offensive; turns to power transition theory and its popular form, Graham Allison’s “Thucydides’s Trap”; examines how power is measured, and what the standard measure rewards and misses; and ends with what all this means for a firm that operates in both the rising and the ruling power.
crumbs: 3  Anarchy and the Balance of Power: Who Sets the Terms When No One Governs

title: 3  Anarchy and the Balance of Power: Who Sets the Terms When No One Governs
section: 3.2 Anarchy, and what it does not mean
text:
3.2 Anarchy, and what it does not mean

Anarchy — in international relations, the absence of any authority above states capable of making binding rules, enforcing agreements between them, or guaranteeing their survival. It describes the structure of the system, not the level of violence within it.

The word is a trap for newcomers, because in ordinary language it means chaos. In realist theory it means nothing of the kind. Most of the time, most states are at peace with most others; they trade, sign treaties, join organisations and settle disputes by negotiation. Anarchy is compatible with all of that. What it denies is that any of it is guaranteed by a higher authority. A treaty is kept because the parties find it in their interest to keep it, not because a court can compel them; a trading relationship continues because both sides value it, not because a sovereign above them will punish defection.
Three consequences follow, in the realist reading, and each matters for firms.
The first is self-help. Because no one else guarantees a state’s survival, each state must ultimately provide for its own security. It may ally with others, but alliances are arrangements of convenience, and a state that relies entirely on an ally has placed its survival in someone else’s hands.
The second is uncertainty about intentions. A state can observe another’s capabilities — its army, its industry, its population — but it cannot observe its intentions with confidence, and intentions can change faster than capabilities. A peaceful neighbour with a large army is a neighbour whose government could change. Because the cost of misjudging a hostile state is so high, states tend to plan for capabilities rather than for stated intentions.
The third is concern for relative gains. Because today’s partner may be tomorrow’s adversary, states care not only about how much they gain from cooperation, but about how much more the other side gains. A trade agreement that makes both countries richer but makes the rival richer faster shifts the balance of capabilities, and in an anarchic system that shift can be a threat.

Relative gains — the concern of a state with its gains from cooperation relative to those of its partner, rather than only with its own absolute gains, arising from the possibility that the partner’s gains will be converted into capabilities used against it (Grieco 1988).

Joseph Grieco’s 1988 article made this the central point of difference between realists and liberal institutionalists such as Keohane (Chapter 2): institutions can solve the problem of cheating, Grieco argued, but they cannot solve the problem that cooperation may help a rival more than oneself. Powell (1991) sharpened the argument by showing that the weight a state places on relative gains is not fixed but depends on circumstances — in particular, on whether the use of force is a live possibility between the two states. Where force is unthinkable, as between Canada and the United States, relative gains matter little and cooperation is easy; where it is conceivable, relative gains matter a great deal.
That is why the concept belongs in a course on international business. Relative-gains thinking is the logic by which trade becomes a security question. A sale of advanced semiconductors to a rival, or of the equipment to make them, may be profitable for the seller and beneficial for the buyer, and still be prohibited, because it narrows a capability gap the seller’s government wishes to preserve. Export controls on advanced chips are not a failure of economic reasoning; they are the application of a different calculus, in which the question is not “are we better off?” but “are we better off relative to them?”. A firm that sells into the gap between two powers’ capabilities should expect its business to be judged by the second question.

title: 3  Anarchy and the Balance of Power: Who Sets the Terms When No One Governs
text:
3.3 Two realisms
Realists agree that anarchy shapes behaviour. They disagree about how much power states want, and the disagreement has direct implications for what to expect from the relationship between the United States and China.

3.3.1 Defensive realism: enough is enough
Kenneth Waltz’s Theory of International Politics (1979) is the founding text of structural, or neo-, realism. Its claim is that the behaviour of states is shaped less by their domestic characteristics — their regimes, their leaders, their ideologies — than by the structure of the system they inhabit: anarchy, plus the distribution of capabilities among the units (Waltz 1979). States are alike in their basic function, which is to survive, and they differ in how well equipped they are to do it.

Balance of power — the distribution of capabilities among the major states of a system, and the tendency, in realist theory, of states to respond to a concentration of power by building their own capabilities or forming coalitions against the stronger state (“balancing”).

In Waltz’s version, states seek an appropriate amount of power: enough to be secure. Seeking more is usually self-defeating, because a state that grows too strong provokes others to balance against it, and ends up less secure than before. The system therefore tends towards equilibrium. Waltz also argued that a bipolar system — two great powers, as in the Cold War — is more stable than a multipolar one, because with only two principal actors there are fewer relationships to manage, fewer opportunities for miscalculation, and no uncertainty about who the main threat is.
Waltz’s theory sits on an older idea that is essential for understanding how conflict can arise without anyone wanting it.

Security dilemma — the situation in which measures a state takes to increase its own security, such as arming or forming alliances, reduce the security of others, who respond in kind, leaving all less secure than before even though none intended aggression (Herz 1950; Jervis 1978).

John Herz named the dilemma in 1950. Robert Jervis’s 1978 article gave it its modern form by asking when it is most severe. His answer turned on two variables: whether offensive and defensive weapons and postures can be distinguished, and whether offence or defence has the advantage. Where defensive preparations look defensive and defence is strong, states can secure themselves without threatening others, and the dilemma is mild. Where they cannot be told apart and offence is favoured, every precaution looks like preparation for attack, and the dilemma is acute.
The security dilemma is the most useful single idea in this chapter for a risk analyst, because it describes escalation without intent. A government imposes an export control to protect a technological lead; the other side reads it as an attempt at containment and responds with restrictions on a critical mineral; the first reads that as coercion and tightens the control. Each step is defensive in the mind of the state that takes it. A firm caught in the sequence does not need either government to want a confrontation in order to lose a market or a supplier.


3.3.2 Offensive realism: as much as possible
John Mearsheimer’s The Tragedy of Great Power Politics (2001), the session’s first big work, accepts Waltz’s starting point but reaches a darker conclusion. It rests on five bedrock assumptions (Mearsheimer 2001):

The international system is anarchic.
Great powers inherently possess some offensive military capability.
States can never be certain about other states’ intentions.
Survival is the primary goal of great powers.
Great powers are rational actors.

None of these, Mearsheimer notes, is individually alarming. Together they imply that great powers fear one another, cannot rely on anyone else for their security, and conclude that the best guarantee of survival is to be as powerful as possible relative to potential rivals. States are therefore not satisfied with an appropriate amount of power. They maximise relative power, and the ultimate goal is hegemony.
Global hegemony, however, is practically impossible, because of what Mearsheimer calls “the stopping power of water”: large bodies of water make it extremely difficult to project land power across oceans. The realistic goal is therefore regional hegemony — domination of one’s own region — together with preventing any other great power from dominating its region. The United States, on this account, is the only regional hegemon in modern history, having achieved dominance in the Western Hemisphere in the nineteenth century, and its foreign policy in the twentieth century can be read as a series of efforts to prevent the emergence of a hegemon in Europe or in North-East Asia.
The prediction for China follows mechanically. If China continues to grow economically, it will seek to dominate Asia as the United States dominates the Western Hemisphere, and the United States, which has spent a century preventing exactly that, will try to stop it. Mearsheimer’s answer to the question of whether China can rise peacefully is no: the result will be intense security competition, with a considerable possibility of war.









Defensive realism (Waltz)
Offensive realism (Mearsheimer)




How much power do states want?
enough for security
as much as possible, relative to others


What restrains them?
balancing by others; expansion is self-defeating
only the limits of their capabilities


Expected US–China outcome
managed competition
intense security competition



A caution belongs here, and the lecture states it twice. Realism predicts competition, not war. In Waltz’s version it often predicts restraint, since overexpansion provokes balancing. Even Mearsheimer’s version predicts security competition, of which war is one possible outcome among several. A risk analyst who reads realism as a forecast of war has misread it; one who reads it as a forecast that the economic relationship will be subordinated to the strategic one has read it correctly.

title: 3  Anarchy and the Balance of Power: Who Sets the Terms When No One Governs
section: 3.4 Power transition and the Thucydides’s Trap
text:
3.4 Power transition and the Thucydides’s Trap
Balance-of-power theory treats an equal distribution of capabilities as the condition of stability. A different tradition reverses the claim.

Power transition theory — the theory, due to A. F. K. Organski, that peace is most secure when a dominant power holds a clear preponderance and that war is most likely when a dissatisfied challenger approaches parity with it (Organski 1958; Organski and Kugler 1980).

Organski’s World Politics (1958) described the international system as a hierarchy rather than a balance. At the top sits a dominant power that built the existing international order and benefits from it; below are great powers, some satisfied with the order and some not. Industrialisation drives the rise of new powers, and their growth is uneven. Danger arises when a challenger that is dissatisfied with the order — that did not write its rules and does not benefit from them as much as it believes it should — draws close to the dominant power in capabilities. At that point the challenger has both the motive and, increasingly, the means to revise the order, and the dominant power has reason to act before its lead disappears. In empirical work, parity is often operationalised as the challenger reaching around 80 per cent of the dominant power’s capabilities, a threshold the practice round places on the chart as a reference line.
Organski and Kugler (1980) took the theory to data in The War Ledger, and a substantial literature followed, including the essays collected in Kugler and Lemke (1996). The tradition connects to Robert Gilpin’s account of hegemonic war, in which the order established by a dominant power becomes misaligned with the underlying distribution of power as others grow, until a war redistributes both (Gilpin 1981). It connects too to Paul Kennedy’s history of the great powers, which argued that dominant powers tend to overextend their commitments relative to their economic base (Kennedy 1987).
Power transition theory has an obvious affinity with Chapter 2. There, the question was whether the rules of the economic order would survive the shrinking share of their authors. Here, the theory supplies a mechanism: a rising power that did not write the rules is likely to be dissatisfied with them, and as its capabilities approach those of the rule-writer, its ability to revise them grows.

3.4.1 Allison’s sixteen cases
Graham Allison’s Destined for War (2017), the session’s second big work, brought the argument to a mass audience under a classical name. Thucydides, the historian of the war between Athens and Sparta in the fifth century BCE, wrote, in the translation Allison uses, that “it was the rise of Athens and the fear that this instilled in Sparta that made war inevitable” (Allison 2017).

From the archive · Thucydides, fifth century BCE
The Peloponnesian War began in 431 BCE and ended, after a long truce and its collapse, with the defeat of Athens in 404. Its historian, Thucydides, was an Athenian general who had been exiled after failing to prevent the loss of a city to Sparta’s forces, and who spent his exile collecting the accounts of both sides.
The sentence Allison made famous comes early in the history, where Thucydides distinguishes the immediate grievances that both sides publicly cited — disputes over Corcyra and Potidaea, over alliances and trade — from what he calls the truest cause, the one least spoken of: the growth of Athenian power and the alarm it caused in Sparta. That distinction between the stated occasion and the structural cause is the analytical move every realist since has borrowed.
It is worth reading what Thucydides does not say. He does not say that rising powers always fight ruling ones; he says this war had this cause. He was writing about a particular conflict between two particular cities, one a maritime and commercial empire and the other a land power with a very different political system. The generalisation to a law of history is Allison’s, and the critics’ first objection is to the generalisation, not to Thucydides.

Allison and the Thucydides’s Trap project at Harvard identify sixteen cases in the past five hundred years in which a rising power challenged a ruling one. Twelve ended in war. The four that did not — among them the United States overtaking Britain in the early twentieth century, and the Cold War rivalry between the United States and the Soviet Union — are presented as evidence that war is not inevitable, but that avoiding it requires deliberate and painful adjustment by both sides.

From the archive · Britain and the United States, 1895–1903
At the end of the nineteenth century the United States overtook Britain as the world’s largest economy, and its navy was growing. The two powers had serious quarrels. In 1895 a boundary dispute between Venezuela and British Guiana brought a sharply worded American demand that Britain accept arbitration, and talk of war on both sides of the Atlantic. Britain accepted arbitration, and a tribunal issued its award in 1899. In 1901 the Hay–Pauncefote Treaty released the United States from an earlier agreement to share control of any canal across Central America, clearing the way for an American-controlled canal at Panama. In 1903 a tribunal settled the boundary between Alaska and Canada largely in the American favour, with the British member siding with the Americans against the Canadian members’ objections.
In each dispute, the ruling power gave way. Britain, facing a rising Germany closer to home and overstretched across its empire, chose to accommodate the rising power in the Western Hemisphere rather than contest it. The case is the strongest evidence that a transition can be peaceful. It is also a reminder of the price: the accommodation was made, in part, at the expense of a third party — Canada — whose interests the ruling power judged less important than the relationship with the rising one.
For a firm, the analogy is uncomfortable and useful. A peaceful transition between great powers is not costless for everyone else. The terms on which it is reached may be paid by actors who were not at the table.



3.4.2 The critics
The Thucydides’s Trap has been criticised on four grounds, and the lecture puts them to the room before showing them.
Case selection. The cases were assembled with knowledge of the outcome. What counts as a “rising” power, a “ruling” power, and a “challenge” is elastic enough that peaceful transitions — which leave less of a trace in history than wars — may be under-counted, inflating the proportion that ended in war. A ratio of twelve to sixteen is only as informative as the rule that produced the sixteen.
Nuclear weapons. No pre-1945 case involved two powers each capable of destroying the other. Nuclear deterrence changes the expected cost of great-power war so drastically that it is not clear any pre-nuclear case is informative about the present. The Cold War, the one transition-like rivalry between nuclear powers in the dataset, did not end in war between the principals.
Interdependence. The United States and China are bound by trade, investment and finance far more tightly than Athens and Sparta were. Liberal theory holds that interdependence raises the cost of conflict and so makes it less likely. The realist reply is that Britain and Germany were also major trading partners in 1914, and fought anyway. Session 04 takes up the debate with data.
Measuring “rise”. The trap depends on knowing when a challenger is approaching parity, and that depends on how power is measured. Beckley (2018) argues that the conventional gross indicators — GDP, population, composite indices of capability — systematically overstate the power of large, populous countries, because they ignore the costs a state bears in governing, feeding, policing and protecting its population. A country with a large GDP and a large population may have much less surplus available for projecting power than the gross figures imply. Beckley proposes measures that account for such costs, and on them the gap between the United States and China looks larger and the transition further off.
The last criticism is the one this session’s practice round can examine directly, because it turns on the choice of measure.

title: 3  Anarchy and the Balance of Power: Who Sets the Terms When No One Governs
text:
3.5 Measuring power
Every theory in this chapter turns on a quantity — the distribution of capabilities, parity, relative power — that none of them can observe directly. Power is a latent concept. What can be observed are its supposed ingredients: people, money, industry, arms. The standard way of combining them in quantitative international relations was devised in the 1960s at the University of Michigan by J. David Singer and his collaborators on the Correlates of War project.

Composite Index of National Capability (CINC) — a yearly index of a state’s material capabilities, equal to the unweighted average of its shares of the state-system total on six indicators: total population, urban population, iron and steel production, primary energy consumption, military personnel and military expenditure (Singer, Bremer, and Stuckey 1972).

The construction has three steps. For every state in the international system in a given year, take six indicators, grouped into three dimensions: demographic (total population, urban population), industrial (iron and steel production, primary energy consumption) and military (military personnel, military expenditure). For each indicator, compute the state’s share of the system total that year. Average the six shares. The result is a number between 0 and 1; summed over all states, it comes to about 1 — not exactly, because a state with a missing component is averaged over the components it has. In the current release, the National Material Capabilities dataset version 7.0, the coverage runs from 1816 to 2022, one row per state-year.
The design has real virtues. It is transparent: anyone can recompute it. It is long: two centuries of comparable data, which is what allows Organski’s and Mearsheimer’s arguments to be confronted with evidence at all. And by using shares of the system total, it sidesteps the problem of comparing military spending in nineteenth-century pounds with twenty-first-century dollars — each year is compared only with itself. Mearsheimer’s own measures of latent power in the Tragedy rely on similar ingredients: for the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, he proxies a state’s wealth with indicators of industrial output such as steel production and energy consumption.

3.5.1 What it rewards
The design also embodies a theory of power, and it is a theory of the 1960s. Two of the six components are population and two are heavy industry. CINC therefore rewards size and smokestacks. A large, populous, industrialising country — one that produces a great deal of steel and burns a great deal of energy — will score highly even if its technology is behind, its productivity low and its military poorly equipped.
The consequence is visible in the replication. CINC shows China passing the United States much earlier than military expenditure or GDP at market exchange rates do. One underlying reality, three measures, three dates. The practice round asks you to find each date for yourself; the point to take into it is that the date of the “transition” is a property of the measure, not only of the world.


3.5.2 What it misses
CINC is equally instructive for what it cannot see. It has no component for technology — the quality of weapons, the sophistication of industry, the capacity to innovate. It has no component for alliances, although a state with many capable allies commands far more power than its own figures suggest. It has nothing on financial power: the role of a state’s currency in international payments, the depth of its capital markets, its control of the institutions through which money moves. And it has nothing on control of networks — the payment systems, cloud platforms and communications infrastructure that Farrell and Newman (2019) identify as instruments of coercion (Chapter 2). These are precisely the forms of power that reach firms most directly, and Sessions 08, 10 and 11 return to them.
The choice of measure is not a technicality, and Beckley’s critique shows why. If power is gross resources, China caught up long ago. If it is net resources after the costs of a large population, or military capability weighted by quality, or control of the networks through which the world economy runs, the picture changes. Each measure is defensible. None is neutral.

title: 3  Anarchy and the Balance of Power: Who Sets the Terms When No One Governs
section: 3.6 Reading two centuries in one chart
text:
3.6 Reading two centuries in one chart
The long-run chart of capability shares is a compressed history of the modern state system, and it is worth knowing what to expect before building it, so that the anomalies are recognisable as anomalies.
The first thing to expect is that the chart is not a chart of a fixed set of countries. The Correlates of War data describe the members of the state system in each year, and membership changes. China and Japan enter the data in 1860. Germany, coded GMY, disappears in 1945 and returns in 1991; in between, the Federal Republic and the Democratic Republic appear as separate states, GFR and GDR. Japan is absent from 1946 to 1951, under occupation. The Soviet Union, by contrast, is coded as RUS throughout, so that Russia, the USSR and Russia again form one continuous series. Each of these is a decision by the data’s authors about what counts as the same state over time, and each produces a visible break or a visible continuity on the chart that has nothing to do with power and everything to do with coding. The codes themselves are a second trap: they look like ISO codes and are not, so that a join with the World Bank data of Chapter 2 on the three-letter code will silently fail for Germany, the United Kingdom and France.
The second thing to expect is that the components are incomplete. Missing values of the six components are coded as -9, not left blank. The index itself has no missing values, because it is averaged over whatever components exist, but any calculation that uses a component directly must exclude the -9s first or it will be wrong in a way that is easy to miss on a chart of shares.
The third is the substantive story. Read with these cautions, the chart shows a sequence that the theories of this chapter were built to explain: a nineteenth-century system in which European powers and then the United States hold the largest shares; the two World Wars as moments when the distribution is violently rearranged; a Cold War in which two powers dominate — Waltz’s bipolarity, visible as data; and, from the late twentieth century, the rise of China’s share. The practice round asks you to date the last of these yourself, and to see how the date moves when the measure does.

3.6.1 Bipolar, multipolar, or something else?
The chart also bears on a question that has occupied realists since the Soviet Union dissolved in 1991: what is the polarity of the system now? The 1990s were widely described as a unipolar moment, with the United States unmatched. Waltz expected that unipolarity would not last, because other states would balance against a power with no counterweight. Whether the present system is returning to bipolarity — the United States and China — or moving to a multipolar one with several significant powers is contested, and the answer depends, once again, on the measure.
The question matters to firms because the two configurations imply different environments. A bipolar system tends to produce two blocs with relatively clear membership, so that the firm’s problem is choosing, or being made to choose, a side, and organising its operations to comply with two sets of rules. A multipolar system produces more hedging states — governments that trade with both sides, refuse to join either bloc, and bargain for advantage between them — and therefore more room for firms to locate operations in third countries that remain open to both. The geography of “connector” economies, which Session 04 examines with trade data, is a direct consequence of which of the two worlds firms are in.

title: 3  Anarchy and the Balance of Power: Who Sets the Terms When No One Governs
section: 3.7 How a firm would know the balance is shifting
text:
3.7 How a firm would know the balance is shifting
The second half of the session’s question — how would a multinational know that the balance is shifting? — has two answers, a structural one and a behavioural one.
The structural answer is the one the practice round builds: track the distribution of capabilities on several measures, and watch the ratios. A challenger’s share approaching the dominant power’s on one measure, while still far behind on others, is a transition in progress and a transition contested; it is the situation in which the security dilemma is most acute, because each side can read the evidence as it wishes. Structural indicators of this kind, in the typology of Session 01, explain why tension is building. They do not say when it will matter.
The behavioural answer is to watch what states do with the rules. A shifting balance shows up first not in war but in the instruments of economic statecraft: export controls, investment screening, sanctions and counter-sanctions, restrictions on data, rules about where a firm may source a component. These are the measures by which states convert relative-gains concerns into policy, and they are observable — in official gazettes, in company disclosures, in the event datasets of later sessions — long before any military confrontation. For a firm, the most reliable signal that the balance is shifting is a change in which rules it is being asked to follow.

title: 3  Anarchy and the Balance of Power: Who Sets the Terms When No One Governs
section: 3.8 What it means for the multinational
text:
3.8 What it means for the multinational
The realist frame leads to five implications for a firm, each of which recurs later in the course.
The balance of power sets the rules of trade. Who can impose sanctions, export controls and market-access conditions depends on who holds capabilities others need: the largest market, the dominant currency, the critical technology. A firm’s exposure to a state’s economic statecraft is a function of how much of its business depends on capabilities that state controls.
A transition changes which rules you follow. A firm operating in both the United States and China increasingly faces two compliance regimes — and, since China adopted its own instruments of counter-sanction in 2020 and 2021, the possibility of penalties in one jurisdiction for complying with the other’s rules. The question “is this transaction legal?” has acquired a second clause: “legal where, and under whose law?”.
Relative gains turn commerce into security. Products that would make a rival stronger — advanced semiconductors, the tools that make them, artificial intelligence, batteries, aerospace — move from the trade ministry’s jurisdiction to the security establishment’s. For firms in these sectors, market access is no longer negotiated mainly on economic grounds, and commercial arguments about mutual benefit carry less weight than they did.
The date of the transition depends on the measure. A board slide that says “China has overtaken the United States” should say on what. On some measures it happened decades ago; on others it has not happened. The decision the slide is meant to inform — whether to expand, hedge, or relocate — depends on which kind of power is relevant to it.
Security dilemmas escalate without intent. A defensive measure by one government — an export control, a military exercise, an investment restriction — is read by the other as offensive and triggers a response that may fall on firms that had nothing to do with the original measure. A firm cannot assume that because neither government wants a confrontation, none will occur.
Mapped onto the five channels of this course, the balance of power runs through every one, but most directly through market access (which markets will remain open to firms from which bloc) and assets and people (where conflict, if it comes, will fall). It reaches inputs through export controls on critical goods, finance and payments through the dominant currency, and data and operations through the control of networks.

title: 3  Anarchy and the Balance of Power: Who Sets the Terms When No One Governs
section: 3.9 What the figure does not license
text:
3.9 What the figure does not license
The target figure — the shares of world material capabilities of the major powers since 1816, with the US–China crossover — is the picture behind both big works. It does not license four conclusions.
CINC measures material capabilities, not influence, intentions or the likelihood of war. A crossover on the chart is not a prediction of conflict. Power transition theory says war is more likely near parity if the challenger is dissatisfied; dissatisfaction is not on the chart.
It overweights size. Population and heavy industry account for four of six components. The index cannot see semiconductors, alliances, the dollar or control of networks — the forms of power that matter most for the economic statecraft firms face.
It ends in 2022. The most recent shifts in the distribution of capabilities are not in it, and for a firm making decisions now the most recent years are the most relevant.
It describes states, not markets. A firm’s exposure depends on where its revenue, suppliers, assets and data sit, not on the system’s distribution of power. Two firms in the same country can face entirely different consequences from the same transition.

title: 3  Anarchy and the Balance of Power: Who Sets the Terms When No One Governs
section: 3.10 A short review of the literature
text:
3.10 A short review of the literature

Realism’s modern structural form begins with Waltz (1979), who explained state behaviour by anarchy and the distribution of capabilities and judged bipolarity the more stable configuration. The security dilemma that underlies much of it was named by Herz (1950) and given its analytical form by Jervis (1978), who related its severity to the offence–defence balance. Grieco (1988) made relative gains the realist objection to liberal institutionalism, and Powell (1991) showed that the weight states put on relative gains depends on whether force is a live option between them. Mearsheimer (2001) pushed the structural argument to its offensive conclusion — power maximisation and regional hegemony — and applied it to China.
A parallel tradition locates danger in hierarchy rather than balance. Organski (1958) introduced power transition theory; Organski and Kugler (1980) and the contributions in Kugler and Lemke (1996) tested it on data. Gilpin (1981) gave a systemic account of hegemonic war, and Kennedy (1987) a historical account of how great powers rise and decline relative to their economic base. Allison (2017) reframed the transition debate for the US–China relationship through sixteen historical cases.
Measurement runs through all of it. Singer, Bremer, and Stuckey (1972) introduced the Composite Index of National Capability and the Correlates of War data on which much of the quantitative literature rests. Beckley (2018) argued that gross indicators overstate the power of populous states and proposed net measures, which change the dating of the US–China transition. Farrell and Newman (2019) identified a form of power — control over network hubs — that no capability index was designed to capture.
The through-line is that every theory of the balance of power is also a claim about how to measure it, and that the measurement is where theories can be checked against the world — and where they most often disagree.

title: 3  Anarchy and the Balance of Power: Who Sets the Terms When No One Governs
text:
3.11 Into the practice round
The practice round rebuilds the distribution of material capabilities among the major powers from 1816 to 2022 using the Correlates of War data, then sets the US–China relationship against the parity and 80 per cent thresholds, and then measures the same transition with military expenditure and GDP. The steps are in the brief that follows. What this chapter adds is the reason each step matters.
When you sum CINC across all states and find that the total is not exactly one, you are seeing the consequence of averaging over the components a state has — a reminder that every index carries its construction with it. When you build the ratio of challenger to leader and set a reference line at 80 per cent, you are operationalising Organski’s theory, and the line is only as meaningful as the theory. When you find the crossover year, and then find two different years on two other measures, you are reproducing Beckley’s critique on your own screen.
Then write the catch, for your team’s firm. A crossover on a capability chart does not tell a multinational that war is coming, that its Chinese revenue is at risk, or that its American suppliers are safe. It tells it that, on one measure that rewards size and heavy industry, the distribution of material capabilities has shifted. The question for the firm is which kind of power its own exposures depend on — markets, technology, currency, networks — and whether the measure on the chart can see it.

title: 3  Anarchy and the Balance of Power: Who Sets the Terms When No One Governs
text:
3.12 In the practice

The target. The shares of world material capabilities (CINC) of the major powers, 1816–2022 — the picture behind Mearsheimer’s and Allison’s argument — and the year China passes the United States. Then: the same transition measured two other ways, dated two other years.

Work in your team. Everyone builds their own workbook; the team hands in one.


3.12.1 1 · Collect — 15 min
NMC v7.0 and the SIPRI workbook should already be in data/raw/; your Session 02 WDI extract too. If not: ../data/README.md.
Provenance log: three lines — NMC (version 7.0, and the codebook’s date), SIPRI (the file name gives the release), WDI (reused; same version as Session 02).



3.12.2 2 · Prepare — 20 min

3.12.2.1 NMC

Connect → Text file → NMC-70-abridged.csv (from NMC-v7-abridged.zip, inside NMCv7.zip). Drag it to the canvas.
Check the columns against the codebook. In v7.0 they are unchanged from v6.0: stateabb (three letters), ccode (number), year, the six components milex, milper, irst, pec, tpop, upop, then cinc and version. Missing component values are coded -9: before you use any component, exclude them (a filter >= 0), or every sum is wrong.
year should be a number (whole), not a date: keep it that way for now.
Sanity check before you build anything: new sheet, year → Columns (continuous), SUM(cinc) → Rows, no filter. Every year should sum to about 1 — in v7.0, between 1.000 and about 1.075. Which years are furthest from 1, and why? (The codebook’s CINC section explains it: the average is taken over the components a state has.)



3.12.2.2 SIPRI

Connect → Microsoft Excel → the SIPRI workbook. Use the Constant (2024) US$ sheet (US$ millions, constant 2024 prices).
Tick Use Data Interpreter: the sheet has five rows of notes above the header (Country, an unnamed column, Notes, 1949 … 2025). Region headings (Africa, North Africa, …) remain as rows with no values: filter them out.
Pivot the year columns (as in Session 02). Rename to Year and Milex. Make Year a whole number with the same name as NMC’s year field — it will be the link.

title: 4  Trade, Conflict and Geoeconomic Fragmentation
text:
4.1 An old promise, and an old embarrassment
The idea that commerce keeps the peace is older than the discipline that now tests it. Montesquieu put it in a sentence in 1748 — peace is the natural effect of trade — and the sentence did a great deal of work for the next century and a half. Richard Cobden built a political career on it: the repeal of the Corn Laws in 1846 and the Anglo-French commercial treaty of 1860 that carries his name were sold, in part, as instruments of peace between nations that had spent much of the previous century fighting each other. The argument was not that merchants are nicer than generals. It was that exchange creates gains, that war destroys them, and that a state which stands to lose a great deal from fighting will think harder before it fights.
The argument’s most famous restatement came at the worst possible moment.
This chapter takes the argument seriously, sets out the realist reply, asks what a century of evidence has settled, and then turns to the question that has replaced it. The old question was whether trade pacifies. The question that matters to a multinational in the 2020s is different: if states have begun to trade more with friends than with rivals, how does a firm find out which side each of its markets is on, and how fast the lines are hardening? That question has an empirical answer, it can be rebuilt from public data, and it is the target of this session’s replication.
crumbs: 4  Trade, Conflict and Geoeconomic Fragmentation

title: 4  Trade, Conflict and Geoeconomic Fragmentation
text:
From the archive · Angell, 1910
In 1910 Norman Angell, a British journalist, published The Great Illusion (Angell 1910). Its claim is usually remembered as “war has become impossible”, which is not what it said. Angell’s claim was narrower and more interesting: that in an economy of credit, contracts and cross-border investment, conquest no longer pays. A victor cannot seize the wealth of an industrial country, because that wealth consists of claims, trading relationships and productive organisation that collapse when they are seized. The economic case for war, he argued, rested on an illusion — the belief that national wealth is a stock of things that can be carried off.
The book sold in enormous numbers and was translated widely. Four years later Britain and Germany — two of each other’s most important trading partners, bound by finance, shipping and insurance as well as by goods — were at war. The war went on for more than four years and destroyed exactly the wealth Angell said it would destroy.
The episode is usually told as a refutation. It is better read as a lesson about which claim was refuted. Angell was largely right that the war would be ruinous for the victors as well as the vanquished. What failed was the inference from war does not pay to states will therefore not make war. Leaders in 1914 were not computing the net present value of conflict, or were computing it with expectations about the war’s length and cost that turned out to be badly wrong. Angell received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1933, as the next European war was being prepared. The commercial peace has lived with the embarrassment of 1914 ever since, and every serious version of the argument is a version that tries to explain it.

title: 4  Trade, Conflict and Geoeconomic Fragmentation
text:
4.2 Four reasons trade might pacify
The modern version of the argument is less a single claim than a family of mechanisms, and they are worth keeping apart because they fail in different ways.

Commercial peace — the proposition that economic interdependence between two states lowers the probability that they will come into militarised conflict with each other. It is a claim about dyads — pairs of states — and it is probabilistic: it predicts fewer disputes, not none.

The first mechanism is opportunity cost. Conflict disrupts trade, and the more a dyad trades, the more it stands to lose. This is Angell’s mechanism with the conquest argument stripped out, and it was formalised by Polachek (1980), who modelled conflict as an activity whose price rises with the gains from trade that it puts at risk. Its weakness is the weakness of 1914: it assumes leaders weigh those costs, and weigh them accurately.
The second is signalling. Interdependent states have a menu of costly actions short of force — threatening, restricting or suspending economic ties — that allow them to reveal how much they care about an issue. A state that is willing to lose trade to make a point is telling its rival something credible about its resolve, and credible information reduces the risk of miscalculation that rationalist accounts of war identify as its main cause. On this account trade matters not because it makes war expensive but because it makes communication possible.
The third is domestic coalitions. Trade creates exporters, importers, port operators, banks and their employees, all of whom have something to lose from a rupture with the partner. They lobby. A government contemplating confrontation faces an organised constituency on the other side, and the larger the trade, the larger the constituency. This mechanism is the one most familiar to a multinational, because the multinational is frequently the constituency.
The fourth is institutions. Trade agreements create committees, forums and dispute-settlement procedures through which grievances can be processed before they escalate, and they create repeated interaction among officials who come to know each other. Mansfield and Pevehouse (2000) found that pairs of states belonging to the same preferential trading arrangement are less prone to militarised disputes, and that the effect strengthens as trade between them grows — a result that has made institutions the most robust strand of the liberal argument.
Statistical work on dyads from the 1990s onwards gave these mechanisms empirical weight. Oneal and Russett (1997), using dyads from 1950 to 1985, titled their findings with some confidence — the classical liberals were right — and the programme culminated in Russett and Oneal (2001), which set interdependence alongside democracy and shared membership of international organisations as the three legs of a “Kantian” peace. Dyads that trade more relative to their GDP experience fewer militarised disputes. That correlation is real. What it means is a different question.

title: 4  Trade, Conflict and Geoeconomic Fragmentation
section: 4.3 The realist reply: interdependence as exposure
text:
4.3 The realist reply: interdependence as exposure
The realist critique does not deny that trade creates gains. It denies that gains are what states care about most. In an anarchic system — the world of Session 03, with no authority above states to enforce agreements — a state’s first concern is survival, and every economic relationship is evaluated for what it does to security.
Seen that way, interdependence is a polite word for vulnerability. If a state depends on a rival for food, fuel or critical components, the rival holds a lever over it. Kenneth Waltz drew the conclusion that great powers will try to limit such dependence, and that where they cannot, they may be tempted to secure supplies by other means (Waltz 1979). The relationship that liberals see as a bond, realists see as a hostage.
The argument has a precise early statement in economics, and it was written by someone watching it happen.
Albert Hirschman, a refugee economist writing during the Second World War, analysed how Germany in the 1930s had organised its foreign trade with the smaller states of south-eastern Europe (Hirschman 1945). The terms were often generous. Germany bought their agricultural exports in quantities no one else would, through bilateral clearing arrangements that tied payment to purchases of German goods. The result was that a large share of each small country’s trade came to depend on a single partner, while each of them was a trivial share of Germany’s. Hirschman separated two effects. The supply effect is the gain in resources that trade brings a state. The influence effect is the power a state acquires over partners for whom the relationship matters much more than it does to the state itself — because breaking it would cost them dearly and cost it little. The influence effect depends not on the volume of trade but on its asymmetry and its concentration, and to measure concentration Hirschman proposed an index that, after a later rediscovery by Herfindahl, became the standard measure of market concentration in competition policy. The intellectual ancestor of every modern dependency dashboard was designed to measure geopolitical leverage.
Two further realist arguments sharpen the point. The first concerns relative gains. In Session 03 we saw why a state in an anarchic system may reject a deal that makes it better off if the deal makes its rival better off by more. Trade usually benefits both partners, but rarely equally, and a state that expects to face its partner as an adversary must worry that today’s gains will fund tomorrow’s threat.
The second is Joanne Gowa’s argument about security externalities (Gowa 1994).

Security externality — the effect of trade on the military potential of the partner. Because the gains from trade raise a partner’s economic capacity, and economic capacity can be converted into military power, trade with an ally strengthens one’s own side while trade with an adversary strengthens the other. States should therefore trade more with allies than with adversaries.

Gowa and Mansfield (1993) tested the prediction and found that alliances do increase trade between their members, and that the effect is stronger in bipolar than in multipolar systems — exactly where the security stakes of strengthening the wrong partner are clearest. The prediction matters for this chapter because it is, word for word, the hypothesis that the fragmentation literature now tests: that trade will reorganise itself along the lines of geopolitical alignment.
The most important refinement of the realist position came from Dale Copeland, and it rescues something from both sides. Copeland’s claim is that what matters is not the level of trade today but expectations of future trade (Copeland 1996, 2015). A dependent state that expects trade to continue has every reason to keep the peace, because the liberal gains are real and are expected to keep flowing. The same state, at the same level of dependence, becomes dangerous when it comes to expect that it will be cut off — because then dependence is a vulnerability about to be exploited, and acting before the window closes can look rational. Interdependence is pacifying or provocative depending on what leaders believe about the future.

From the archive · Washington and Tokyo, 1941
Copeland’s most cited illustration is the road to Pearl Harbor. Through the 1930s Japan depended on the United States for a large part of its oil and of other strategic materials, while it was waging war in China. As Japan advanced into Indochina, Washington tightened export controls step by step, and in the summer of 1941 the United States froze Japanese assets, which in practice cut Japan off from American oil; Britain and the Netherlands, which controlled the other accessible supplies, followed.
Japan’s leaders now faced a dependence that had turned, in their reading, from an asset into a countdown: stocks of oil would run down, the navy would lose the capacity to act, and the terms on offer from Washington — withdrawal from China — were ones they would not accept. In December 1941 they attacked the American fleet at Pearl Harbor and moved south against the oil-producing Dutch East Indies.
The episode does not show that trade causes war; Japan’s expansion was the cause of the embargo before the embargo became a cause of the attack. What it shows is the mechanism Copeland identifies. The same trading relationship that had given Japan a reason for restraint gave it, once expectations of continued supply collapsed, a reason for haste. For a firm the lesson transfers directly: the moment of maximum danger in a dependent relationship is not when trade is high, but when one side comes to believe it is about to end.

title: 4  Trade, Conflict and Geoeconomic Fragmentation
section: 4.4 What the dyads say, and why they disagree
text:
4.4 What the dyads say, and why they disagree
By the end of the 1990s the two camps had produced findings that pointed in opposite directions. Oneal and Russett (1997) found interdependence pacifying. Barbieri (1996), using dyads from 1870 to 1938 and measures that distinguished the salience of a relationship from its symmetry, found that extensive interdependence was associated with more militarised disputes, not fewer, and later extended the case against the liberal view at book length (Barbieri 2002). Much of the disagreement turned out to be about measurement — trade relative to whose GDP, counted from whose customs records, over which years, against which definition of a dispute — which is a warning this course will repeat in every practice round.
Edward Mansfield’s review in the Oxford Handbook of International Political Economy is the best short guide to where the debate now stands (Mansfield 2021). Four of its points organise everything that follows.
The first is that the relationship runs both ways. Conflict reduces trade: states that expect to fight trade less, and states that are fighting trade hardly at all. A negative correlation between trade and conflict is therefore what we would observe whether trade causes peace, peace causes trade, or both are driven by something else — a shared alliance, a shared regime type, geographical distance. This is reverse causality in its classic form, and it is fatal to any naive reading of a dyadic correlation. It returns in this session’s replication in a new form: when trade between two blocs falls, we must ask whether the trade fell because the relationship deteriorated, or whether the deterioration is what the falling trade is measuring.
The second is that institutions matter. The finding of Mansfield and Pevehouse (2000) on preferential trading arrangements has proved more durable than the bare correlation between trade and peace, perhaps because institutions supply the information and the repeated interaction that the signalling and coalition mechanisms require.
The third is that context matters. The pacifying effect of trade differs with regime type, with the level of development, and with the distribution of power between the partners. A finding pooled across all dyads in all decades is an average over very different relationships, and an average can describe none of them well.
The fourth is the one that matters most for a business school: the question has changed. As great-power competition returned, research turned from asking whether trade pacifies to asking how states use trade as an instrument of conflict. That is the question of Sessions 08, 09 and 10 — cyber, economic diplomacy and sanctions — and it is the reason this session ends not with dyadic dispute data but with the geography of trade itself.
crumbs: 4  Trade, Conflict and Geoeconomic Fragmentation

title: 4  Trade, Conflict and Geoeconomic Fragmentation
text:
4.5 Bilateral ties, multilateral exits
One contribution reshaped the debate by asking which trade matters. Martin, Mayer, and Thoenig (2008) — economists rather than political scientists — separated two quantities that earlier work had often lumped together.

Bilateral versus multilateral openness — bilateral openness is how much two states trade with each other; multilateral openness is how much each trades with the rest of the world. The first raises what the pair loses from fighting each other. The second lowers it, because a state with many alternative partners can replace the trade a conflict destroys.

The logic is that of any outside option. If country A trades heavily with B and with almost no one else, a war with B is ruinous. If A trades heavily with B but also with fifty other countries, losing B is costly but survivable: the fifty others become substitutes. Their model predicts, and their empirical work supports, both effects at once: bilateral trade lowers the probability of a bilateral conflict, and multilateral openness raises it.








Effect on the risk of conflict between A and B




Bilateral trade between A and B
lowers it: more to lose from fighting each other


Multilateral openness of A and B with everyone else
raises it: substitutes make losing the partner cheaper



The implication is uncomfortable for the liberal view and was meant to be. Globalisation lowers the cost of bilateral conflict. The very process that multiplied trading relationships after 1990 made each individual relationship less essential, and therefore made breaking any one of them cheaper. A world of many alternative suppliers is a world in which a state can afford to fall out with one of them.
There is a corollary for the multinational that is easy to miss. Martin, Mayer and Thoenig describe the cost of switching for states, aggregated across an economy. A government that decides to reduce its dependence on a rival can point to a world of substitutes. The firm whose particular supplier sits in that rival, whose tooling is calibrated to that supplier’s components, whose certifications name that plant, does not get the aggregate substitution elasticity. It gets its own contracts, which do not become cheaper to break because the national economy has alternatives. Geopolitical decisions are taken at the level where switching is cheapest and paid for at the level where it is dearest.

title: 4  Trade, Conflict and Geoeconomic Fragmentation
section: 4.6 From “does trade pacify?” to “how is trade used?”
text:
4.6 From “does trade pacify?” to “how is trade used?”
The fourth of Mansfield’s points has a theoretical counterpart that has become central to the study of geoeconomics. Farrell and Newman (2019) observe that globalisation did not produce a flat network of equal partners. It produced hubs: the dollar clearing system, the messaging network banks use for cross-border payments, a handful of firms that control critical technologies, a small number of undersea cables and cloud providers. States with jurisdiction over a hub acquire two kinds of power over everyone who must pass through it. The panopticon effect is the ability to see — to gather information from the flows that cross the hub. The chokepoint effect is the ability to deny — to cut a target off from the network.
This is Hirschman’s influence effect, rebuilt for a networked economy. It also turns the liberal argument on its head. In the liberal story, dense economic ties reduce conflict by raising its cost. In the account of weaponised interdependence, dense ties are the instruments through which conflict is conducted. Interdependence does not stop states competing; it changes the terrain on which they compete, and the multinational, which builds and uses those networks, finds itself standing on that terrain.
The policy response has been to reorganise the networks themselves — to reduce exposure to a rival’s chokepoints and to build one’s own. That reorganisation has a name.

title: 4  Trade, Conflict and Geoeconomic Fragmentation
text:
4.7 Fragmentation: three words, three policies
The vocabulary of the early 2020s distinguishes three policies that are often run together in public debate, and a firm that cannot tell them apart will misread its own exposure.
Friend-shoring — a term popularised in US policy debate in 2022, most prominently by the US Treasury Secretary — proposes to move supply chains towards trusted partners: to keep trading, but with friends. De-risking — the European Commission’s term, adopted in 2023 to describe its approach to China — proposes to reduce dependence on a rival in critical goods and technologies while preserving trade overall. De-coupling is the end point that both of the others say they are trying to avoid: separate economic blocs with little exchange between them.

Geoeconomic fragmentation — a policy-driven reversal of global economic integration, in which states redirect trade, investment, technology and payments according to geopolitical alignment rather than cost (Aiyar et al. 2023). It is distinguished from ordinary changes in trade patterns by its cause: it is driven by security and alignment, not by prices or technology.

The definition, from an IMF Staff Discussion Note that set out the research agenda, contains a claim that is hard to test: that the cause is geopolitical. A fall in trade between two countries may be the result of a tariff, a sanction, a shift in comparative advantage, a change in exchange rates, or a firm’s decision to build a factory closer to its customers. Fragmentation is a hypothesis about why trade patterns change. What the data can show directly is only whether they change along geopolitical lines — whether the lines that matter for trade start to coincide with the lines that matter for foreign policy.
That narrower question is the one Gopinath and her co-authors set out to answer.

title: 4  Trade, Conflict and Geoeconomic Fragmentation
section: 4.8 How Gopinath and co-authors draw the lines
text:
4.8 How Gopinath and co-authors draw the lines
Gopinath et al. (2025), first circulated as an IMF working paper (Gopinath et al. 2024), ask whether the global economy has begun to split into blocs since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Their design has three steps, and the replication rebuilds a simplified version of each.
First, define the blocs. Countries are grouped into a US-leaning bloc, a China-leaning bloc and a non-aligned group on the basis of their foreign-policy alignment as revealed by voting in the UN General Assembly. The choice is deliberate. Alliances are too sparse to classify most countries; trade itself cannot be used, because trade is the outcome; and General Assembly votes are cast by nearly every state on hundreds of resolutions a year, recorded publicly and comparable across countries. Section 2 of the paper states exactly which measure, which reference period and which cut-offs the authors use. Read it carefully, because the version built in the practice round is a simplification, and the size of the simplification is part of what you must report.
Second, compare trade within and between blocs before and after the invasion. The comparison is made in a gravity framework — the workhorse model of international trade, in which bilateral trade is explained by the economic size of the partners, the distance between them and a set of other frictions — so that the change attributed to bloc membership is the change left over once the usual determinants of bilateral trade have been accounted for. The paper also examines foreign direct investment, where the same question is asked of announced investment projects.
Third, look for connectors. Non-aligned countries whose trade with both blocs grew after 2022 are candidates for rerouted trade: goods that once moved directly between the blocs may now move through a third country, sometimes after some processing, sometimes after very little. Countries such as Mexico and Vietnam are the obvious candidates, and they appear in the lecture as illustrations.
The main finding is that after the invasion trade between the two blocs fell relative to trade within them, by a margin the paper estimates precisely and which you should take from the paper itself rather than from any summary, including this one; foreign direct investment shows a similar pattern. The authors are careful in two directions. The fragmentation they measure is real and is concentrated in strategic sectors. It is also small compared with the Cold War, when trade between the Western and Soviet blocs was a small fraction of what it is now. Both halves of that conclusion matter to a firm. The first says the lines are hardening. The second says that the world is a long way from two separate economies, and that a strategy built on the assumption of complete de-coupling is a strategy built for a world that does not yet exist.
The design deserves the scrutiny a referee would give it. Bloc membership is fixed at a reference date, so countries that drift — and some do — are classified by where they stood, not where they are going. The non-aligned group is large and heterogeneous; it contains countries that lean slightly towards one side and countries that genuinely balance between them. The before-and-after comparison is anchored on a single event, and anything else that happened in 2022 is a candidate explanation. None of this undermines the paper. It defines what the paper licenses, which is the subject of the final section.

title: 4  Trade, Conflict and Geoeconomic Fragmentation
text:
4.9 Turning alignment into a number
The replication depends on a single variable that most students have never met, and it is worth understanding how it is made, because every choice in its construction travels into the figure.
A General Assembly roll call records, for each resolution, whether each state voted yes, no or abstained. The simplest way to measure the alignment of two states is to count how often they vote the same way. Agreement scores of this kind have been used since the 1960s, and their limits were documented by Signorino and Ritter (1999), who showed that the common measures confound genuine similarity with the base rate of agreement on resolutions everyone supports. A deeper problem is comparability over time. The agenda changes from one year to the next. If the Assembly votes on more resolutions about the Middle East in one year and more about decolonisation in another, a change in a state’s agreement with the United States may reflect the agenda rather than the state.
Bailey, Strezhnev, and Voeten (2017) solve the problem with a spatial model. Each state is assumed to have a position — an ideal point — on an underlying dimension, and each resolution divides the dimension into the positions that favour it and those that oppose it. The model estimates both states’ positions and resolutions’ cut-points from the pattern of votes. Comparability over time comes from resolutions that are repeated in essentially identical form across years: because the same text is voted on again, it anchors the scale, and movement by a state relative to those anchors is movement by the state. Voeten (2000) had earlier shown that after the Cold War the main dimension of Assembly voting separates states by their stance towards the US-led liberal order — which is why the dimension can be read as alignment with, or against, the United States.

Ideal point — a state’s estimated position on a single underlying dimension of UN General Assembly voting, derived from all its roll-call votes and designed to be comparable over time. Higher values indicate positions closer to those of the United States. It measures revealed foreign-policy alignment in the Assembly; it does not measure trade, alliance membership, military co-operation or friendship.

The data come from the Dataverse record maintained by Erik Voeten and co-authors (Voeten 2026). Version 39, released in July 2026, estimates ideal points by calendar year, where older releases used Assembly sessions; the file still carries a session column, and the calendar year is the session number plus 1945. That change of meaning is exactly the sort of detail that belongs in a provenance log, because a figure built on the older file and a figure built on the newer one can disagree for reasons that have nothing to do with geopolitics. In 2021, the reference year used in the practice round, the file covers 193 countries, with the United States at 2.41 and China at −0.41 on the scale.
An ideal point is a continuous variable. A bloc is a category. Getting from one to the other requires a rule, and the rule is a modelling choice. The practice round uses a simple one: a country is US-leaning if it is closer to the United States than to China by more than a chosen margin, China-leaning if the reverse holds, and non-aligned otherwise. The margin is a parameter, which means it can be moved — and when it moves, countries change bloc and the figure changes with them. A result that survives a range of reasonable margins is evidence of fragmentation. A result that appears at one margin and vanishes at another is evidence of the margin.
The trade side of the figure has its own decisions. The source is the IMF’s International Trade in Goods by partner country, the dataset formerly known as the Direction of Trade Statistics (International Monetary Fund 2026). It reports, for each reporting country and each partner, the value of goods exports and imports in US dollars. Two things about it shape the replication. The first is the mirror problem: A’s reported exports to B are not equal to B’s reported imports from A, because of timing, of valuation (exports are recorded free on board, imports including cost, insurance and freight), of re-exports and of confidentiality. A figure must pick one side and say which; the practice round uses exporter-reported exports throughout. The second is that the values are in current US dollars. When commodity prices rise, the dollar value of trade rises without a single extra barrel or tonne crossing a border, and 2022 was a year of very high energy and food prices. Trade “within” a bloc that includes large energy exporters can rise for reasons that have nothing to do with alignment.
The final step is the index. Each series — trade within the US-leaning bloc, within the China-leaning bloc, between the two, and involving the non-aligned — is divided by its own value in a base year and multiplied by a hundred. Indexing removes the enormous differences in level between the series and lets the eye compare their trajectories, which is what fragmentation is about. It also hands enormous weight to the base year. Index to 2021 and the post-COVID rebound of 2021 is built into the denominator; index to 2019 and it is not. The paper’s choice and the replication’s choice should be stated, and if they differ, the difference should be logged.
