title: 4  Trade, Conflict and Geoeconomic Fragmentation
section: 4.10 What fragmentation does to a multinational, channel by channel
text:
4.10 What fragmentation does to a multinational, channel by channel
The course follows five channels through which geopolitical risk reaches a firm. Fragmentation touches all of them, but not equally, and a firm that can say which channel matters most for its own business has already done most of the analysis.
Market access is the most direct. A firm whose markets sit in different blocs faces the prospect that the rules governing its sales — tariffs, export controls, procurement preferences, product standards — will diverge between them. The first practical step is unglamorous: classify the firm’s five most important countries by alignment, as the team milestone of this session asks, and look not only at where they sit but at whether they are drifting. A market that is non-aligned today and drifting is a different exposure from one that is non-aligned and stable.
Inputs are where friend-shoring and de-risking bite. Fragmentation in the data is concentrated in strategic sectors — semiconductors, critical minerals, advanced machinery, energy — and so is the policy pressure. A firm making consumer goods and a firm making semiconductor equipment live, in effect, in two different worlds: the first may see little change beyond rising transport and compliance costs, the second may find its suppliers, customers and technology licences reorganised by law. The connectors matter here twice over. A supplier in a connector country may be the cheapest route around a bloc boundary. It may also be the next target of rules-of-origin enforcement and transshipment investigations, because governments that wish to make fragmentation stick have every reason to close the routes around it.
Finance follows the same lines. The between-bloc decline Gopinath and co-authors find in foreign direct investment is the investment counterpart of the trade finding, and it reaches firms through investment screening, restrictions on outbound investment in sensitive technologies, and the cost of capital for projects that straddle the boundary. Payments, too, run through hubs of the kind Farrell and Newman (2019) describe, and access to them is a matter of jurisdiction.
Assets and people are exposed in the connector countries and in the blocs’ borderlands. A plant built to serve both blocs from a non-aligned location is a bet that the location will stay non-aligned and that both blocs will continue to accept goods from it. Staff who move between blocs face visa regimes, export-control rules on what technical knowledge they may carry, and in extreme cases detention risk.
Data and operations fragment as well: rules on data localisation, on cloud providers and on cross-border transfers increasingly follow the same alignment, and a firm whose systems are integrated across blocs may find that integration itself becomes a compliance problem.
Across all five channels the same distinction from Martin, Mayer and Thoenig applies. The aggregate economy has substitutes; the firm has contracts. When a government decides that de-risking is affordable because the country’s imports can be sourced elsewhere, it is making a claim about averages. The firm’s own exposure is whatever its supply chain happens to be, and its own substitutes may be few, slow and expensive. The distinction between de-coupling and de-risking matters here too. If the data show de-risking — selective reductions in strategic sectors with overall trade preserved — then a blanket strategy of exit from the other bloc overreacts. If they show de-coupling, a strategy of waiting overreacts in the other direction. On the evidence so far the picture is closer to the former, and the right response is sectoral: know which of your products sit in the strategic categories where fragmentation is concentrated.

A tempting but wrong conclusion is that non-aligned markets are safe because they are on neither side. They are where between-bloc trade is being rerouted, and they are therefore where enforcement, scrutiny and secondary sanctions will concentrate. Non-alignment is a position in a contest, not an exemption from it.

title: 4  Trade, Conflict and Geoeconomic Fragmentation
section: 4.11 A short review of the literature
text:
4.11 A short review of the literature

The commercial peace has a long pre-history in political philosophy and a short history as a testable proposition. Angell (1910) gave it its most influential popular form and its most notorious timing. The modern empirical literature begins with Polachek (1980), who modelled conflict as an activity priced by the gains from trade it endangers. Oneal and Russett (1997) and Russett and Oneal (2001) established the dyadic correlation between interdependence and peace, alongside democracy and international organisations; Barbieri (1996) and Barbieri (2002) challenged it with longer series and different measures, and much of the subsequent dispute concerned measurement as much as theory. Mansfield and Pevehouse (2000) showed that preferential trading arrangements dampen conflict, and Mansfield (2021) is the most recent and compact review of the whole field.
The realist tradition starts from Hirschman (1945), whose distinction between the supply and influence effects of trade, and whose concentration index, remain the foundation of the study of economic dependence as power. Waltz (1979) placed dependence within structural realism as a vulnerability states will seek to limit. Gowa and Mansfield (1993) and Gowa (1994) identified the security externalities of trade and showed that allies trade more with each other. Copeland (1996), developed at length in Copeland (2015), reconciled the two camps by making expectations of future trade the variable that decides whether interdependence restrains or provokes. Martin, Mayer, and Thoenig (2008) separated bilateral from multilateral openness and showed that globalisation can lower the cost of bilateral conflict.
The contemporary turn is from trade as a restraint to trade as an instrument. Farrell and Newman (2019) recast interdependence as a network with hubs that confer panopticon and chokepoint power. Aiyar et al. (2023) defined geoeconomic fragmentation and set out its channels; Gopinath et al. (2024), published as Gopinath et al. (2025), provided the first systematic evidence that trade and investment have begun to reorganise along lines of foreign-policy alignment. The measurement of that alignment rests on a parallel literature: Signorino and Ritter (1999) on the pitfalls of agreement scores, Voeten (2000) on the post-Cold War structure of General Assembly voting, and Bailey, Strezhnev, and Voeten (2017) on dynamic ideal points comparable over time. Le Billon and Shykora (2020) extends the analysis from manufactured goods to commodities, showing how supply chains themselves carry conflict.
The through-line is a shift in what is being explained. The older literature asked whether economic ties prevent war. The newer one asks how the expectation of conflict reorganises economic ties — and therefore treats trade data not as a cause of peace but as a record of how states expect each other to behave.

title: 4  Trade, Conflict and Geoeconomic Fragmentation
section: 4.12 What the figure will not tell the firm
text:
4.12 What the figure will not tell the firm
The practice round rebuilds, from ideal points and IMF trade data, a version of the figure at the centre of Gopinath et al. (2025): trade within and between blocs, indexed to the period before the invasion. If the build goes well, the lines will separate after 2022 in the direction the paper reports. The temptation will be to read that separation as a finding about geopolitics. It is a finding about a classification, a currency and a date, and each of those carries part of the result.
It is a correlation with a date. Sanctions on Russia, the post-pandemic rebound and the surge in commodity prices all move trade values in 2022, and all of them move trade between some blocs more than within others. A simple index cannot separate them; the paper’s gravity specification goes some way towards doing so, and the replication does not. Bloc membership is a modelling choice: move the margin and countries move between blocs, and if the gap between the lines moves with them, the gap is partly an artefact of where the lines were drawn. Values are not volumes: a bloc rich in energy exporters will show trade rising in 2022 because oil and gas were expensive, not because its members drew closer. And the figure is aggregate: a multinational’s products may sit in a sector where fragmentation is far stronger than the average, or in one where it is absent.
What the figure can do is narrower and still useful. It can show whether the broad pattern Gopinath and co-authors report is visible in raw data, with transparent choices that anyone can reproduce and change. It can show which of a firm’s markets sit in which bloc under a stated rule, and how fragile that classification is. It can identify the connectors through which between-bloc trade appears to be flowing, which is where both the opportunities and the enforcement risks are concentrated.
The question to carry into the practice round is therefore the one the course asks of every replication. Suppose the lines separate exactly as the paper says. What does that figure not license a multinational to conclude? It does not license the conclusion that geopolitics caused the separation, that the firm’s own sector follows the aggregate, that its non-aligned markets are safe, or that the bloc boundaries drawn at one margin in one year will be the boundaries that matter in five. The answer you give — in one sentence, on the catch slide — is the part of the round that most resembles the judgement a risk analyst is paid to make.

title: 4  Trade, Conflict and Geoeconomic Fragmentation
text:
4.13 In the practice

The target. Gopinath, Gourinchas, Presbitero & Topalova (2025): trade between geopolitical blocs against trade within them, before and after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. You define the blocs yourself from UN General Assembly ideal points, then watch what happens to the finding when you move the line.

Work in your team. One extract per team; everyone builds their own workbook.


4.13.1 1 · Collect — 10 min
Ideal points and codebook from Dataverse; your IMF IMTS extract of bilateral goods exports, annual, 2015–latest. If not done: ../data/README.md.
Provenance log: one line per file. For the ideal points, log version 39 and the change to calendar-year estimation. For IMF, log the date of the extract and the exact indicator you chose.



4.13.2 2 · Prepare — 25 min

4.13.2.1 A · Classify countries into blocs (ideal points)

Connect → Text file → IdealpointestimatesFP_2026FP.csv. The ISO 3-letter code, the year and the ideal point are iso3c, year and IdealPointFP (see the codebook). Rename iso3c → iso3 and IdealPointFP → IdealPoint (right-click → Rename): the steps below use those names.
New sheet. Filter year = 2021 — the last full year before the invasion. (Gopinath et al. may use a different reference: check, and log the difference.)
Read the ideal points of the US (USA) and China (CHN) off the data. Create two parameters, US ref and CHN ref (Float), and type those two values in.
Create a third parameter Margin (Float, start at 0.5) and the calculated field:
Bloc =
IF ABS([IdealPoint] - [CHN ref]) - ABS([IdealPoint] - [US ref]) > [Margin] THEN "US-leaning"
ELSEIF ABS([IdealPoint] - [US ref]) - ABS([IdealPoint] - [CHN ref]) > [Margin] THEN "China-leaning"
ELSE "Non-aligned"
END
iso3 → Rows, Bloc → Rows, IdealPoint → Text. Sort by ideal point. Does the classification look right for countries you know? Adjust Margin until you can defend it — and write down the value and why.
Export the classification as a derived file: Worksheet → Export → Crosstab to Excel (or View Data → Export All to CSV). Save it as data/derived/blocs_2021.csv — not in raw/. Add a provenance line: derived from the ideal points, Margin = …, base year 2021.



4.13.2.2 B · Relate trade to blocs — the dyad model

New data source: Connect → Text file (or Excel) → your IMF extract. Identify the exporter, partner, year and value columns — in the IMF’s SDMX layout COUNTRY, COUNTERPART_COUNTRY, TIME_PERIOD, OBS_VALUE — and rename them exporter, partner, year, value. Keep only INDICATOR = XG_FOB_USD.
Remove aggregate partners (“World”, “Advanced Economies”, regions — codes starting with G or TX, e.g. G001 World): filter them out, and log which.
In the data source pane, drag blocs_2021.csv onto the canvas: Tableau creates a relationship. Click the noodle → relate exporter = iso3.
Drag blocs_2021.csv onto the canvas a second time. Relate partner = iso3. Rename this copy Partner blocs and its Bloc field Partner bloc; rename the first copy’s field Exporter bloc.
IMTS uses ISO3 codes, so the relationship works directly. If your download shows names instead, you need a concordance table — log it.





4.13.3 3 · Replicate — 25 min

4.13.3.1 Sheet 1 · “Trade within and between blocs”

The pair type:
Pair type =
IF [Exporter bloc] = "Non-aligned" OR [Partner bloc] = "Non-aligned" THEN "Involves non-aligned"
ELSEIF [Exporter bloc] = [Partner bloc] THEN "Within bloc"
ELSE "Between US- and China-leaning"
END
The index, 2021 = 100:
Trade index = SUM([value]) / WINDOW_SUM(SUM(IF [year] = 2021 THEN [value] END)) * 100
year → Columns as a discrete dimension (blue); Trade index → Rows; Pair type → Colour. Right-click Trade index → Edit Table Calculation → Compute Using → year, so each pair type is indexed to its own 2021.
Reference line at 100. Annotate 2022.
Title with the finding. Caption: both sources with versions, and “Blocs: ideal-point distance to US vs China, 2021, margin = …”.



4.13.3.2 Sheet 2 · “Who sits where?” — the classification on a map
iso3 (geographic role Country/Region, ISO 3166-1 alpha-3) on the map, coloured by Bloc. Mark your team firm’s five main countries with a group (Create → Group, “Our markets”).




4.13.4 4 · Compare and break — 20 min

Compare. Put Sheet 1 beside the paper’s figure. Their data are quarterly and their estimate controls for other determinants of trade; ours is annual and raw. Does the direction match? Is the gap between “within” and “between” of a similar order? Write one difference and its likely cause.
Break the bloc definition. Move Margin (0.25, 1.0), re-export, refresh. Which countries change bloc? Does the gap between the lines survive? This is the most important answer of the round.
Break the side of the trade. If your extract has the mirror series (imports reported by the partner), rebuild the index with it. Same picture?
Extend — connectors. Create a set of non-aligned countries (Create → Set, Top tab: top 10 by growth in exports to both blocs, 2021 → latest — or pick by hand from a table). Which are they? Is any of them among your firm’s markets?




4.13.5 5 · The catch — 10 min
One slide:








Original
Ours
The catch




Gopinath et al.’s within/between figure
Sheet 1, and the same chart with another Margin
One sentence: what this figure does not license your team’s multinational to conclude



A member drawn at random presents in two minutes.



4.13.6 Hand in
On ZoneCours before leaving, one per team: .twbx (including the derived blocs_2021.csv), provenance log, slide. Formative.
The one rule: your log records at least one place where the data disagreed with the paper — and your slide says how your blocs differ from theirs.



4.13.7 What loses credit

Joining on country names (Türkiye, Côte d’Ivoire, Korea…)
Leaving “World” or regional aggregates among the partners
An index computed across pair types instead of within each one
A bloc threshold that is not reported on the slide

title: 5  International Institutions: Who Finances, Insures and Referees the Firm
text:
5.1 A hotel in New Hampshire, and what it still decides
Ask a manager which international institutions matter to her firm and the first answer is usually the United Nations. Ask instead who lent the money for the port her goods leave from, who insured the plant her company built in a country whose currency may not be convertible next year, who will hear the case if that country’s government takes the plant, and who decided which firms were allowed to bid for the contract to build the port in the first place — and the list becomes long, specific and almost entirely economic. The World Bank, its private-sector arm, its insurer, its arbitration centre; a regional development bank in Manila, Abidjan or London; and, increasingly, a bank in Beijing or Shanghai that did not exist when today’s graduate students were in primary school.
This chapter is about those institutions. It treats them in two ways at once, because a multinational has to. They are business infrastructure: sources of long-term finance, guarantees, political risk insurance, contracts and dispute settlement in exactly the markets where private finance is scarcest and political risk highest. And they are arenas of power: bodies governed by states, whose votes are unequally distributed, whose rules are bargained, and whose decisions — as the session’s big work shows — can be bought. A firm that relies on such an institution to manage its geopolitical risk is relying on a rule; it is also relying on the coalition of states that keeps the rule in force. The question that runs through the chapter is which of the two it is really relying on, institution by institution and issue by issue.
The story starts, as the order it describes did, in July 1944.
crumbs: 5  International Institutions: Who Finances, Insures and Referees the Firm

title: 5  International Institutions: Who Finances, Insures and Referees the Firm
text:
From the archive · Bretton Woods, 1944
In July 1944 delegations from forty-four countries met at a resort hotel in Bretton Woods, New Hampshire, to design the post-war monetary order. The war in Europe was not over. The two plans on the table were British and American: John Maynard Keynes proposed an International Clearing Union with its own unit of account and pressure on creditor as well as debtor countries to adjust; Harry Dexter White, for the US Treasury, proposed a more modest stabilisation fund to which members would contribute and from which they could draw. The American plan largely prevailed, for the reason a realist would give: the United States was the creditor, and the creditor wrote the rules.
The Articles of Agreement of the International Monetary Fund were adopted on 22 July 1944, alongside those of the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development, and entered into force in December 1945. The design choice that matters most for this chapter was made then and has never been reversed: each member’s quota — its subscription to the Fund — determines both how much it can borrow and how many votes it has. Money and voice were tied together from the first day. Eighty years later the argument about whether the new institutions of Asia and the BRICS complement or contest the Bretton Woods order is, at bottom, an argument about that tie.
crumbs: 5  International Institutions: Who Finances, Insures and Referees the Firm

title: 5  International Institutions: Who Finances, Insures and Referees the Firm
section: 5.2 Why would states under anarchy build institutions at all?
text:
5.2 Why would states under anarchy build institutions at all?
Session 03 left us with a system that has no government above states, and Session 04 with trade reorganising itself along geopolitical lines. Yet the same system is thick with institutions. Two traditions explain why, and they make opposite predictions for a firm.
The liberal institutionalist answer, given its canonical form by Keohane (1984), is functional. States that would gain from cooperation often fail to achieve it because they cannot observe each other’s behaviour, cannot make credible promises, and fear being exploited. Institutions lower the transaction costs of agreement, supply information about compliance, and lengthen the shadow of the future by turning one-off bargains into repeated games. Keohane’s point was that this logic survives the decline of the hegemon that created the institutions: once built, they are cheaper to maintain than to replace, and states keep obeying them because reneging would be costly.
The realist answer, set out most sharply by Mearsheimer (1994), is that institutions reflect the distribution of power. The strong build them to serve their interests, and when an institution’s rules collide with a powerful state’s interests, the rules give way. On this view an institution has no independent effect on behaviour; it is a stage on which power is exercised, and its apparent successes are cases in which states would have behaved the same way without it.

International institution — a persistent set of rules, usually with an organisation to administer them, that states have agreed to and that prescribes behaviour, constrains activity and shapes expectations. The economic institutions in this chapter add a balance sheet: they lend, guarantee, insure or invest, and their votes are attached to capital.

Neither account is a strawman, and a firm does not need to choose between them in general. It needs to know which institution, on which issue, behaves like which. A MIGA guarantee, an IFC loan covenant and an ICSID award are rules that have, on the whole, been honoured; the WTO’s Appellate Body is a rule whose enforcement collapsed when its most powerful member stopped appointing judges. That is an empirical question, and the rest of the chapter treats it as one.
A third idea is needed to read the last decade. Morse and Keohane (2014) observed that dissatisfied states do not only lobby inside an institution; they also go around it. They may move an issue to a different existing body — regime shifting — or build a new one — competitive regime creation. They called the result contested multilateralism.

Contested multilateralism — the use of multilateral institutions to challenge the rules, practices or missions of other multilateral institutions, either by shifting an issue to an existing alternative forum or by creating a new institution to compete with the old one (Morse and Keohane 2014).

The Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank was their leading example of the second strategy, and it is where this chapter ends up. To see why it was built, one has to start with the votes inside the institutions it was built beside.
crumbs: 5  International Institutions: Who Finances, Insures and Referees the Firm

title: 5  International Institutions: Who Finances, Insures and Referees the Firm
text:
5.3 The votes behind the money
The International Monetary Fund lends to governments, never to firms. It matters to a multinational because its programmes set the conditions in which the firm operates: whether the host currency floats, whether capital may leave, whether subsidies and public-sector wages are cut, whether the government can pay its suppliers. A country in an IMF programme has its macroeconomic policy partly written in Washington.
The Fund now has 191 members. Its governance follows the 1944 design: quotas determine votes. As of 30 April 2026 the United States held 16.49% of total voting power, Japan 6.14% and China 6.08%; the other founding BRICS each held less than 3% (International Monetary Fund 2026). Article III of the Articles requires an 85% majority of total voting power for any change in quotas, so a member holding more than 15% can block a quota reform alone — and only one member does.

Voting power and capital — in a shareholder-governed institution, a member’s votes are a function of its capital subscription (plus, usually, a small equal allocation of basic votes). Voting power is therefore a lagging indicator of economic weight: it moves only when members agree to reallocate capital, and those whose share would fall can often block the reallocation.

The lag is the hinge of the session. China’s economy is far larger relative to the American economy than a vote of 6.08% against 16.49% suggests, and reform has been slow. The Sixteenth General Review of Quotas, approved in December 2023, raises total quotas by half but does so equiproportionally: every member’s share stays where it was. Even that increase had not taken effect by October 2026 — the IMF had extended the deadline for members’ consents to 15 November 2026 — and the realignment of shares was left to a Seventeenth Review for which, at the time of writing, guiding principles had been endorsed but no formula agreed. The same pattern holds at the World Bank: in the IBRD the United States held 15.98% of votes, Japan 6.88% and China 5.75% as of 30 June 2026 (World Bank Group 2026).
Two other institutions shape the conditions of business without lending a cent. The World Trade Organization, founded in 1995 with 166 members today, holds the tariff bindings and non-discrimination rules on which a firm’s market access rests. Its Appellate Body has had no members since 30 November 2020, because appointments require consensus and the United States has withheld it; a subset of members now appeal through an interim arbitration arrangement instead. The rule still exists; whether it binds depends on which members have opted in. The OECD’s relevance is quieter. Its Arrangement on Officially Supported Export Credits, in force since 1978, limits the terms that participating governments’ export-credit agencies may offer, so that exporters compete on price and quality rather than on subsidised finance — and China is not a participant. Its Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises give anyone a route to complain about a firm’s conduct through National Contact Points. And its Inclusive Framework negotiated the global minimum tax that now shapes where multinationals book profits.

title: 5  International Institutions: Who Finances, Insures and Referees the Firm
section: 5.4 The World Bank Group as the firm’s toolkit
text:
5.4 The World Bank Group as the firm’s toolkit
The World Bank is usually described as a development institution, which it is. For a multinational it is also five distinct services, run by five legally distinct institutions with overlapping but different memberships.
The IBRD (1944) lends to middle-income and creditworthy governments; the International Development Association (1960) gives grants and concessional credits to the poorest. Neither lends to firms. Both matter to firms because the money they lend is spent buying goods, works and services, and the World Bank’s Procurement Framework, in force since July 2016, requires that much of that buying be done through open international competition, with notices published on United Nations Development Business and the Bank’s own site. Procurement is the least glamorous and most overlooked business channel of the multilateral system; for an engineering, construction or equipment firm it is often the largest.
Procurement has a disciplinary side. Firms found to have engaged in fraud, corruption, collusion or coercion in Bank-financed contracts are debarred, and their names published. Since the Agreement for Mutual Enforcement of Debarment Decisions of 9 April 2010, a debarment of more than one year by the World Bank Group, the Asian Development Bank, the African Development Bank Group, the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development or the Inter-American Development Bank Group is enforced by the other four. A sanction at one bank becomes a sanction at five — which makes integrity compliance in one country a condition of market access in dozens.
The International Finance Corporation (1956) invests in the private sector directly: loans, many in local currency, equity stakes, guarantees, and the mobilisation of other investors. Its Managed Co-Lending Portfolio Program lets institutional investors — insurers, pension funds, sovereign funds — lend alongside IFC in a portfolio that mirrors its own. For a firm, IFC is a co-investor whose presence lowers the cost of other finance and signals to the host government that the project has a powerful friend.
The Multilateral Investment Guarantee Agency (1988) is the institution in this chapter most directly in the business of geopolitical risk. It insures cross-border investors and lenders against five political perils, and in fiscal year 2026 it issued a record US$10.6 billion of guarantees for sixty projects, bringing its gross exposure to US$41.4 billion (Multilateral Investment Guarantee Agency 2026). Since July 2024 the Group’s guarantee products have been brought together in a single platform housed at MIGA.

Political risk insurance — cover for a cross-border investor or lender against losses caused by government action or political violence: currency inconvertibility and transfer restriction, expropriation, war and civil disturbance, breach of contract by the host government, and non-honouring of a sovereign financial obligation. Multilateral cover adds something private cover cannot: the insurer’s shareholders include the host state.

That last clause is the deterrence argument for multilateral insurance. A host government that expropriates a MIGA-insured investor is not only in dispute with a foreign firm; it is in dispute with an agency of which it is itself a member, which will pay the claim and then seek recovery from it, and whose other members include the governments that decide its access to World Bank lending. The insurance works, in part, because the coalition behind it is large. It also means that the insurer is governed by states: in MIGA the United States held 14.81% of votes as of 30 June 2026 (World Bank Group 2026), and the cover a firm can buy reflects what that coalition is willing to underwrite.
The International Centre for Settlement of Investment Disputes (Convention in force 1966) provides the forum. A firm whose host state has consented — usually through a bilateral investment treaty — can bring a claim against the state before an arbitral tribunal rather than the state’s own courts. ICSID had registered 1,118 cases by mid-2026, and of the cases registered in fiscal year 2026 a quarter concerned oil and gas and almost a fifth mining; more than three in five were brought under bilateral investment treaties (International Centre for Settlement of Investment Disputes 2026).

Investor–state arbitration — a procedure in which a foreign investor brings a claim directly against a host state before an international tribunal, under consent given in a treaty, a contract or a national investment law. The award is binding; whether it is paid depends on the state.

The forum is a rule a state can leave. Bolivia denounced the ICSID Convention in 2007, Ecuador in 2009 and Venezuela in 2012; Ecuador rejoined in 2021, and Honduras, which gave notice in 2024, rejoined in 2026. The investor protection a firm buys when it structures an investment through a treaty jurisdiction is real, but it is protection under a regime whose membership moves with the politics of host states.

title: 5  International Institutions: Who Finances, Insures and Referees the Firm
section: 5.5 Does influence inside an institution have a price?
text:
5.5 Does influence inside an institution have a price?
Everything so far assumes that the institutions apply their rules to all comers. The realist suspicion is that they do not — that the votes in the tables above are used, and that influence is traded. The session’s big work offers the sharpest test of that suspicion, and it does so in the institution whose decisions bind every firm in the world.
The UN Security Council has fifteen members: five permanent, with a veto, and ten elected by the General Assembly for two-year terms by regional group, five each year, without immediate re-election. Before 1966 there were six elected seats. Substantive decisions need nine votes and no permanent-member veto, and measures adopted under Chapter VII of the Charter — sanctions, arms embargoes, authorisations of force — bind every member state, and therefore every firm operating in one. The arithmetic gives the elected members leverage: the permanent five cannot pass anything without at least four of them.
Kuziemko and Werker (2006) asked whether that leverage is paid for. Their identification idea is the reason the paper is the session’s big work. Rotation onto the Council follows regional queues and informal norms, not a country’s need for aid in a particular year. So instead of comparing members with non-members — who differ in a hundred ways — they compare a country with itself, in the years before, during and after its term. If aid rises during the term and falls back afterwards, the seat is the likeliest explanation: poverty, alliances and politics do not rotate on a two-year cycle.

Event time — time measured relative to an event rather than by the calendar: year 0 is the first year of a Council term, −1 the year of the election, +2 the first year after the term. Re-indexing every country’s series to its own event aligns cases that happened decades apart and lets one ask what typically happens around the event.

They found that US aid to a developing country rises substantially when it rotates onto the Council — by about 59% in the paper’s headline estimate — and that aid through the UN rises too, more modestly. The increase is concentrated in the term years and disappears afterwards. And it is larger in years when the Council matters more, measured by how much the press covered it. That last result turns a pattern into a mechanism: if aid followed membership regardless of what the Council was doing, rotation might proxy for something else; that it tracks the salience of Council business is what makes vote buying the most plausible reading.
The distinction between finding and interpretation matters for the practice round: the paper shows that aid moves with membership and with salience; bribery is the authors’ word for the most plausible mechanism, not something the data observe.
For this chapter the decisive step is what came next. The same research programme looked inside the economic institutions. Temporary Council members receive more World Bank projects (Dreher, Sturm, and Vreeland 2009a) and IMF programmes with fewer conditions attached (Dreher, Sturm, and Vreeland 2009b); Vreeland and Dreher (2014) assemble the evidence across channels. Kilby (2009) showed that World Bank disbursements respond less to a borrower’s compliance with conditions when the borrower is aligned with the United States. Stone (2011) built a general account of how the dominant shareholder exercises informal influence over the IMF when its interests are at stake, while leaving the formal rules to operate otherwise. The voting tables of the previous section are not trivia. Who holds the votes shapes who gets the money — and the money decides where the contracts, the co-investment and the insurance are.

title: 5  International Institutions: Who Finances, Insures and Referees the Firm
section: 5.6 Regions with banks of their own
text:
5.6 Regions with banks of their own
The World Bank model was copied, region by region, with a different balance of shareholders each time. The Inter-American Development Bank (1959) was the first; its private-sector arm, now IDB Invest, has operated since 1986, and in 2024 its governors approved a capital increase of US$3.5 billion tied to an “originate-to-share” model in which the bank originates loans and sells much of them on to private investors. The African Development Bank followed in 1964, the Asian Development Bank in 1966, the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development in 1991, to finance the transition of the former Soviet bloc. The European Investment Bank (1958) is the EU’s own bank, owned by its member states, and the Islamic Development Bank (operations from 1975) serves the members of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation, with separate arms for private investment, trade finance and export-credit and political risk insurance. Sub-regional banks fill in the map — CAF in Latin America, owned mainly by its borrowers; the Eurasian Development Bank in the post-Soviet space, founded by Russia and Kazakhstan.
Each has a private-sector window, a trade-finance programme that guarantees the letters of credit of local banks so that international banks will confirm them, and a procurement market. And each tells a geopolitical story through its shareholder register. Japan and the United States each held 15.6% of the Asian Development Bank’s shares at the end of 2025; the United States holds about 30% of the votes in the Inter-American Development Bank; Nigeria is the largest single voter in the African Development Bank; Saudi Arabia holds the largest share of the Islamic Development Bank.
Three features of the regional banks matter to a firm in ways the World Bank’s rules can obscure. The first is that procurement eligibility is foreign policy. The Asian and Inter-American banks restrict contracts to firms and goods from member countries; the EBRD’s are open to firms from any country; the African Development Bank opens contracts financed by its concessional fund to all while restricting those financed by the bank itself to members. Whether a Canadian, Chinese or Turkish firm may bid on a road in Bangladesh or Bolivia depends on whether its home state paid in.
The second is that a development bank can become an instrument of sanctions. On 4 April 2022 the EBRD’s Board of Governors suspended Russia’s and Belarus’s access to the bank’s resources and decided to close its offices in Moscow and Minsk (European Bank for Reconstruction and Development 2022). Both remain shareholders. A firm that had counted on EBRD co-finance in either country lost it overnight, through a decision taken by votes in which the host state took part and lost.
The third is that shareholding moves, slowly. The EBRD has expanded into sub-Saharan Africa, with Benin, Côte d’Ivoire and Nigeria becoming countries of operation in 2025; the Asian Development Bank amended its charter for the first time, with effect from March 2026, to lend more against the same capital; the Eurasian Development Bank cut Russia’s share below half at the end of 2022. Each move redraws the map of where a firm finds support, and on whose terms.

Multilateral development bank — a bank owned by several states that borrows on capital markets against its members’ paid-in and callable capital and lends, invests and guarantees for development purposes. Its rating, and therefore its cost of funds, depends on the creditworthiness of its shareholders and on its standing in the dollar and euro bond markets.

title: 5  International Institutions: Who Finances, Insures and Referees the Firm
section: 5.7 Building beside the old house: the new institutions
text:
5.7 Building beside the old house: the new institutions
The new institutions of the last decade are a response to the lag between votes and weight. They come in three kinds: development banks, reserve pools, and the national policy banks of China.

From the archive · London and Beijing, March 2015
On 12 March 2015 the British government announced that it intended to join China’s proposed Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank as a founding member — the first major Western economy to do so. Within weeks other European governments had followed, among them France, Germany and Italy. The United States and Japan stayed out, and are still out. On 29 June 2015 the bank’s Articles of Agreement were signed in Beijing by fifty countries; they entered into force on 25 December 2015, and the bank opened on 16 January 2016 with fifty-seven founding members.
For this chapter the episode is a demonstration of Morse and Keohane’s mechanism. China had sought a larger voice in the IMF and the World Bank for a decade, without a realignment of shares. It then built an institution in which it held the largest share by design — and invited the Europeans in. Once they were in, the new bank could not easily be dismissed as a Chinese instrument, and the old ones lost their monopoly on legitimacy in infrastructure finance. Competitive regime creation does not need to replace the incumbent to change the bargaining inside it.

The Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank has an authorised capital of US$100 billion. Its membership had reached 111 approved members by October 2026, 106 of them full members (Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank 2026). China holds 30.5% of subscriptions and 26.37% of votes; India, the second-largest member, holds 7.53% and Russia 5.92%. The Articles require a “super majority” — two-thirds of governors representing at least three-quarters of total voting power — for the most important decisions, among them capital increases and the election of the president. China’s quarter of the votes is therefore a veto, as the United States’ sixth of the IMF’s is. The board is non-resident, a deliberate contrast with the full-time resident boards of the Bretton Woods institutions. The bank signed co-financing frameworks with the World Bank and the Asian Development Bank in its first months and co-financed many of its early projects with them; it lends to private as well as sovereign borrowers, and offers non-sovereign loans in a range of local currencies.
The New Development Bank was created by the five original BRICS under an agreement signed at Fortaleza on 15 July 2014 and is headquartered in Shanghai. Its initial subscribed capital of US$50 billion was divided equally among the founders, and voting power equals subscribed shares; the founders’ combined votes may not fall below 55%, and non-borrowing members’ combined votes may not exceed 20% (BRICS Governments 2014). Bangladesh, the United Arab Emirates, Egypt, Algeria and, in 2026, Uzbekistan have since joined; several other countries have been admitted but have not yet completed accession. Its 2022–2026 strategy set a target of 30% of financing in local currencies. The equal-shares rule is the most interesting design choice in the new architecture: it prevents China from dominating the bank by capital, at the price of limiting how much capital the bank can raise.
The reserve pools are less visible to firms but matter to the country risk they face. The BRICS Contingent Reserve Arrangement, signed on the same day in Fortaleza, commits US$100 billion — China 41, Brazil, India and Russia 18 each, South Africa 5 — to members facing balance-of-payments pressure; but only 30% of a member’s maximum access is available without an IMF programme in place. The Chiang Mai Initiative Multilateralisation among the ASEAN members, China, Japan and Korea, in force since 2010, is a US$240 billion network of currency-swap commitments, 40% of which has been available without an IMF link since 2021; its surveillance unit, AMRO, became an international organisation in 2016. Both are regional insurance that defers, for most of its value, to the Fund they were meant to supplement.

IMF-delinked portion — the share of a regional financing arrangement that a member can draw without having an IMF programme in place. It measures how far the arrangement is an independent lender of last resort rather than a co-financier of the Fund: 30% for the BRICS Contingent Reserve Arrangement, 40% for the Chiang Mai Initiative Multilateralisation.

The third kind of new institution is not multilateral at all. China’s two policy banks, the China Development Bank and the Export-Import Bank of China, both created in 1994, and the Silk Road Fund, established in December 2014, are the financial core of the Belt and Road Initiative announced in 2013. AidData’s tracking of Chinese official finance counts US$1.34 trillion of loans and grants to 165 low- and middle-income countries between 2000 and 2021 (AidData 2023). Its terms differ from those of the multilateral banks in ways that matter: Horn, Reinhart, and Trebesch (2021) show that a large part of China’s overseas lending has gone unreported to the international debt statistics, much of it on commercial rather than concessional terms and often collateralised; Dreher et al. (2022) trace its aims and effects project by project. For a non-Chinese firm the opportunities are case by case. Contracts on Chinese-financed projects have often gone to Chinese contractors, and the standards that govern them are set bilaterally rather than by the published policies of a multilateral board.
BRICS itself, finally, is not an institution: it has no charter and no secretariat, and its two treaty bodies are the NDB and the CRA. Its expansion matters to a firm as a map of alignment. Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran and the United Arab Emirates became members on 1 January 2024 and Indonesia in January 2025; Saudi Arabia is listed by the BRICS chairs but has never formally confirmed its membership, and its status is best described as ambiguous. A category of partner countries, created at the Kazan summit in October 2024, numbered ten by mid-2025. The New Delhi summit of September 2026 added no members or partners and asked for continued work on cross-border payments in local currencies — work, not a launched system.

title: 5  International Institutions: Who Finances, Insures and Referees the Firm
text:
5.8 Complement or counter-hegemony?
The question every analyst asks of the new institutions is whether they complement the Bretton Woods order or contest it. Put that way, it has no answer; split into four tests, it does.
On votes, the new banks give emerging economies the voice that quota reform at the Fund has not — and reproduce its structure. China’s veto in the AIIB mirrors the American veto in the IMF; the NDB avoids a dominant shareholder only by fixing equal shares among the founders. A realist reading these tables would not be surprised.
On standards, the evidence leans towards complement. The AIIB adopted its own environmental and social framework and co-financed many of its first projects with the established banks; Wang (2017) and Humphrey (2022) both stress how much of the older banks’ operating model the new ones borrowed. The contest is sharper outside the multilateral banks, in bilateral Chinese lending that sits outside the OECD export-credit rules and the cross-debarment agreement, on terms that are often confidential.
On currency, local-currency lending by the AIIB and the NDB reduces the currency mismatch that has ruined many infrastructure borrowers, which any development economist would call a complement. The BRICS work on local-currency settlement is something else: an effort to reduce members’ dependence on the dollar and the payment chokepoints through which sanctions are enforced (Session 10).
On sanctions, the test came in March 2022. Within a week of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the AIIB announced that all activities relating to Russia and Belarus were on hold and under review, and the NDB put new transactions in Russia on hold — Russia being one of its five founders. Both banks depend on dollar funding markets. When the choice was between a founding member and access to the market that funds them, they chose the market. That is the strongest single piece of evidence that the new multilateral banks are, for now, inside the system they were thought to contest.
The verdict, then, is both, and the reason is structural. The new institutions do not need to replace the old ones to change the bargaining inside them; they need only to exist as an outside option. Ikenberry and Lim (2017) frame the AIIB as institutional statecraft that pursues influence partly through the existing order rather than against it. Humphrey and Michaelowa (2013) had already shown, for Latin America, that borrowers with access to a bank controlled by borrowers prefer it to the banks controlled by creditors. A host state with several lenders can shop among them, and the conditions any one of them attaches bind less.

title: 5  International Institutions: Who Finances, Insures and Referees the Firm
section: 5.9 What the firm should do with all this
text:
5.9 What the firm should do with all this
Across the course, geopolitical risk reaches a firm through five channels: market access, inputs, finance, assets and people, and data and operations. The economic institutions of this chapter touch all five, but they open four specific business channels — procurement, finance, insurance and dispute settlement — and each comes with its own geopolitical risk.
Procurement is a market-access channel. The projects financed by the World Bank, the regional banks, the AIIB and the NDB buy through published procedures; a firm that tracks project pipelines and procurement notices sees demand years before it reaches the market. The risk is eligibility: whether the firm may bid at all depends on its home state’s shareholding, and a cross-debarment for misconduct in one country closes the channel everywhere.
Finance and co-investment belong to the finance channel. IFC, IDB Invest, the EBRD and the private-sector windows of the Asian and African banks lend and invest alongside firms, increasingly in local currency and increasingly by mobilising institutional investors. A development bank in the capital structure lowers the cost of other finance and raises the political cost to a host government of interfering. The risk is conditionality and its politics: the institution’s own standards bind the project, and its decisions respond, as the previous sections showed, to the preferences of its largest shareholders.
Insurance and guarantees protect assets and people. MIGA, the World Bank Group’s guarantee platform, the Islamic Development Bank’s insurer and the trade-finance programmes of the regional banks turn political risk into a premium. The risk is that the cover is itself political: what a multilateral insurer will underwrite, and in which countries, reflects its shareholders’ view of those countries.
Dispute settlement — ICSID and the treaty network behind it — protects assets against the host state. The new institutions have built nothing comparable. The risk here is exit: states denounce the Convention, terminate treaties, or decline to pay awards, and the protection is only as strong as the regime’s membership.
Three further risks cut across the channels. Sanctions exposure runs through the institutions as well as around them: suspension at the EBRD, freezes at the AIIB and the NDB. Alignment is signalled by membership — BRICS status, AIIB or EBRD shareholding, a Belt and Road memorandum, a vote at the Council — and an analyst can read it. Competing standards mean that a project bankable by one lender may not be bankable by another.
An institution is a risk mitigator when the coalition that sustains it is stable, and a risk source when it is not. A firm’s dashboard should track the coalition, not only the rule: who holds the votes, who sits on the Council, who has been suspended, who has joined which club.

A guarantee, a co-financing agreement or a treaty is a promise by a coalition of states. Read the coalition before the contract.

title: 5  International Institutions: Who Finances, Insures and Referees the Firm
text:
5.10 How the concept becomes data
Institutions leave good data: they publish their rules, members and votes. Voting power is the simplest series: the IMF publishes each member’s quota and votes, the World Bank Group publishes country voting tables for each of its institutions, and the AIIB publishes each member’s subscription and voting power (International Monetary Fund 2026; World Bank Group 2026; Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank 2026). A comparison of China’s and the United States’ shares across the IMF, the IBRD and the AIIB, dated and sourced, is a one-sheet summary of the session’s argument. Activity is the second series: MIGA’s annual issuance and exposure, ICSID’s caseload by sector and legal basis, the regional banks’ commitments, AidData’s project-level record of Chinese official finance. Membership and its changes — accessions, suspensions, denunciations — are the third, and the easiest to turn into events.
The fourth kind of data is the one the practice round uses: an institution’s own rules, turned into a natural experiment. The rotation of elected Council members is set by the UN Charter and by regional custom. The UN publishes the list of elected members; the United States publishes its aid by country and year. Neither file contains the quantity Kuziemko and Werker study. It has to be built by joining the two on a country code, re-indexing every country-year to the start of a term, and expressing aid relative to the country’s own pre-term level — which is where the session’s Tableau skill comes in.

The level-of-detail expression in the practice computes each country’s pre-term baseline once per term, whatever else is in the view. That is the event-study idea in one calculation: every country is its own control, and the comparison is made within each term before it is averaged across terms.

title: 5  International Institutions: Who Finances, Insures and Referees the Firm
section: 5.11 A short review of the literature
text:
5.11 A short review of the literature

The theoretical frame is the exchange between Keohane (1984), for whom institutions persist because they reduce the costs of cooperation, and Mearsheimer (1994), for whom they reflect the distribution of power and constrain it little. Ikenberry (2011) reads the post-war order as an American project that bound its creator as well as others, which is why its institutions outlived the moment of American dominance. Morse and Keohane (2014) supply the concept that organises the last decade — contested multilateralism, through regime shifting and competitive regime creation.
On the politics inside the Bretton Woods institutions, Woods (2006) examines how the IMF and the World Bank’s relations with their borrowers are shaped by their largest shareholders, and Stone (2011) models the informal influence of the dominant shareholder alongside the formal rules. The empirical programme on the price of influence starts with Kuziemko and Werker (2006) on US and UN aid to elected Security Council members, and extends to World Bank projects (Dreher, Sturm, and Vreeland 2009a), IMF conditionality (Dreher, Sturm, and Vreeland 2009b) and World Bank disbursements (Kilby 2009); Vreeland and Dreher (2014) synthesise it. Humphrey and Michaelowa (2013) show that shareholder composition shapes borrowers’ choices among development banks.
On investment protection, Büthe and Milner (2008) find that international trade agreements raise FDI into developing countries by making policy commitments more credible, and Simmons (2014) shows that developing countries signed bilateral investment treaties, and tied their hands most tightly, when their bargaining position was weak — after which investors sued governments with surprising regularity. On the new institutions, Wang (2017) gives an early assessment of the AIIB and the NDB as complements to and potential competitors of the established banks; Ikenberry and Lim (2017) read the AIIB as Chinese institutional statecraft; Humphrey (2022) places both in a broader account of multilateral development banks under geopolitical change. On Chinese official finance, Dreher et al. (2021) build the project-level dataset and estimate its growth effects, Dreher et al. (2022) extend the analysis of its aims and impacts, and Horn, Reinhart, and Trebesch (2021) document the scale of lending absent from official debt statistics.

title: 5  International Institutions: Who Finances, Insures and Referees the Firm
text:
5.12 Into the practice round
The practice round rebuilds Kuziemko and Werker’s evidence in event time: US aid to developing countries in the three years before, the two years of, and the two years after a Security Council term, each country measured against its own pre-term level. If the paper’s pattern survives your data — flat before, higher during the term, back down afterwards — you will have seen, in a chart you built yourself, influence being priced inside an international institution.
Read the chart with the discipline of the earlier sections. It is evidence about one institution, one donor, and the decades the data cover. It does not show that the World Bank, MIGA, the AIIB or the NDB sell their decisions; the follow-up literature makes a case for some of them, with its own designs and its own limits. It does not tell a firm how a particular host government on the Council will vote, or whether a sanctions resolution will survive the next change of government in a permanent member. And because the aid series you will download is a later release than the one the authors used, in different constant dollars, your figure will not match theirs exactly; the log you keep is where that disagreement is recorded.
The question to ask at the end — what does this figure not license a multinational to conclude? — is the institutional version of the session’s opening question. The chart shows that the coalition behind a rule can be bought. A firm that relies on the rule should therefore know who is in the coalition, what they are being offered, and how long the offer lasts.

5.13.2 2 · Prepare — 20 min

Connect to the aid file and to unsc_elected_members.xlsx. In the Country Summary, filter Transaction Type Name = Obligations (a data-source filter), exclude Fiscal Year = 1976tq, then make Fiscal Year a number and rename it Year; rename constant_amount to Aid.
Drag the aid table to the canvas, then double-click it to open the physical layer, and drag the term table next to it: inner join on Country Code = Iso3 (or on country name only if you have checked every match — see the trap list in TABLEAU-TOOLKIT.md). Route A teams: use the replication file’s own country, year and aid fields. > Why a join, not a relationship? The next step is a row-level calculation that uses Year from > one table and Term start from the other. Relationships do not allow that.
Check the row count before and after the join and write both in your log. The join should multiply rows: each country-year now appears once per term of that country.
Keep only aid recipients (drop regional aggregates such as “World”, “Africa Region” — every Country Name ending in “Region”), and check that aid is in constant dollars (constant_amount, not current_amount). If it is not, say so in the log — the ratio to baseline below limits the damage, but does not remove it.

5.13.3.1 Calculated fields

5.13.3.2 Sheet 1 · “Aid in event time”

Filter [Event time] to −3 … +3 (make it a dimension, discrete).

Differ. Put your Sheet 1 beside the paper’s event-time evidence. Same shape? Same size? Write one difference and its most likely cause (release of the aid data, years covered, the sample of countries, constant vs current dollars, levels vs logs).

title: 6  Private Authority, Standards and Global Regulation
text:
6.1 Count the rules in a telephone
Pick up a mobile phone and ask how many rules it obeys. Its radio speaks a language specified by 3GPP, a partnership of standards organisations in which the engineers of competing telecommunications firms draft the technical specifications for each generation of mobile networks. Its wireless connection follows a family of specifications developed under the IEEE, a professional association of engineers. Its charging port follows a specification written by an industry forum. The factory that assembled it is probably certified to ISO 9001 for quality management and ISO 14001 for environmental management; its data centre partners to ISO/IEC 27001 for information security. The company that sold it reports its emissions under the Greenhouse Gas Protocol, a standard developed by a research institute and a business council, and its suppliers of tin, tantalum, tungsten and gold carry out due diligence on conflict minerals under frameworks developed by an intergovernmental organisation and audited by private firms.
Now ask how many of those rules were written by a government. Very few, and in most cases none. Some have since been made compulsory or referenced in procurement and trade law, but they were drafted and revised by engineers, auditors, industry associations and non-governmental organisations. The multinational that sells the phone spends far more of its compliance effort on these rules than on any treaty.
Session 05 looked at intergovernmental institutions — the organisations states build and in which states vote. This chapter is about the other half of global governance, the rules that come from somewhere other than states, and about why that half is increasingly geopolitical.
For a multinational, private authority is two things at once. It is a risk: a standard written elsewhere, by actors the firm does not control, can become a condition of access to a market. And it is a lever: a firm that shapes a standard shapes the market the standard governs, and may write its own technology, its own processes and its own costs into the rules its competitors must follow. The question this chapter asks is the one in the session’s title: who writes the rules a multinational actually follows, with whose power — and does trade spread those rules up or down?
crumbs: 6  Private Authority, Standards and Global Regulation

title: 6  Private Authority, Standards and Global Regulation
text: Private authority — the capacity of non-state actors (firms, industry associations, standards bodies, non-governmental organisations) to make rules that others treat as binding, even though no state has enacted them and no court may enforce them directly.
crumbs: 6  Private Authority, Standards and Global Regulation

title: 6  Private Authority, Standards and Global Regulation
text:
6.2 Where private authority comes from
For most of the twentieth century, private authority in international affairs was close to a contradiction in terms: international relations studied states, and rule-making was what states did. The concept entered the field in the 1990s, as globalisation multiplied the transactions that crossed borders faster than states could agree on rules to govern them.
Susan Strange made the argument most sharply. In The Retreat of the State she contended that markets, firms and a variety of non-state actors had come to exercise authority over outcomes — prices, investment, technology, credit — that had once been the preserve of governments, and that the study of international political economy had to follow power wherever it actually lay (Strange 1996). Cutler, Haufler, and Porter (1999) gave the concept its name in an edited volume on private authority in international affairs, focusing on the inter-firm arrangements — industry norms, business associations, private regimes — through which firms govern their own transactions. Hall and Biersteker (2002) extended it to a broader set of actors, from credit-rating agencies to transnational NGOs and even illicit networks, and asked a question that has never been fully settled: what makes private authority authority, rather than simply market power or persuasion?
The usual answer is legitimacy combined with consequences. A rule has authority when those it governs accept that it ought to be followed, and when failing to follow it has costs. Private rules acquire those costs through markets rather than courts. A supplier that is not certified loses the contract; a forest company whose timber is not certified loses access to the retailers whose customers demand certification; a firm whose emissions report does not follow the recognised protocol loses credibility with investors.

“Voluntary” does not mean “optional”. A standard required by a firm’s buyers, insurers or investors is, for that firm, as compulsory as a law — and sometimes more so, because a law can be challenged in court and a lost customer cannot.

Voluntary describes how a standard is adopted — no state compels it. It does not describe how much choice the firm has once its customers have adopted it.
crumbs: 6  Private Authority, Standards and Global Regulation

title: 6  Private Authority, Standards and Global Regulation
text:
6.3 The governance triangle
If rules can come from states, firms and NGOs, it helps to have a map. Kenneth Abbott and Duncan Snidal provide one (Abbott and Snidal 2009). They study what they call regulatory standards-setting schemes — arrangements that write standards for business conduct, monitor compliance, and sometimes certify it — and place each scheme in a triangle whose three corners are the three types of actor that can write rules.

Regulatory standards-setting (RSS) scheme — in Abbott and Snidal’s terms, an arrangement through which states, firms, NGOs or combinations of them set standards for the conduct of firms, and often monitor or certify compliance. Its position in the governance triangle is given by the share each of the three actor types has in its governance.

Schemes near a corner are run by one type of actor. An industry code of conduct, drafted by firms for firms, sits near the firm corner. A certification scheme created by an activist organisation sits near the NGO corner. A traditional intergovernmental rule sits near the state corner. Schemes in the interior are hybrids. The Forest Stewardship Council, founded in 1993, brings together environmental organisations, social organisations and firms in a multi-stakeholder structure, and sits on the edge between NGOs and firms. The UN Global Compact, launched in 2000 by the UN Secretary-General as a set of principles to which firms commit, brings states, firms and civil society together and is often placed near the centre. ISO itself is harder to place: its members are national standards bodies, some of them government agencies and many of them private associations whose committees are staffed largely by industry experts — which is why the placement of ISO standards is a useful argument to have in class rather than a fact to memorise.
The triangle’s most important feature is not on the diagram. Abbott and Snidal stress the shadow of the state: even schemes run entirely by private actors are shaped by the possibility that states will regulate if private actors do not, and by states’ decisions to endorse, require, reference or ignore private schemes. Firms write codes of conduct partly to pre-empt legislation; NGOs create certification schemes partly because they have despaired of getting legislation; and states frequently pick up private standards and give them legal force, at which point the scheme moves across the triangle without a word of its text changing.

From the archive · Brussels, 2022
For years, mobile phones in Europe were sold with a variety of incompatible chargers. The European Commission encouraged manufacturers to converge voluntarily, and a memorandum of understanding among major producers in 2009 led much of the market towards a common connector — but not all of it, and not permanently, as connectors evolved and one large manufacturer kept its own.
Meanwhile an industry body, the USB Implementers Forum, had written the specification for a new reversible connector, USB Type-C. It was a private standard in the purest sense: drafted by firms, adopted voluntarily, and spreading because device makers found it convenient.
In 2022 the European Union adopted a directive amending its Radio Equipment Directive to require a common charging port (European Parliament and Council of the European Union 2022). From the end of 2024, new mobile phones and a range of other portable devices sold in the EU had to charge through USB Type-C, with laptops following in 2026. A specification written by an industry forum became, by a single legislative act, a legal requirement for access to a market of several hundred million consumers. Because few manufacturers wish to design one version of a phone for Europe and another for everywhere else, the EU rule had consequences far beyond the EU.
In the governance triangle the specification did not change at all. What changed was its position: it moved from the firm corner towards the state corner, carried by the shadow of the state that had been hanging over it for more than a decade. And it illustrates in one case both of the chapter’s main arguments — that private standards can become conditions of market access, and that the jurisdiction which turns them into law extends its rules well beyond its borders.

For a firm, the triangle is useful because a scheme’s position predicts its behaviour. A scheme near the firm corner is easier for firms to change, and correspondingly less trusted by NGOs and regulators. A scheme with strong NGO participation is more legitimate in the eyes of activist consumers and harder for any single firm to steer. A scheme that a state has begun to reference in law is a scheme that may become mandatory, and a firm that ignores it is betting against the shadow.

title: 6  Private Authority, Standards and Global Regulation
text:
6.4 Who writes an international standard?
The triangle tells us what kinds of actor write rules. It does not tell us whose rules win when actors from different countries meet in the same room. That is the question Walter Mattli and Tim Büthe ask of the two principal international standards bodies for products, ISO and the International Electrotechnical Commission (Mattli and Büthe 2003).
Some institutional background makes the question concrete. ISO was founded in 1947, and its members are national standards bodies — one per country. Standards are drafted in technical committees and their subcommittees and working groups, where experts nominated by the national bodies — overwhelmingly engineers employed by firms — negotiate the text. Each national body takes positions on drafts and votes on them. The process looks consensual and technical, and in one sense it is. But the experts who sit at the table, the national positions they carry, and the timing with which they bring proposals all determine whose existing practice becomes the international standard. A firm whose product already conforms to the standard that emerges has a head start; a firm whose product does not must redesign.
Mattli and Büthe compare three explanations of who wins. On the first, technological rationality, the technically best solution wins whoever proposes it — the engineers’ view of themselves. On the second, the primacy of power, the standard favours the states with the largest markets — the realist’s view of everything. Mattli and Büthe argue for a third.

Institutional complementarity — in Mattli and Büthe’s account, the fit between a country’s domestic standard-setting institutions and those of the international body. A hierarchical, coordinated national system, which speaks with one voice and passes information efficiently between firms and the national delegation, matches the structure of ISO and IEC and wins more influence than a fragmented, decentralised one, regardless of market size.

Their evidence pointed to the advantage of the European national standards bodies, which are hierarchical and coordinated, over the fragmented, decentralised system of the United States, in which many private standards developers compete and no single body aggregates national preferences. The result was striking because it cut against the realist expectation: the country with the largest market was not the most effective at shaping international product standards. Influence over “technical” rules depends on how a country and its firms are organised to take part, not only on how big they are. Büthe and Mattli (2011) later generalised the argument to accounting standards as well as product standards, showing that the same logic of institutional fit shapes who wins in the private bodies that write rules for global financial reporting.
The lesson for a firm is practical and somewhat uncomfortable. Participation is costly — it takes the time of senior engineers over years — and its benefits are diffuse and delayed. It is easy to conclude that someone else will look after the standard. But if a competitor’s national standards body is better organised than one’s own, and that competitor’s engineers are in the room, the standard will reflect their technology, and the firm that stayed away will pay to comply with it. In standards, absence is a decision.

title: 6  Private Authority, Standards and Global Regulation
text:
6.5 Standards as geopolitics
For most of the post-war period, the politics of standards was the politics of firms and of national standards bodies, and it rarely reached foreign ministries. That has changed. The competition over telecommunications standards, over battery and charging standards, over the rules for artificial intelligence and for the flow of data, has become a competition between blocs, each trying to make its domestic rules the world’s.
The reason is that standards confer advantages that outlast the meeting at which they were agreed. A standard that incorporates patented technology generates licence revenue for as long as it is used; one that matches a country’s industrial practice lowers its firms’ costs and raises its competitors’; one that embeds choices about data access or encryption shapes what governments can see. And standards are sticky, so early influence compounds. When governments came to see technical standards as a component of technological leadership, and technological leadership as a component of national power, standard-setting acquired the stakes of geopolitics — and the bodies in which standards are written, which had been designed for engineers, found themselves hosting a contest between states.
The European Union’s version of this contest has been described most fully by Anu Bradford as the Brussels effect (Bradford 2020). The EU rarely sets out to impose its rules on the world. It regulates its own market. But when a large market sets a strict rule, firms that sell in it face a choice: produce two versions of their product, one for the strict market and one for everyone else, or produce one version that meets the strictest rule and sell it everywhere. Where production cannot easily be divided — because of economies of scale, because the product is a single global platform, or because maintaining two compliance systems costs more than over-complying in lax markets — firms adopt the strict rule globally, and then often lobby their home governments to adopt it too, so that their less global competitors bear the same costs. Bradford identifies the conditions under which the effect operates: a large market, the regulatory capacity to write and enforce rules, a preference for strict rules, regulation of targets that cannot easily leave the market (consumers rather than mobile capital), and non-divisibility of production. Data protection, chemical safety, competition law and product standards are her main cases; the common charger is a small, clean example.
The Brussels effect is a mechanism of unilateral regulatory globalisation, but it shares a logic with private standards. In both cases, rules travel along the channels of trade, carried by firms that find it cheaper to adopt one rule everywhere than to maintain many. That shared logic is precisely what the big work of this session tests.
