title: 6  Private Authority, Standards and Global Regulation
section: 6.6 Of, by, as: what standards do to organisations
text:
6.6 Of, by, as: what standards do to organisations
Standards are usually associated with stability and sameness: a standard exists so that things will be the same everywhere. Nils Brunsson, Andreas Rasche and David Seidl argue that this view misses most of what is interesting about them (Brunsson, Rasche, and Seidl 2012). They organise research on standards around three perspectives.
The first is standardisation of organisations: standards that tell firms how to be organised. ISO 9001 and ISO 14001 are the archetypes. They do not specify what a product must be like or how much pollution a plant may emit. They specify that a firm must have a management system — documented procedures, objectives, responsibilities, internal audits, management reviews and a commitment to continual improvement. The second is standardisation by organisations: the bodies that write standards, how they work, and how they compete with each other for adopters. The third is standardisation as organisation: standards as a way of organising markets and fields without formal hierarchy, coordinating the behaviour of thousands of firms that have no contract with each other and no common owner.
Their central point is that standards are dynamic. They are revised, contested, interpreted differently in different places, and — most important for anyone using certification as evidence — decoupled from practice.

Decoupling — the separation between the formal structures an organisation adopts to signal conformity to external expectations and the practices it actually follows. A firm certified to a management standard may change its documents and its audits while leaving its operations largely as they were.

The idea is older than the study of standards. Meyer and Rowan (1977) argued that organisations adopt formal structures because those structures are regarded as legitimate in their environment, not necessarily because they make the organisation more efficient, and that organisations protect themselves by decoupling those structures from the technical core of their work. A certificate can be a ceremony.
Whether ISO 14001 certificates are mostly ceremony is an empirical question, and the evidence is mixed in an informative way. Potoski and Prakash (2005) found that US facilities certified to ISO 14001 reduced their pollutant emissions somewhat more than comparable uncertified facilities — the standard’s “weak sword”, in their phrase, could still cut, because third-party audits and the reputational stakes of certification gave it some force. Christmann and Taylor (2006), studying firms in China, found that whether certification was implemented substantively or symbolically depended on the firm’s circumstances, and in particular on whether its customers monitored what it actually did. Certification backed by demanding buyers was more likely to change practice; certification sought only for its signal was more likely to be decoupled. The implication for a multinational is direct. If it relies on its suppliers’ certificates as evidence of environmental performance, the certificate’s value depends on whether anyone — the multinational included — looks behind it.
crumbs: 6  Private Authority, Standards and Global Regulation

title: 6  Private Authority, Standards and Global Regulation
text:
6.7 Agents and entrepreneurs
Private authority does not all arise in the same way, and its origin matters for how durable it is. Jessica Green draws the key distinction (Green 2013).

Delegated versus entrepreneurial private authority — delegated authority exists when states hand rule-making or implementation to private actors, who act as their agents; entrepreneurial authority exists when private actors create rules on their own initiative and others choose to adopt them.

Green’s field is carbon governance, and it supplies clean illustrations of both. Under the Clean Development Mechanism of the Kyoto Protocol, private bodies were accredited to validate and verify emission-reduction projects: they exercised authority that states had delegated to them, within rules states had written. The Greenhouse Gas Protocol, by contrast, was created by a research institute and a business council without any state mandate, and became the dominant framework for corporate carbon accounting because firms, investors and eventually regulators adopted it.
The distinction tells a firm what to watch. Delegated authority is as durable as the delegation: the state that handed it over can take it back, rewrite it or abolish the programme, and when the Kyoto mechanisms gave way to new arrangements under the Paris Agreement, the authority of the bodies that served them changed with them. Entrepreneurial authority is as strong as the number of its users. It grows through adoption and network effects, and it can be displaced by a competing standard that attracts more adopters — or captured by a state that writes it into law, at which point it becomes something closer to delegated authority after the fact.
Benjamin Cashore’s analysis of forest certification shows how entrepreneurial schemes gain the authority to make rules (Cashore 2002). He calls them non-state market-driven governance systems: they have no state backing, and their authority derives from the market — from retailers and consumers who demand certified products, and from the firms in the supply chain who must therefore decide whether to comply. The Forest Stewardship Council, created by environmental groups with stricter rules, was soon met by industry-backed schemes with laxer ones, and the competition between them became a contest over which would be accepted as legitimate by the buyers whose purchases conferred authority. Private authority, on this view, is not given; it is won, one supply chain at a time, and it can be lost the same way.
crumbs: 6  Private Authority, Standards and Global Regulation

title: 6  Private Authority, Standards and Global Regulation
section: 6.8 Race to the bottom, or trading up?
text:
6.8 Race to the bottom, or trading up?
With the concepts in place, the session’s central question can be stated precisely. Trade intensifies competition among producers in different countries. Does that competition push standards down or up?
The worry is the race to the bottom. If firms can produce anywhere and sell everywhere, governments compete for investment and exports, and one way to compete is to lower the costs that regulation imposes. Environmental standards are an obvious candidate: lax rules make production cheaper, and countries that compete hard for exports may tolerate pollution that richer or less trade-dependent countries would not. The argument predicts that greater openness to trade will be associated with weaker environmental governance.
The alternative was named by David Vogel (Vogel 1995).

California effect — the tendency of trade to spread stricter rules from strict to less strict jurisdictions. When a large, rich market imposes demanding standards on the products sold in it, producers elsewhere who wish to sell there adopt those standards, and may then press their own governments to adopt them too. Trade becomes a mechanism of “trading up”.

The name comes from American environmental history. California, with severe air-quality problems and a large car market, set vehicle emission standards stricter than federal ones; manufacturers that wanted to sell in California built cars to meet them, and other states followed. Vogel contrasted it with the Delaware effect — the race to the bottom in corporate chartering law, in which American states competed to attract company registrations by offering laxer rules, and Delaware won. The two effects are not contradictory. They describe different regulatory targets. Where the rule governs a product that must cross a border to be sold, the importing market can impose it, and trade tends to spread strict rules upward. Where the rule governs a process or a legal form that can be relocated, jurisdictions compete for the mobile target, and trade can push rules down.
Environmental management standards sit in an interesting middle position. ISO 14001 governs a process — how a plant manages its environmental impacts — and not a product. No importing government can require it at the border. But buyers can, and that is where the question becomes empirical.

From the archive · Rio and Geneva, 1992–1996
ISO 14001 was born of a particular moment. In the run-up to the UN Conference on Environment and Development in Rio de Janeiro in 1992, business leaders organised to present a constructive business response to global environmental concerns, and international standardisation was one of the avenues they explored. ISO and the IEC set up an advisory group on the environment to consider whether international standards for environmental management were needed.
They were not starting from nothing. The British Standards Institution had published BS 7750, a national standard for environmental management systems, in 1992, building on the management-system model that the ISO 9000 quality standards, first published in 1987, had made familiar to firms worldwide. In 1993 the European Union adopted its own Eco-Management and Audit Scheme. ISO created a new technical committee for environmental management, TC 207, in 1993, and in 1996 it published ISO 14001.
The standard reflected its parentage. Like ISO 9001, it specified a management system rather than a performance level: a certified firm commits to comply with applicable law and to improve continually, but the standard sets no emission limit of its own. That design made it adoptable anywhere, by firms in any sector and any regulatory environment — and it made it, from the first, vulnerable to the charge that certification and performance could diverge. It was revised in 2004 and again in 2015, and it became the most widely adopted environmental management standard in the world.
The episode illustrates Mattli and Büthe’s argument in miniature. The international standard grew out of a European national standard and a European regulatory scheme, drafted in a committee where coordinated national bodies with a working model to propose were well placed to shape it. Firms in countries with that model already in place adopted the international standard more easily — a pattern documented by Delmas (2002), who traced how differences in institutional environments made adoption faster in Europe than in the United States.

Aseem Prakash and Matthew Potoski put the race-to-the-bottom hypothesis to a direct test (Prakash and Potoski 2006a). ISO 14001 is a useful instrument because it goes beyond what many domestic laws require, is adopted voluntarily, and is counted, country by country, every year. Using a panel of 108 countries over seven years, they asked whether a country’s adoption of ISO 14001 depends on adoption in its export markets — the countries to which it sells.
Their finding is that trade linkages encourage ISO 14001 adoption when a country’s major export markets have themselves adopted it. Exporters to markets where certification is widespread certify more; exporters to markets where it is rare do not. Trade, on this evidence, does not drive environmental governance down. It transmits the standards of customers to their suppliers — a California effect operating through private rather than public regulation, with buyers rather than governments doing the imposing. The argument was developed at book length in Prakash and Potoski (2006b), which treats voluntary programmes like ISO 14001 as “green clubs” whose value to members depends on the credibility of the club’s standards and the visibility of membership to outsiders.
The mechanism is consistent with earlier work on the diffusion of quality certification. Guler, Guillén, and Macpherson (2002) showed that ISO 9000 certificates spread across countries through trade and investment ties with countries where certification was already common, alongside the influence of states and of imitation among firms. Christmann and Taylor (2001) found, among firms in China, that environmental self-regulation was more likely where firms were linked to multinational owners or exported to developed-country customers. Across these studies the picture is consistent: private standards travel along supply chains, from buyer to supplier, and the supply chains themselves determine where they go.
For the firm, the conclusion is one of the most practical in the course. A private standard can become a de facto condition of access to a market without a single law changing. Monitoring “regulatory” risk therefore means monitoring not only what governments legislate but what one’s customers’ home markets adopt.

title: 6  Private Authority, Standards and Global Regulation
text:
6.9 Turning a certificate into data
The practice round rebuilds the two figures that carry Prakash and Potoski’s argument: the diffusion of ISO 14001 across countries over time, and each country’s adoption against the adoption level of its export markets. Every step of the construction involves a choice that affects what the figure shows.
The data on certification come from the ISO Survey of Management System Standard Certifications, which counts valid certificates by country and year for the main management-system standards. Two features of the survey should temper any reading of it. It counts certificates issued by certification bodies, not firms or sites, and its coverage of certification bodies has changed across editions, so that a sudden jump in one country in one year may reflect a change in reporting rather than a wave of adoption. And from 2025 it is compiled from the IAF CertSearch database, a change of method that belongs in a provenance log. The 2015 revision of ISO 14001 adds a further wrinkle: as certificates to the old version expired and were reissued, transition years can show dips that have nothing to do with firms abandoning the standard.
A count of certificates is not an adoption rate. A large economy has more certificates because it has more firms, and a map of raw counts is mostly a map of economic size. The practice round therefore normalises by GDP, expressing adoption as certificates per billion US dollars of output. That is one reasonable choice among several — per firm, per unit of manufacturing output, per unit of exports would each tell a somewhat different story — and the scaling Prakash and Potoski themselves use should be checked against the paper. If it differs, the difference is logged, not hidden.
The trade side requires a measure of export-market adoption for each country: how much ISO 14001 adoption there is, on average, among the countries it sells to. The natural measure is a weighted average of partners’ adoption rates, with each partner weighted by its share of the country’s exports. Bilateral exports come from the IMF’s International Trade in Goods by partner country (International Monetary Fund 2026), the dataset already used in Session 04. The weighting is the substance of the argument, not a technical detail. The California effect predicts that what matters is adoption among the markets a country actually sells to, in proportion to how much it sells to them. An unweighted average of all partners would give a country’s smallest customers as much influence as its largest and would test a different, much weaker hypothesis.
A scatter of own adoption against export-market adoption can show whether the two move together, not why; the paper’s panel model with controls and the replication’s descriptive cloud differ precisely there, and the final section returns to the gap.
The most instructive check is a placebo. ISO 9001, the quality-management standard, is demanded by buyers everywhere and has no environmental content at all. If adoption of ISO 9001 tracks export-market adoption of ISO 9001 just as closely as ISO 14001 tracks its own, then the export-market pull may have little to do with environmental governance and a great deal to do with the general practice of supply chains demanding certificates of their suppliers. That would not overturn the finding that trade spreads private standards upward. It would change what the finding means — from “trade spreads environmental governance” to “trade spreads certification”, which is a different and less encouraging claim.

title: 6  Private Authority, Standards and Global Regulation
section: 6.10 What private authority means for the multinational, channel by channel
text:
6.10 What private authority means for the multinational, channel by channel
The five channels through which the course traces geopolitical risk all run through private authority, and in each the firm is both a rule-taker and a potential rule-maker.
Market access is the most direct channel. A certificate required by buyers is a condition of entry as real as a tariff, and it is set by the buyers and, behind them, by their home markets. When a large market writes a private standard into law, as the EU did with the common charger, the condition of access hardens and its reach extends through the Brussels effect to markets far beyond the one that legislated. A firm that monitors only government regulation will see these changes late. The practical discipline is to track what one’s customers’ home markets adopt, both privately and in law, because the evidence of this chapter says that is where one’s own future requirements will come from.
Inputs are where the multinational becomes the imposer rather than the imposed upon. A firm that requires its suppliers to certify is exercising private authority over them, and the evidence on decoupling says that the value of that requirement depends on whether the firm monitors behind the certificate. A supplier’s ISO 14001 certificate is evidence that a management system exists. It is not, by itself, evidence that the supplier pollutes less, and a firm that treats it as such is exposed when the gap between certificate and practice becomes public.
Finance increasingly runs on private standards too — carbon accounting, sustainability reporting frameworks, credit ratings — each written by a private or hybrid body, each conditioning access to capital, and several being absorbed into law, which moves them across the triangle and changes who can change them.
Assets and people are exposed through the standards that govern labour and human rights in supply chains. A plant certified under a scheme that later loses legitimacy is an asset whose value in the eyes of customers has fallen overnight.
Data and operations are where standards have become most explicitly geopolitical. Telecommunications standards, information-security standards, rules for artificial intelligence and for cross-border data flows are now contested between blocs. A firm whose products embed one bloc’s standards may find them excluded from the other’s procurement, and a firm whose engineers sit on the committees writing the next generation of a standard is not only shaping its own costs but taking part, whether it likes it or not, in a contest between states.
Across the five channels, the strategic choice is the same, and it has three options. The firm can adopt a standard written elsewhere, accepting the cost of compliance as the price of access. It can shape the standard, investing in participation in the bodies that write it — the lesson of Mattli and Büthe is that this investment pays only if the firm and its national body are organised to use it. Or it can resist, backing a competing standard or lobbying against legal adoption — a bet that the rival standard will win enough users, or that the shadow of the state will not fall. The choice depends on where the scheme sits in the governance triangle, on whether its authority is delegated or entrepreneurial, and on whether the firm’s own customers are among those who confer it.
crumbs: 6  Private Authority, Standards and Global Regulation

title: 6  Private Authority, Standards and Global Regulation
section: 6.11 A short review of the literature
text:
6.11 A short review of the literature

The study of private authority in international political economy begins with Strange (1996), who argued that authority over economic outcomes had shifted from states to markets and firms, and with Cutler, Haufler, and Porter (1999) and Hall and Biersteker (2002), who gave the concept its name and extended it from inter-firm regimes to NGOs, rating agencies and other non-state actors. Abbott and Snidal (2009) organised the resulting landscape into the governance triangle and introduced the shadow of the state; Green (2013) distinguished delegated from entrepreneurial private authority and traced both in carbon governance; Cashore (2002) showed how non-state, market-driven schemes such as forest certification gain the authority to make rules through the purchasing decisions of firms and consumers.
The politics of who writes international standards is the subject of Mattli and Büthe (2003), whose argument for institutional complementarity over technological rationality and raw power was generalised in Büthe and Mattli (2011) to the private regulation of products and financial reporting. Bradford (2020) documented the unilateral mechanism by which strict EU rules become global through firms’ preference for a single production standard; the EU’s common-charger directive (European Parliament and Council of the European Union 2022) is a recent and transparent instance of a private specification hardened into law.
On standards as organisation, Brunsson, Rasche, and Seidl (2012) set out the three perspectives — of, by and as organisation — and the dynamism of standards in practice, drawing on the institutionalist insight of Meyer and Rowan (1977) that formal structure may be decoupled from activity. Whether ISO 14001 changes behaviour is addressed by Potoski and Prakash (2005), who find modest emission reductions among certified US facilities, and by Christmann and Taylor (2006), who show that substantive rather than symbolic implementation depends on monitoring by customers.
On the race to the bottom, Vogel (1995) named the California effect and set it against the Delaware effect. Prakash and Potoski (2006a) provided the cross-national test at the centre of this session, finding that trade spreads ISO 14001 from export markets to exporters, and Prakash and Potoski (2006b) developed the theory of voluntary programmes as clubs. The diffusion mechanism is corroborated for quality standards by Guler, Guillén, and Macpherson (2002), for Chinese firms by Christmann and Taylor (2001), and for the differing paths of Europe and the United States by Delmas (2002). The through-line is that private rules travel along supply chains, and that the power to write them lies with those organised to take part.
crumbs: 6  Private Authority, Standards and Global Regulation

title: 6  Private Authority, Standards and Global Regulation
section: 6.12 What the map will not tell the firm
text:
6.12 What the map will not tell the firm
The practice round produces a map of ISO 14001 adoption that changes as the years advance, small multiples of its diffusion by region, and a scatter of each country’s adoption against the adoption of its export markets. If the build goes well, the scatter will slope upward, as Prakash and Potoski’s argument predicts. The temptation will be to read that slope as proof that trade spreads environmental governance. It is evidence of something narrower.
The scatter is a correlation, not a test. Countries whose export markets certify heavily are richer, more industrialised and more embedded in multinational supply chains than others, and any of those differences could produce the slope on its own; the paper’s panel model controls for some of them, the cloud of points controls for none. Certificates are not performance: the evidence on decoupling says that a certified plant may or may not pollute less than an uncertified one, and the figure says nothing about which. The data carry the scars of their collection: certification-body coverage changes between survey editions, the 2015 revision produces transition dips, and the switch to IAF CertSearch is a change of method. And the measure depends on choices — normalising by GDP rather than by firms or exports, weighting partners by exports rather than equally — that the comparison step asks you to break deliberately.
What the figures can show is whether the broad pattern the paper reports is visible in public data with transparent choices; how unevenly a private standard has diffused across the world; and, through the ISO 9001 placebo, whether the pull of export markets is specific to environmental governance or general to certification. Each of these matters to a firm deciding whether to certify, whether to require certification of its suppliers, and how much to trust the certificates it receives.
The question for the catch slide is the course’s usual one, applied to private rules. Suppose the scatter slopes upward exactly as the paper says. What does it not license a multinational to conclude? It does not license the conclusion that a certified supplier is environmentally better than an uncertified one, that certification caused a country’s export success, that a standard voluntary today will stay voluntary, or that the rules the firm’s markets follow were written by anyone the firm can vote for. The answer you give — one sentence — is a judgement about where authority lies, and it is the judgement a multinational must make every time it decides whether to adopt, shape or resist a rule it did not write.

title: 7  Measuring Risk: How a Political Judgement Becomes a Number
text:
7.1 The thermometer in the wrong room
Every geopolitical risk score that reaches a board has a pedigree, and the pedigree is usually hidden. A consultancy reports that a country’s risk has “risen to 71”; a bank’s dashboard turns a cell from amber to red; an index published by a central bank spikes in the week an invasion begins. Each of these numbers is the last link of a chain that started with a concept nobody can observe directly — the probability that politics will damage a firm’s business — and passed through a sequence of choices about texts, words, coders, units, weights and scales. The choices were made by someone, for reasons, and most of them could have been made differently.
This chapter is about seeing that chain, so that a score one is sold can be audited and a score one builds can be defended. Two words carry most of the weight, and they are worth fixing at the start.
The two are independent in one direction only. A measure can be perfectly reliable and entirely invalid: a thermometer that everyone reads identically, hanging in the wrong room. It cannot be valid without being reasonably reliable, because a measure that returns different numbers for the same object is measuring, in part, the person who applied it. The history of measurement in the social sciences is largely a history of trading one against the other — cheap, mechanical procedures that are perfectly reliable and of uncertain validity, against slow human judgement that captures meaning and disagrees with itself.
crumbs: 7  Measuring Risk: How a Political Judgement Becomes a Number

title: 7  Measuring Risk: How a Political Judgement Becomes a Number
text:
Validity — the degree to which an indicator measures the concept it claims to measure. Is the share of newspaper articles mentioning war threats a measure of geopolitical risk, or of editors’ attention to geopolitics, or of the number of journalists posted to a war zone?


Reliability — the degree to which the same procedure, applied by someone else to the same material, yields the same number. Would a second coder, following the same rules, put the same article in the same category? Would the same dictionary, run next year on the same archive, return the same count?
crumbs: 7  Measuring Risk: How a Political Judgement Becomes a Number

title: 7  Measuring Risk: How a Political Judgement Becomes a Number
text:
7.2 The chain, link by link
Write the chain out once, so that its parts have names. A measure of geopolitical risk passes from a concept (“geopolitical risk”) to an indicator (the share of articles that discuss geopolitical tensions), drawn from a source (a fixed set of newspapers), processed by a coding rule (a list of words grouped into categories), summarised by an aggregation (a monthly share, rescaled so that a base period averages 100) and delivered in a presentation (a line with spikes labelled “9/11” and “Iraq invasion”). Every one of the risk measures in this course can be written in that form, and every link is a place where the number can part company with the concept.
At the concept link, the danger is that nobody has said what is being measured. “Political risk” in the business literature has meant expropriation, contract repudiation, currency inconvertibility, civil unrest, regulatory change and, more recently, sanctions and export controls — things with different causes, different probabilities and different remedies. An indicator that pools them may be a reasonable summary of the newspapers and a poor guide to any one of the decisions it is meant to inform.
At the indicator and source links, the danger is selection. Newspapers report what is new and dramatic, in the countries their readers care about, in the language they print in. The ten newspapers behind the Caldara–Iacoviello index are American, British and Canadian; a war in a country with no correspondents may barely register. That is a property of the index, not a flaw, but a user must carry it into every inference.
At the coding link, the danger is the gap between words and meaning: a rule that counts “war” cannot tell a war from a price war or a trade war.
At the aggregation link, the danger is that choices about scaling and weighting, innocuous one at a time, decide the result. A share of articles behaves differently from a count when the number of articles changes; an average across countries weighted by GDP tells a different story from an unweighted one. And at the presentation link — the one most often forgotten — the labels on the spikes tell the reader what to see, and the absence of labels on the troughs tells them what not to.

From the archive · Inferences from enemy propaganda, 1941–1945
The systematic analysis of text as evidence about political intentions did not begin with computers. During the Second World War, analysts in the United States — among them a group at the Federal Communications Commission’s foreign broadcast monitoring service — read German radio propaganda not for what it said but for what its saying implied. If the propaganda ministry began preparing the public for a particular kind of news, what did the regime expect to happen? If a theme disappeared from broadcasts, what had changed in the regime’s own calculation?
Alexander George later reconstructed this work and asked how well the analysts’ inferences had held up once the German archives could be checked (George 1959). His account made two points that every risk analyst should know. The first is that the useful inferences were rarely about the manifest content — the frequency of a word — and usually about what the content revealed of the speaker’s situation and purposes, which required a model of the speaker. The second is that the analysts were most often wrong when they forgot that the text had been produced for an audience, by an actor with reasons to mislead it. A newspaper is not a propaganda ministry, and an earnings call is not a broadcast to a wartime public. But both are texts written by people with purposes, and an index built from them inherits those purposes.

title: 7  Measuring Risk: How a Political Judgement Becomes a Number
section: 7.3 Content analysis: from reading to inference
text:
7.3 Content analysis: from reading to inference
The discipline that formalised these practices is content analysis. Its early textbook definition called it a technique “for the objective, systematic, and quantitative description of the manifest content of communication” (Berelson 1952). The modern definition, Krippendorff’s, is broader and more demanding.

Content analysis — a research technique for making replicable and valid inferences from texts (or other meaningful matter) to the contexts of their use (Krippendorff 2018). Replicable: a second analyst following the same procedure should reach the same result. Valid: the inference must hold about the context, not merely about the texts.

The shift from “description” to “inference” matters. Nobody builds a geopolitical risk index because they want to know how often the word “missile” appears in newspapers. They want to infer something about the world the newspapers describe — and, in the case of a multinational, about the likelihood that the world will change in ways that touch the firm. The texts are evidence; the context is the object.
Krippendorff breaks the procedure into steps, and they map cleanly onto both the published indices and the coding exercise in this session. Unitising decides what a single unit is: an article in the GPR and EPU indices, a transcript in Hassan and colleagues’ measure, a headline in this session’s own coding. Sampling decides which units enter: every article in ten newspapers, every earnings call of listed firms that hold one, forty headlines drawn at random from a news query. Recording or coding assigns each unit to a category, by a dictionary or by human coders following a protocol. Reducing summarises the codes — counts, shares, monthly averages. Inferring draws the conclusion about the context: geopolitical risk is high this month; this firm faces unusual political risk this quarter; the countries in which a firm operates are in the news for military build-ups rather than for elections.

7.3.1 Manifest and latent content
The distinction that does most of the work in practice is between what a text says and what it is about. Manifest content is on the surface: the words, their frequency, their co-occurrence. Latent content requires interpretation: whether a headline reports a threat or an act, whether a statement is ironic, whether a reference to war is literal. Dictionaries read manifest content; human coders can read latent content. The trade-off between them is the trade-off between reliability and validity seen from another angle. A dictionary is perfectly reliable — run it twice and it returns the same count — and blind. A human coder sees meaning, and two human coders see slightly different meanings.
The best measures use both. They encode the analyst’s judgement in a dictionary that a machine can apply to millions of documents, and then audit the machine with humans who read a sample and check whether the dictionary’s classifications match what the texts are about. That design — a dictionary audited by people — is common to all three of the indices this session examines, and the quality of the audit is the best single guide to the quality of the index.

section: 7.4 Three dictionaries, three theories of risk
text:
7.4 Three dictionaries, three theories of risk
The three measures on the table share a family resemblance and differ in ways that matter.










GPR
EPU

7.4.1 Geopolitical risk as newspaper attention
Caldara and Iacoviello define geopolitical risk as the threat, realisation and escalation of adverse events associated with wars, terrorism and tensions between states that affect the normal and peaceful course of international relations (Caldara and Iacoviello 2022). Their index counts, each month, the share of articles in a fixed set of newspapers that contain words from eight categories: war threats, peace threats, military build-ups, nuclear threats, terror threats, beginning of war, escalation of war and terror acts. The first five form a sub-index of threats, the last three a sub-index of acts. The series is rescaled so that its average over a base period equals 100, and national indices are built by requiring that the article also mention the country.
The theory of risk embedded in this procedure is explicit: geopolitical risk is what informed newspaper readers in a few large democracies are being told to worry about. The split between threats and acts is not a technical detail. It distinguishes the risk that something will happen from the fact that it has, and the two behave differently — threats can rise for months before an act, and an act can resolve uncertainty as well as create it. The coding protocol of this session borrows the eight categories, with a rule that acts beat threats.


7.4.2 Policy uncertainty as a three-way conjunction
Baker, Bloom and Davis built the Economic Policy Uncertainty index on a different logic (Baker, Bloom, and Davis 2016). An article counts only if it contains a term from each of three sets: one about the economy, one about policy and one about uncertainty. The conjunction is the clever part. A filter on “uncertainty” alone would capture weather and sport; a filter on “policy” alone would capture every legislative report. Requiring all three narrows the count to articles that discuss uncertainty about economic policy, at the cost of missing articles that discuss it without using any of the listed words.
What distinguishes the EPU work methodologically is the audit. The authors had human readers code a large sample of articles and compared the human judgements with the dictionary’s, tuning the policy term set to reduce errors in both directions — articles the dictionary flagged that humans judged irrelevant, and articles humans judged relevant that the dictionary missed. The audit does not make the index perfect. It makes its error rates known, which is the more useful property. The global index used in this session is a GDP-weighted average of national indices; the data file offers two weightings, current-price and purchasing-power-parity GDP, and the choice between them is a small instance of the aggregation decisions discussed below.


7.4.3 Political risk as what managers discuss
Hassan, Hollander, van Lent and Tahoun asked a question the newspaper indices cannot answer: how much political risk does an individual firm face, and does it matter for what the firm does (Hassan et al. 2019)? Their text is not newspapers but the transcripts of quarterly earnings conference calls, in which senior managers present results and answer questions from analysts. The choice is deliberate. An earnings call is the place where a firm’s own leadership, under questioning from people paid to find weaknesses, talks about what worries it.
Their dictionary is not written by hand. It is learned. The authors took a body of political texts and a body of non-political texts and identified two-word combinations — bigrams — that are frequent in the first and rare in the second. A bigram such as a reference to a particular kind of legislation is political; a bigram such as a reference to a production process is not. They then counted, in each transcript, the political bigrams that appear close to a synonym of “risk” or “uncertainty”, weighted them by how distinctively political they are, and divided by the length of the transcript. The result, PRisk, is a firm-quarter measure of the share of the conversation devoted to political risk.

Dictionary method — a measurement procedure that assigns texts to categories by counting words or phrases from a pre-specified list. The list may be written by the analyst (GPR, EPU) or learned from labelled texts (PRisk). Either way it is a theory of what the concept looks like in language, and its validity depends on whether that theory holds in the texts to which it is applied.

The proximity requirement deserves a moment. Counting political bigrams alone would measure how much a firm talks about politics — which may reflect opportunity as much as risk, or simply a chief executive’s interests. Requiring that the political language appear near the language of risk and uncertainty turns a measure of political attention into a measure of political risk. It is the same logic as EPU’s three-way conjunction, applied at the level of a sentence rather than an article. The authors also construct the companion measures in the data file — non-political risk, sentiment and risk by political topic — so that a user can ask whether a firm’s political risk moves independently of its overall risk and its overall mood.
The dependence of a dictionary on its domain is not a hypothetical worry. Loughran and McDonald showed that the general-purpose word lists then in common use classified much of the ordinary vocabulary of corporate filings as negative — words such as “liability”, “tax” or “cost” that in a financial report are neutral descriptions — and built a finance-specific list in response (Loughran and McDonald 2011). Tetlock’s earlier work on newspaper pessimism and stock prices had shown that a dictionary measure of tone could carry real information about markets (Tetlock 2007). The two papers together make the point that runs through this chapter: a dictionary can work, but only for the texts it was built for, and its transfer to a new domain is an empirical question, not an assumption.

title: 7  Measuring Risk: How a Political Judgement Becomes a Number
text:
7.5 What the firm-level measure found
Hassan and colleagues validated PRisk in three ways, and the structure of the validation is as instructive as the result. First, the aggregate of PRisk across firms moves over time with the newspaper-based EPU index, which is what one would expect if both capture the same underlying variation in political uncertainty. Second, the measure picks out the topics one would expect at the times one would expect — firms talk about political risk in a given domain when policy in that domain is in motion. Third, and most persuasively, firms with high PRisk behave as theory predicts firms facing political risk should behave: they cut investment and hiring, and they become more active politically, lobbying more and donating more to politicians. A measure that predicted nothing about behaviour would be a curiosity. A measure that predicts the behaviour the concept implies has passed a test of validity that no amount of reliability could substitute for.
The finding that surprised the authors, and that matters most for a multinational, concerns where the variation lies. Most of the variation in political risk is not common to all firms at a given time, nor common to all firms in a sector; it is specific to the firm. Two companies in the same industry, in the same quarter, can face very different political risk, because they sell to different governments, depend on different regulations, source from different countries or hold different licences.
The implication is uncomfortable for anyone who buys a country-risk score. An aggregate index — however carefully built, however well audited — measures what is common. The political risk that actually reaches a particular firm is mostly what is not common. A board that tracks a national index and believes it is tracking its own exposure is watching the weather report for a region while the risk is in the plumbing of its own building.
This is where the five channels used throughout the course earn their place. Political risk reaches a multinational through market access (who may sell what to whom), inputs (what can be bought, and from where), finance (who will lend, insure, settle), assets and people (what can be seized, damaged or detained) and data and operations (what can be stored, transferred or shut down). An index built from newspapers measures, at best, the climate in which these channels operate. A firm-level measure such as PRisk measures how much a firm’s own managers are worried, which integrates the channels from the inside. Neither tells the firm which channel is exposed. That is the job of the team composite index, built at the end of this chapter, which is assembled channel by channel for a named firm.

title: 7  Measuring Risk: How a Political Judgement Becomes a Number
text:
7.6 Two coders and a protocol
The obvious measure of reliability is percent agreement: the share of items on which two coders chose the same category. It is intuitive and misleading. Two coders who never read the headlines and simply assigned codes at random, in proportion to how often each category occurs, would agree often — and very often if one category dominates. In a sample where four headlines in five are not about geopolitics at all, two coders who both write “not geopolitical” for every item will agree on most of them, while having measured nothing.
Cohen’s coefficient corrects for this by comparing observed agreement with the agreement that chance alone would produce, given each coder’s own distribution of codes (Cohen 1960).

Cohen’s kappa — a measure of agreement between two coders on a nominal scale, corrected for chance: \(\kappa = (p_o - p_e)/(1 - p_e)\), where \(p_o\) is the observed share of agreements and \(p_e\) the agreement expected if the two coders assigned categories independently at their own marginal rates. A kappa of 1 is perfect agreement; 0 is agreement no better than chance; negative values are worse than chance.

The expected agreement is computed from the margins of the agreement table. If coder A puts \(n_{A,k}\) of \(N\) items in category \(k\) and coder B puts \(n_{B,k}\) there, the chance that both pick \(k\) for the same item, if they choose independently, is the product of their shares; summing over categories gives
\[
p_e = \sum_k \frac{n_{A,k}}{N}\cdot\frac{n_{B,k}}{N}.
\]
Take forty headlines, collapsed into three categories — not geopolitical, threat, act — with coder A’s codes in the rows and coder B’s in the columns:

The coders agree on the diagonal, \(20 + 8 + 5 = 33\) items, so \(p_o = 33/40 = 0.825\). Chance agreement is \((24 \cdot 22 + 10 \cdot 12 + 6 \cdot 6)/40^2 = 684/1600 = 0.4275\). Kappa is therefore \((0.825 - 0.4275)/(1 - 0.4275) \approx 0.69\). An agreement rate that sounds excellent — better than four in five — shrinks by almost a fifth once the agreement the coders would have reached without reading is removed. The shrinkage is driven by the dominant category: because both coders put more than half the headlines in “not geopolitical”, much of their agreement there was to be expected.
What counts as good enough is a convention, and the conventions differ. Landis and Koch proposed a set of labels that have become widely used, under which values between 0.61 and 0.80 are “substantial” (Landis and Koch 1977). Krippendorff, for his alpha — a generalisation that handles more than two coders, missing data and ordinal or interval scales — asks for at least 0.800 before data are relied on, and accepts values from 0.667 only for tentative conclusions (Krippendorff 2018; Hayes and Krippendorff 2007). By the first convention the worked example is respectable; by the second it would support only a tentative claim.

7.6.1 What disagreement is for
The worst thing to do with disagreement is to average it away — to take the mean of two codes, or to pick one coder’s version at random. Disagreements are where the concept is fuzzy, and they are information. Read each one. Some will be errors: a coder misread a headline, or forgot a decision rule. Others will reveal that the protocol did not anticipate a case — a headline about sanctions, a cyber operation, a military exercise that might be a build-up or might be routine. Those are the valuable ones. The right response is to revise the protocol, write down the new rule, and then adjudicate.
The protocol used in this session contains a deliberate gap of exactly this kind. Sanctions, export controls and trade wars are not among Caldara and Iacoviello’s eight categories, so the protocol tells coders to assign them to “not geopolitical” and flag them. For a multinational in the 2020s, that is a strange place for them to be. A headline about export controls on semiconductors may matter more to a firm’s inputs channel than a headline about a distant military exercise. The gap is not a mistake in the GPR index, which measures what it says it measures; it is a reminder that an index built for one purpose — tracking the risk of war and terrorism as perceived by newspaper readers — may not be the index a firm needs.

title: 7  Measuring Risk: How a Political Judgement Becomes a Number
text:
7.7 Big data: detection, not measurement
The coding exercise draws its headlines from the GDELT Project, which monitors news media worldwide in many languages and turns them into searchable records. It is the most visible example of what is usually called big data in political risk: a source that promises coverage — every country, every day — and speed, without a research assistant reading anything.
The promise is real, and the traps are four. The first is selection. GDELT records what is reported, by the sources it monitors, in the languages it processes. Its coverage of sources has changed over time, so a rising count of articles about a country may mean more sources rather than more events. The second is duplication: a single wire-service story is republished by hundreds of outlets, and a naive count treats each republication as evidence. The third is machine coding: automated classification of events misreads irony, quotation and historical reference, and errs in ways that are not random — it is worse in some languages than in others, and worse for some kinds of event. The fourth is the most seductive. “N = all” is never all. A very large sample drawn by a biased process is still biased, and the large number only makes the estimate more confidently wrong.
The fourth trap has been formalised. Meng showed that the error of an estimate from a large non-random sample depends on the correlation between being in the sample and the quantity being measured, and that even a tiny such correlation can make a sample of millions worth less than a small random sample (Meng 2018). The parable everyone cites is the story of a search-based model of influenza that, after an initial success, substantially overestimated flu prevalence for long stretches, because the behaviour generating the data changed while the model did not (Lazer et al. 2014). Neither example is about geopolitics; both describe exactly what can happen to an event count built from online news.

More data is not better measurement. A dataset of millions of machine-coded news records is a sample drawn by a process nobody controls, measured with error nobody has fully characterised. Forty headlines drawn at random from a well-defined query and coded by two people with a written protocol can be more valid for a specific question — not because forty is more than millions, but because you know what the forty are.

The working rule for a risk analyst follows. Use big data for detection: something is happening, here, now, and it is worth a closer look. Use small, carefully coded data for measurement: how much is happening, compared with what, and whether it has changed. The two jobs are complementary. A monitoring system that flags a spike in news about a firm’s supplier country is doing detection well. A board paper that reports that “risk in the supplier country has doubled” on the strength of the same spike is doing measurement badly.

section: 7.8 Composite indicators and the arithmetic of judgement
text:
7.8 Composite indicators and the arithmetic of judgement
The third measurement task of the session is the one that a multinational is most likely to perform itself: combining several indicators into one number. Country-risk ratings, governance indices, supplier-risk scores and the team’s own exposure index are all composite indicators. They are attractive for the same reason they are dangerous: they compress several dimensions into one figure that a board can read at a glance, and they hide, in the compression, a series of decisions that determine the ranking.
The standard guide is the handbook produced by the OECD and the European Commission’s Joint Research Centre (OECD and European Commission Joint Research Centre 2008). It sets out ten steps, from the theoretical framework to the presentation of results. Five of them decide most of the outcome.
The theoretical framework says which dimensions of risk the index captures and why. Without one, the index becomes a collection of whatever data were available — which is to say, an index whose content was chosen by the data suppliers rather than by the analyst. For the team composite, the framework is the five channels: each indicator must be defended as a measure of exposure through a named channel, or it does not belong.
Missing data is where indices quietly lie. The country GPR indices cover 44 countries; the country EPU indices about twenty. A composite that drops every country missing an indicator will cover only large, well-documented economies — and the countries it silently drops are, very often, the risky ones, about which fewer people write. Imputing a value is a claim about a country nobody measured; flagging the gap is honest and less tidy. Whatever is chosen should be visible in the output.
Normalisation puts indicators measured in different units on a common scale. The simplest method, min–max, maps each indicator to the interval from 0 to 1:
\[
x^{*} = \frac{x - \min x}{\max x - \min x}
\qquad\text{or, where higher is safer,}\qquad
x^{*} = \frac{\max x - x}{\max x - \min x}.
\]
The second form matters more than it looks. The Worldwide Governance Indicators’ measure of political stability is scored so that higher means more stable; in a risk index it must be inverted, or a stable country will score as risky. The indicators also changed scale in their 2025 edition, moving to a 0–100 score and recalculating their history, so that values from different editions cannot be mixed; the methodology behind the indicators is set out in Kaufmann, Kraay, and Mastruzzi (2011). Other normalisations — z-scores, ranks, distance to a reference country — produce different rankings from the same data, because they treat outliers and gaps differently. Min–max is sensitive to the extremes: a single country with an extraordinary value compresses everyone else into a narrow band.
Weighting and aggregation combine the normalised indicators. The usual form is a weighted average,
\[
CI = \frac{\sum_j w_j \, x^{*}_j}{\sum_j w_j},
\]
and the weights can be equal, derived statistically (from principal components, say), or set by experts. Each choice is defensible and none is neutral. Equal weights are a judgement that every dimension matters equally, which is rarely what anyone believes. Statistical weights reward the indicators that move together, which may simply be the redundant ones. Expert weights encode the expert.
The aggregation rule carries a further assumption that is easy to miss.

Compensability — the property of an aggregation rule under which a high score on one dimension can offset a low score on another. Additive aggregation is fully compensatory: a country with excellent governance and an active war can average to “medium”. Geometric aggregation is partially compensatory, penalising unbalanced profiles; non-compensatory rules rank countries without allowing any trade-off at all.

For a risk index, full compensability is often the wrong assumption. A firm does not experience the average of a country’s risks; it experiences the worst of them that touches its operations. Excellent contract enforcement does not compensate for a plant inside a war zone. Additive aggregation is still the default, because it is simple and transparent, but an analyst who uses it should be able to say why the dimensions can trade off — or at least show the profile behind each score so that the reader can see when they cannot.

From the archive · The Human Development Index, 1990 and 2010
The most influential composite indicator of the past half-century was designed to argue with a single number. The first Human Development Report, published by the United Nations Development Programme in 1990 under the direction of Mahbub ul Haq, proposed the Human Development Index as an alternative to ranking countries by income per head (United Nations Development Programme 1990). It combined three dimensions — a long and healthy life, knowledge and a decent standard of living — each normalised against minimum and maximum values, and averaged them with equal weights. Its authors were explicit that the index was a simplification built to change a conversation, and it did.
Twenty years later the 2010 report changed the aggregation from an arithmetic to a geometric mean of the three dimension indices and revised the indicators of education and income (United Nations Development Programme 2010). The reason given was compensability: under the arithmetic mean, a country could make up for poor health with high income, one for one; under the geometric mean, poor performance in one dimension weighs more heavily. The change re-ranked countries. Ravallion then showed that the new formula implied trade-offs between longevity and income that few would accept if they were stated openly — in effect, valuations of an extra year of life that varied enormously with a country’s income, and were very low in the poorest countries (Ravallion 2012).
The episode is a compact lesson in everything this section argues. The weights and the aggregation rule were value judgements; changing them changed the ranking; and the implicit prices they carried became visible only when someone did the algebra. A firm’s exposure index embeds trade-offs of the same kind — between, say, sanctions exposure and political instability — and the board deserves to see them stated.

title: 7  Measuring Risk: How a Political Judgement Becomes a Number
section: 7.9 Sensitivity: the ranking that one weight overturns
text:
7.9 Sensitivity: the ranking that one weight overturns
The last of the decisive steps is the one most often skipped. Sensitivity analysis asks how much the results move when the choices change: a different normalisation, different weights, a different treatment of missing data, a different aggregation rule. Saisana, Saltelli and Tarantola set out how to do this systematically, by treating each methodological choice as an uncertain input and examining the distribution of ranks it produces (Saisana, Saltelli, and Tarantola 2005). The simplest version needs no special software. Record the ranking under equal weights; then under each indicator alone; then count how many countries move by more than a few places. A country that stays near the top under every reasonable choice is robustly high-risk. A country whose rank swings from fifth to twenty-fifth depending on one weight is not “fifth”; it is a country about which the index has no firm opinion.
This is why the practice round builds the team composite with weights a reader can move. The point is not interactivity for its own sake. It is that a composite which hides its weights is an opinion dressed as a measurement, and a composite whose weights are visible and adjustable is an argument the reader can test.

A minimal sensitivity report for any composite: the ranking under the chosen weights; the ranking under equal weights; the ranking under each indicator alone; the number of units whose rank changes by more than a stated threshold; and a sentence on the unit most sensitive to the weights and why.

title: 7  Measuring Risk: How a Political Judgement Becomes a Number
section: 7.10 A short review of the literature
text:
7.10 A short review of the literature

Content analysis as a social-science method was codified in the mid-twentieth century. Berelson (1952) gave the classic definition centred on manifest content, and George (1959) reconstructed the wartime analysis of enemy propaganda that showed both the power and the dangers of inference from text. Krippendorff (2018) is the standard modern treatment, recasting the method around replicable and valid inference and setting out the reliability apparatus; Hayes and Krippendorff (2007) make the case for Krippendorff’s alpha as a general standard. The chance-corrected agreement coefficient is Cohen (1960), and the labels most often attached to its values are Landis and Koch (1977).
Automated text analysis in political science and economics has grown into a large literature. Grimmer and Stewart (2013) is the essential warning and guide for political texts — their principle that automated methods amplify rather than replace human reading, and must be validated for every application, is the spine of this chapter. Gentzkow, Kelly, and Taddy (2019) survey text as data in economics. In finance, Tetlock (2007) showed that dictionary measures of media tone carry information about markets, and Loughran and McDonald (2011) showed how badly general-purpose dictionaries misread specialised documents.
The three indices at the centre of the session are Caldara and Iacoviello (2022) for geopolitical risk, Baker, Bloom, and Davis (2016) for economic policy uncertainty and Hassan et al. (2019) for firm-level political risk; the last is notable both for its learned dictionary and for its demonstration that most political risk is firm-specific. On big data, Lazer et al. (2014) is the cautionary tale and Meng (2018) the formal account of why sample size does not rescue a biased selection process.
Composite indicators have their own methodological literature. OECD and European Commission Joint Research Centre (2008) is the practitioner’s handbook and Saisana, Saltelli, and Tarantola (2005) the statement of sensitivity and uncertainty analysis as a quality test. Kaufmann, Kraay, and Mastruzzi (2011) document the Worldwide Governance Indicators, a composite of composites. The Human Development Index (United Nations Development Programme 1990, 2010) and the critique of its implicit trade-offs in Ravallion (2012) are the clearest case study of how aggregation rules carry value judgements.

title: 7  Measuring Risk: How a Political Judgement Becomes a Number
section: 7.11 What the figure will not tell the firm
text:
7.11 What the figure will not tell the firm
The practice round produces three figures — the firm-level measure against the newspaper-based one, the team’s own coded index and the draft composite for the team’s firm — and each comes with a sentence it does not license. The first comparison is two indicators of a similar concept built from different texts, dictionaries and levels of aggregation; where they part company, the question is which link of which chain explains the gap.
The line of average firm-level political risk set against policy uncertainty does not tell a particular multinational how much political risk it faces. It is an average over listed firms that hold earnings calls in English, which is mostly to say American listed firms, over a period that ends in early 2022. The most important finding of the paper it replicates is that most of the variation in political risk is specific to the firm — and that is precisely the variation an average removes. A board can use the line to see when political uncertainty was high for corporate America as a whole; it cannot use it to see its own exposure, which would require scoring its own calls, or at least those of its closest peers.
The team’s coded index, with its kappa, does not license a claim about how geopolitical the news about a country is. It is forty headlines from a three-month window of an online news monitor whose sources are weighted towards English-language media, coded against a protocol that by design places sanctions and export controls outside geopolitics. What it licenses is a statement about how reliably two trained readers can apply that protocol — and a list of the places where the protocol needs to change before anyone relies on it.
The composite exposure index does not license a ranking presented as fact. It licenses a ranking under stated weights, together with the weight that would overturn it. The question to carry into the practice round, and into every risk score a multinational is sold, is the five-part audit this chapter has built: what concept, from which sources, coded by whom or by what, normalised and weighted how, and how sensitive to each of those choices. A score that can answer all five is a measurement. A score that cannot is somebody’s opinion, with decimals.

title: 8  Cyber Geopolitics: Restraint, Rivals and Weaponised Networks
text:
8.1 The war that was supposed to happen
For most of the past three decades, the public conversation about cyberspace and international politics has been conducted in the future tense. A “cyber Pearl Harbor” would switch off a country’s power grid; a handful of skilled operators would humble a great power; the next war would be won or lost before a shot was fired. The scenarios were vivid, and they were not absurd: modern economies do run on networked systems, and those systems can be broken. What the scenarios lacked was a record. They were claims about what could happen, offered in the absence of systematic evidence about what had.
The opposite caricature is just as easy to state. On this view cyber operations are simply crime and espionage conducted with better tools — a nuisance for security departments, of no strategic consequence, and no business of a course on geopolitics. It, too, is a claim about evidence, and it, too, is usually made without any.
This chapter takes the question to the data. It does so through the work of Brandon Valeriano and Ryan Maness, who built a dataset of cyber incidents between rival states and asked what the record actually shows (Valeriano and Maness 2015), and through the argument of Henry Farrell and Abraham Newman that the networks globalisation built are not flat, and that states with jurisdiction over their hubs can turn them into instruments of coercion (Farrell and Newman 2019). The two works answer different questions. The first asks how states use offensive cyber operations against each other. The second asks how states use the architecture of the global economy — including its digital architecture — to watch and to deny. A multinational needs both answers, because it sits inside the architecture and in the path of the operations.
The question for the firm is narrower and more practical than the question for the strategist. It is not whether cyberspace is a new domain of war. It is through which channels inter-state rivalry in cyberspace reaches a firm’s operations, and how its decision architecture should absorb it. The answer, this chapter argues, is that the firm is rarely the intended target of strategic cyber operations, frequently their collateral, and increasingly a piece of the infrastructure over which states compete.

title: 8  Cyber Geopolitics: Restraint, Rivals and Weaponised Networks
text:
8.2 Three activities that look alike
Three kinds of activity are routinely run together under the heading “cyber attack”, and the first task is to separate them.
Espionage steals information: state secrets, negotiating positions, intellectual property, the personal data of officials. Its typical actors are intelligence services and their contractors, and its typical intrusion — into a ministry, a defence supplier or a law firm advising on a merger — is designed never to be noticed. Disruption and degradation interrupt or damage systems: a denial-of-service attack that floods a ministry’s website, malware that wipes the disks of a company’s computers, an operation that manipulates an industrial control system. Its actors are military and intelligence units and the proxies they sponsor. Crime extracts money: ransomware that encrypts a hospital’s records, fraud against a bank’s payment systems. Its actors are criminal groups.

Cyber operation — the use of computer code or network access by an organised actor to obtain information from, disrupt, degrade or manipulate a target’s information systems. Espionage, disruption and crime are all cyber operations; they differ in purpose and actor, not in technique. The same intrusion may serve any of the three.

The boundaries blur, and the blurring is itself a geopolitical fact. States tolerate criminal groups that operate from their territory against foreign targets, hire them, shelter them, and occasionally use their tools. An intrusion that begins as espionage leaves access that can later be used for disruption. A ransomware campaign run by a criminal group may serve a state’s purposes by sowing disorder in a rival’s economy, without the state having ordered it. When a ransomware attack by a criminal group believed to operate from Russia forced the shutdown of the Colonial Pipeline in the United States in May 2021, it was crime in its motive and geopolitics in its consequences: the question of what the Russian state knew, tolerated or could have prevented became a matter between governments.
For a multinational the distinction matters because the three activities call for different responses. Espionage is a threat to the firm’s intellectual property and its negotiating position, and the defence is largely technical and organisational. Disruption is a threat to its operations, and the defence includes resilience — the ability to keep working when systems fail. Crime is a threat to its cash and its reputation, and it is the one where law enforcement, insurers and the firm’s own willingness to pay become part of the calculation. A risk register that lists “cyber” as a single line has not yet done the first piece of analysis.

From the archive · Estonia, 2007
In April 2007 the Estonian government moved a Soviet-era war memorial, the Bronze Soldier, from the centre of Tallinn to a military cemetery. The decision provoked protests by members of the country’s Russian-speaking minority and an angry response from Moscow. Over the following weeks a wave of distributed denial-of-service attacks hit Estonian government websites, banks, newspapers and political parties. Estonia, among the most digitised societies in Europe, found its online services intermittently unreachable.
Estonian officials pointed to Russia. The Russian government denied involvement, and the public record never established a chain of command; much of the traffic came from botnets and from individuals mobilised on Russian-language forums. The episode thus contained, in compressed form, nearly every feature that later analysts would identify in state cyber conflict: an existing political rivalry, an operation of low technical sophistication and limited physical harm, high political salience, and attribution that remained contested.
Its institutional legacy was substantial. NATO’s Cooperative Cyber Defence Centre of Excellence was established in Tallinn the following year, and under its auspices a group of international lawyers produced the Tallinn Manual, an attempt to state how existing international law applies to cyber operations (Schmitt 2013). The episode was widely described at the time as the first cyber war. With hindsight it looks more like the first clear case of what Valeriano and Maness would call restraint: a rival state’s displeasure expressed through disruption that stopped well short of destruction.

title: 8  Cyber Geopolitics: Restraint, Rivals and Weaponised Networks
text:
8.3 The restraint thesis
Valeriano and Maness built their dataset around a simple design choice that shapes everything they found. They did not try to catalogue every cyber operation in the world. They took pairs of states with a history of enduring hostility — rivals, in the sense the international-conflict literature has used for decades — and recorded the cyber incidents between them. The unit is the incident, nested in campaigns; the population is rival dyads; the evidence is public. The dataset has since been extended as the Dyadic Cyber Incident and Campaign Data, whose version 2.0 covers incidents beginning between 2000 and 2020 and is the replication data for this session (Maness et al. 2022).

Cyber incident (in DCID) — an individual cyber operation launched by one state against another within a rival dyad, with a start date, a method, a target type, an objective and a severity score. Incidents can be grouped into campaigns, sustained series of operations with a common purpose. The unit is the incident between rivals, not the operation in general.

The choice of rivals as the population is a theoretical commitment, not a convenience. The study of international conflict has long found that a small number of pairs of states account for a large share of militarised disputes, and that these enduring rivalries have their own dynamics: hostility persists, crises recur, and each side interprets the other’s moves in the light of a long history. If cyber operations are a new instrument of old conflicts, rivalries are where they should appear; if they are something genuinely new — an instrument that lets any state hurt any other cheaply — they should appear outside rivalries too. Restricting the data to rivals makes the first hypothesis testable and the second invisible — a limitation that the comparison dataset in the practice round makes concrete.
From that record they drew four propositions.
The first is restraint. States use cyber operations far less often, and far less destructively, than the “cyber war” narrative predicts. Most incidents in the data are of low severity: defacements of websites, denial-of-service attacks, espionage. Operations that destroy physical property or take lives are rare. The image of cyberspace as a domain of constant, escalating attack does not survive contact with a systematic count.

Cyber restraint — the empirical pattern, and the theoretical argument, that states with offensive cyber capabilities use them sparingly and at low severity against their rivals, holding back the most destructive options. Restraint is a claim about strategic severity, not about frequency of nuisance or about commercial cost.

The second is that cyber conflict follows regional rivalries. The dyads that account for most of the incidents are those that were already hostile before anyone had a network: the United States and China, Russia and its neighbours and the West, Israel and Iran, India and Pakistan, the two Koreas. Cyber operations do not create new conflicts; they are a tool in old ones. That finding matters for anyone who expected the low cost of entry to cyber operations to flatten the international hierarchy. The states that are most active in cyberspace are, by and large, the states that were already contending.
The third proposition explains the first: why states hold back. The fourth is that cyber operations have limited coercive effect. They rarely change the target’s behaviour. They are better at signalling displeasure and at gathering intelligence than at compelling a rival to do something it would otherwise not do — a conclusion that the same authors developed at greater length in later work on cyber strategy (Valeriano, Jensen, and Maness 2018).
The restraint thesis did not arrive in an empty field. Thomas Rid had argued, provocatively, that cyber war in the sense of an act of force that is violent, instrumental and political had never occurred, and that what was called cyber war was better understood as sabotage, espionage and subversion — old activities in a new medium (Rid 2012, 2013). Erik Gartzke made a related argument from the logic of force: an attack that cannot be followed up by conventional power changes nothing durable, so cyber operations are likely to be adjuncts to force rather than substitutes for it (Gartzke 2013). Lucas Kello took the opposite position, arguing that the cyber revolution genuinely strained the concepts of international relations because it blurred war and peace into a condition of permanent, sub-threshold “unpeace” (Kello 2013, 2017). Valeriano and Maness’s contribution was to bring data to an argument that had been conducted largely through concepts and anecdotes, and the data came down closer to Rid and Gartzke than to the prophets of catastrophe.
