title: 8  Cyber Geopolitics: Restraint, Rivals and Weaponised Networks
text:
8.4 Why states hold back
The reasons for restraint are worth taking one at a time, because each has an analogue in the firm’s own calculation.
Escalation. A destructive cyber operation against a rival invites a response, and the response need not stay in cyberspace. A state that switches off a rival’s grid has made a move whose consequences it cannot control. In a relationship where both sides have conventional and sometimes nuclear forces, the incentive to stay below the threshold that would provoke them is strong.
Revelation. A cyber capability depends on a vulnerability the target has not fixed. Using it reveals it, and once revealed it can be patched — in the target’s systems and everyone else’s. The most sophisticated capabilities are therefore wasting assets, worth more held in reserve than spent.
Blowback. Malicious code, once released, can be captured, analysed and reused. A weapon that can be reverse-engineered and turned back on its maker, or on the maker’s allies and firms, is a weapon to be used with care.
Access. The value of being inside a rival’s networks is often greater than the value of damaging them. A state that can read a rival’s communications has every reason not to do anything that would alert the rival to its presence. Espionage, in this sense, restrains disruption.
These incentives are not the whole story. Ben Buchanan has argued that intrusions made for defensive purposes — to understand a rival’s capabilities, or to pre-position against a future threat — look identical, from the target’s side, to preparation for attack, and that this creates a security dilemma in which each side’s prudence alarms the other (Buchanan 2017). Restraint in the use of destructive operations is compatible with constant, mutual intrusion, and the intrusions themselves are a source of instability.
The war in Ukraine has tested the restraint thesis harder than anything in the dataset, which ends in 2020. Russian cyber operations against Ukraine have been extensive since 2014, and they intensified around the full-scale invasion of February 2022. The best systematic study of the earlier period found that cyber operations had little discernible effect on events on the battlefield (Kostyuk and Zhukov 2019), which is consistent with the fourth proposition: cyber operations are weak instruments of compulsion even in war. Whether the restraint thesis holds as of today is an open question, and it is the right question to ask of the replication. A pattern measured to 2020 is evidence about 2000–2020; extending it requires data the dataset does not contain.
The most famous exception proves the rule in an instructive way. The operation later known as Stuxnet, discovered in 2010, sabotaged centrifuges at Iran’s uranium-enrichment plant at Natanz by manipulating the industrial control systems that ran them. It was widely attributed to the United States and Israel, neither of which has formally acknowledged it. It is the clearest case in the public record of code causing physical destruction to a rival’s strategic asset, and it fits the restraint thesis better than the catastrophe narrative: it was narrowly targeted, designed to look like malfunction rather than attack, and aimed at delaying a programme rather than at provoking a war. It also illustrates blowback. The code escaped the plant’s isolated network, spread to computers around the world, and was analysed in detail by security researchers, so that its techniques became available to everyone. For firms, the lesson was that industrial control systems — the machinery of plants, pipelines and utilities — were now a target class, and that the code designed to attack one of them could end up on their own networks.

Low strategic severity is not low commercial cost. An operation that barely registers on a scale of harm between states — a wiper that destroys no infrastructure and kills no one — can halt a company’s production for weeks. The restraint thesis is about what states do to each other. The firm’s question is what happens to the firms that happen to be in the way.

title: 8  Cyber Geopolitics: Restraint, Rivals and Weaponised Networks
text:
8.5 Weaponised interdependence
Valeriano and Maness study offensive operations. Farrell and Newman study something quieter and, for a multinational, probably more consequential: the way in which the networks of the global economy can be used by the states that sit at their centre (Farrell and Newman 2019).
Their starting observation is that the networks globalisation built — for finance, for communications, for the internet’s physical and logical infrastructure — are not flat meshes in which every node is equal. They are highly asymmetric, with a few hubs through which most traffic passes. Network economics explains why: hubs are efficient, and efficiency attracts more traffic, which makes the hub more central still. The internationalisation of the 1990s was conducted on the assumption that this centralisation was a technical fact with no political content. Farrell and Newman’s argument is that the assumption was wrong. A state that has jurisdiction over a hub can use it.

Panopticon effect — the use of jurisdiction over a network hub to see what flows through it: to gather information about the activities of other states, firms and individuals whose traffic passes through the hub.


Chokepoint effect — the use of jurisdiction over a network hub to deny others access to it: to cut a bank out of a payment system, a firm out of a software supply, a country out of a market for critical components.

The two effects need each other. The panopticon tells a state where to apply the chokepoint, and the chokepoint gives the panopticon its teeth. Farrell and Newman’s cases make both concrete. The disclosures by Edward Snowden in 2013 showed the extent to which American intelligence agencies had used the concentration of global internet traffic and data storage in American firms and on American territory to collect information at scale — the panopticon. The disconnection of sanctioned Iranian banks from the SWIFT financial-messaging network in 2012, after the European Union adopted the necessary legal measures, showed how a hub located in one jurisdiction could be used to deny a whole country’s banking system its normal connection to the world — the chokepoint.
The implication for a multinational is uncomfortable in two ways. The first is that the firm’s exposure to geopolitical risk depends on where the hubs it uses are located and whose law applies to them. A firm whose payments clear through one jurisdiction, whose data are stored with providers subject to another, and whose software updates arrive from a third has three sets of exposure to the coercive choices of three states, most of which have nothing to do with the firm.
The second is more uncomfortable still: the firm itself can be the hub. A cloud provider, a payment network, a telecommunications operator, a maker of widely used software — each is infrastructure that its home state can watch through or weaponise, and that rival states therefore have reason to treat as a target, to exclude, or to replace with a domestic alternative. A firm in that position is not a bystander to geopolitical competition. It is part of the terrain. This is the bridge from this session to sanctions in Session 10, where the chokepoint becomes a legal instrument, and to space in Session 11, where the hubs are in orbit.

title: 8  Cyber Geopolitics: Restraint, Rivals and Weaponised Networks
text:
8.6 Attribution: evidence about evidence
Every dataset of state cyber operations rests on an act of attribution. Somebody has to say who did it. And attribution in cyberspace has four properties that make it unlike the identification of the attacker in almost any other kind of conflict event.

Attribution — the identification of the actor responsible for a cyber operation, at three levels: the machines used, the individuals or groups who operated them, and the state, if any, that directed or sponsored them. Public attribution is the decision to announce the third.

It is slow. Forensic analysis takes weeks or months; public attribution by governments often comes a year or more after the event. It is probabilistic. Technical indicators — the code, the infrastructure, the working hours of the operators, the language settings left in a file — can be faked, borrowed or reused, and a careful operator plants false ones. It is political. Governments decide when to attribute publicly, to whom, and with how much of their evidence, and they decide in the light of their relations with the accused state and their wish to protect their own sources. And it is selective. What is attributed publicly is what someone wanted known.
Rid and Buchanan put the point sharply: attribution is what states make of it (Rid and Buchanan 2015). It is not a technical fact waiting to be discovered but a judgement, assembled from technical, operational and strategic evidence, and communicated for a purpose. Lindsay offered a partial corrective: for the most consequential operations the set of capable actors is small, and the attribution problem is therefore less severe than it is for routine intrusions — which is one reason deterrence of major attacks remains possible (Lindsay 2015). Both views lead to the same conclusion about data.
An event dataset of cyber operations is a record of public attributions, not a record of operations. That sentence is the most important caveat of the practice round. It has predictable consequences for what the data show. States that attribute publicly — mostly Western democracies, with active security services and a free press — appear more often as victims than states that do not. Operations by allies against each other are rarely attributed in public and are therefore nearly invisible. Operations that succeeded in remaining undetected are, by definition, absent. A dyad with no incidents in the data may be a dyad with no operations, or a dyad in which neither side chose to say anything.

title: 8  Cyber Geopolitics: Restraint, Rivals and Weaponised Networks
text:
8.7 When the firm is collateral
The restraint thesis concerns the intentions of states. The cost to firms is driven by something else: the technical reach of what states release.

From the archive · NotPetya, June 2017
On 27 June 2017, the eve of a Ukrainian public holiday, malware spread through the update mechanism of a Ukrainian accounting program widely used by businesses operating in the country. It looked like ransomware, displaying a demand for payment, but its encryption could not be reversed: it was a wiper dressed as a ransom note. Within hours it had spread beyond Ukraine through the internal networks of any company that ran the software at a Ukrainian site. In February 2018 the governments of the United States and the United Kingdom, among others, publicly attributed the operation to the Russian military.
The apparent target was Ukraine. The victims included some of the largest firms in the world. The shipping company Maersk lost the use of systems across its global operations. The pharmaceutical company Merck and the food company Mondelez reported very large losses, as did logistics and manufacturing firms in many countries. None of them had a quarrel with anyone; they had a subsidiary, an office or a supplier in Ukraine, running a program everybody used (Greenberg 2019).
The aftermath carried a second lesson. When the companies claimed under their property insurance, insurers invoked the war exclusions that such policies had carried for generations, arguing that an operation by a state’s military was an act of war. The litigation lasted years and did not go uniformly the insurers’ way; in Merck’s case, New Jersey courts held that the traditional exclusion, written with armed conflict in mind, did not cover the attack. The market’s response was to write explicit exclusions for state-backed cyber operations into its contracts, which the Lloyd’s market required from 2023. The effect is that a firm’s cyber cover may now end exactly where geopolitics begins.

Three lessons follow for the firm. The first is that proximity in cyberspace is technical, not political. Firms were hit by NotPetya because they ran a piece of software in a country at war, not because anyone chose them. A firm’s exposure to a state’s cyber operations depends on its network architecture — what it connects to, what it updates from, what its subsidiaries can reach — as much as on its political profile.
The second is that insurance is not a backstop. A risk transfer that excludes the scenario the board is most worried about does not transfer that risk. The question to ask of a cyber policy is not whether it covers “cyber attacks” but what it says about operations attributed to states — and who decides the attribution.
The third is that the board owns it. Securities regulators increasingly require listed firms to disclose material cyber incidents and to describe how their boards oversee cyber risk. In the United States, rules adopted in 2023 require listed companies to report material incidents promptly and to describe their risk management and governance of cybersecurity in their annual reports (U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission 2023). The geopolitical part of cyber risk — the part that arises from the rivalry of states — is thereby made a matter of corporate governance, whatever the firm’s own view of it.

title: 8  Cyber Geopolitics: Restraint, Rivals and Weaponised Networks
section: 8.8 Digital sovereignty and the splintering network
text:
8.8 Digital sovereignty and the splintering network
Weaponised interdependence has a defensive mirror. States that fear the panopticon and the chokepoint of others respond by asserting control over the networks within their own jurisdiction: where data must be stored, who may access them, which foreign equipment may be installed, which vendors may operate. The vocabulary varies — digital sovereignty, data localisation, trusted vendors, technological self-reliance — and the effect is the same. The single global network on which the internationalisation of the 1990s assumed firms could operate is splintering into jurisdictions with different rules.
Three instruments matter most for a multinational. Data-localisation and transfer rules require that certain data be stored within a country or restrict their movement abroad; the invalidation by the Court of Justice of the European Union in 2020 of the framework that governed transfers of personal data from the European Union to the United States showed how quickly a legal basis for a firm’s data architecture can disappear. Security reviews and vendor bans exclude foreign suppliers from critical networks; the restrictions imposed on Huawei’s telecommunications equipment by the United States and a number of its allies from 2019 onward forced operators to redesign and in some cases to strip out networks they had already built. Access laws give governments the power to compel firms under their jurisdiction to hand over data, including data stored abroad; the United States’ CLOUD Act of 2018 is the best-known example, and it sits awkwardly beside European data-protection law.
For the firm, these instruments generate three kinds of cost. Duplication: separate data centres or cloud regions per jurisdiction, separate supply chains for network equipment, separate compliance regimes. Conflicting obligations: one state’s law requires a disclosure that another’s forbids, and the firm must choose which to break. Vendor risk: a supplier banned in one market may be mandatory, or at least dominant, in another, so that a single global architecture becomes impossible. None of these costs arises from a cyber operation. All of them arise from the geopolitics of cyberspace.
crumbs: 8  Cyber Geopolitics: Restraint, Rivals and Weaponised Networks

title: 8  Cyber Geopolitics: Restraint, Rivals and Weaponised Networks
section: 8.9 Where cyber risk sits in the firm
text:
8.9 Where cyber risk sits in the firm
The five channels through which geopolitical risk reaches a multinational help locate cyber risk precisely. It runs most obviously through data and operations: the operation that halts production, the localisation rule that forces a redesign. It runs through assets and people, when intellectual property is stolen or staff in a jurisdiction are compelled to provide access. It runs through finance, when insurers exclude state-backed operations and when payment hubs become chokepoints. It runs through inputs, when a vendor is banned or a software supply chain is compromised — NotPetya travelled through a software update. And it runs through market access, when a firm is excluded from a market as a security risk, or when its home state’s use of the firm as a hub makes it unwelcome abroad.
Inside the firm, the risk is distributed across several actors, and the distribution is part of the problem. The board sets risk appetite and oversees disclosure; its distinctive question is which state actors would want our data or our downtime, and why? The chief information security officer turns threat intelligence into controls and owns incident response, but typically reports through a technology function with limited geopolitical analysis. The chief risk officer is the natural integrator of cyber risk with country, sanctions and supply-chain risk — the view the team project takes. The insurer prices the risk and, increasingly, draws the line at state-backed operations. And regulators impose disclosure, localisation and vendor rules from outside. A firm in which each of these actors holds a piece of the picture and nobody holds the whole has a decision architecture designed for crime and espionage, not for geopolitics.
What changes on Monday, for a firm with a plant in a country that sits in one of the densest cells of the rivalry matrix? Not, in the first instance, its technology. The first change is to the map: an inventory of which systems at that site connect to which systems elsewhere, which software is updated from which vendors, and which data cross which borders — because it is along those connections that an operation aimed at a government travels into a firm. The second is to segmentation: a subsidiary in a contested jurisdiction whose network can reach the group’s core systems is a bridge for anyone who compromises it, and the cheapest geopolitical control a firm can buy is often a wall between the two. The third is to contracts: what the insurance policy says about operations attributed to states, what the cloud provider’s terms say about government access in each jurisdiction, and what suppliers have agreed about notifying the firm when they are compromised. The fourth is to governance: who in the firm is responsible for asking, before an investment rather than after an incident, which states would want the firm’s data or its downtime. None of these is a technical fix. All of them follow from treating cyber risk as a geopolitical exposure rather than an IT problem.

title: 8  Cyber Geopolitics: Restraint, Rivals and Weaponised Networks
text:
8.10 From concept to data
The replication target is the descriptive picture at the heart of Valeriano and Maness’s book: incidents by year, by method and by severity, and the matrix of who targets whom. Rebuilding it from DCID version 2.0 is mostly a matter of reading the codebook carefully, and the codebook repays the reading because it is where the concepts of this chapter become columns.
The unit is one incident between an initiating state and a target state within a rival dyad. The dyad’s two states are recorded as names, ordered by their Correlates of War codes, so that the first state of the pair is not the initiator; the initiator is recorded separately, as a code, and the target is whichever state of the dyad did not initiate. The method is coded on a scale that runs from vandalism through denial of service and network intrusion to network infiltration, with sub-codes for kinds of malicious software. Severity is coded on a scale the codebook defines from 0 to 10, of which the released file uses only the values 0 to 6 — a discrepancy worth logging and, if the codebook’s scale applies, consistent with restraint. The type of target distinguishes private and non-state targets from governmental ones, civilian and military, and the objective distinguishes disruption, short- and long-term espionage and degradation. The September 2022 release contains 433 incidents with start dates from September 2000 to January 2021.
Two properties of the data follow directly from the arguments above. The first is that the population is rival dyads. A cell of the initiator × target matrix that is empty does not mean “no cyber conflict”; it means “no rivalry in the data”, because pairs of states that are not coded as rivals never enter. The second is that the incidents are public attributions. The matrix is therefore a picture of who has been publicly accused of operating against whom — itself a geopolitical artefact, shaped by which governments attribute and when.
The comparison dataset, the European Repository of Cyber Incidents, makes both properties visible (Zettl-Schabath et al. 2025). It records incidents with state and non-state initiators, including criminal, hacktivist and unattributed operations, and in its version 1.3 it contains 3,414 incidents with start dates from 2000 to 2024 — several times the size of DCID. Restricting it to incidents attributed to state or state-affiliated actors leaves 1,014; restricting it to states alone leaves 329. The gap between those numbers, and between all of them and DCID’s 433, is a measure of how much the answer to “how much cyber conflict is there?” depends on the definition of the population and of attribution.

title: 8  Cyber Geopolitics: Restraint, Rivals and Weaponised Networks
section: 8.11 A short review of the literature
text:
8.11 A short review of the literature

The debate over whether cyberspace is a domain of war was framed in the early 2010s. Rid (2012) and Rid (2013) argued that cyber war had not taken place and would not, reclassifying cyber operations as sabotage, espionage and subversion; Gartzke (2013) argued from the logic of force that cyber operations would complement rather than replace conventional power; Kello (2013) and Kello (2017) argued, against both, that the cyber revolution unsettled the conceptual foundations of international relations. The legal question of how existing international law applies to cyber operations is set out in Schmitt (2013).
Systematic evidence arrived with Valeriano and Maness (2015), whose dataset of incidents between rival states supported a thesis of restraint and regional rivalry. The dataset has been extended through successive releases, of which Maness et al. (2022) is the current public version; Maness and Valeriano (2016) examine whether cyber incidents shift the broader conflict and cooperation between rivals, and Valeriano, Jensen, and Maness (2018) develop the argument that cyber operations are weak instruments of coercion. Kostyuk and Zhukov (2019) tested cyber operations in the war in eastern Ukraine against battlefield events and found little effect. Buchanan (2017) sets out the cybersecurity dilemma created by intrusions that are defensive in purpose and threatening in appearance.
On attribution, Rid and Buchanan (2015) treat it as a political judgement assembled from technical and strategic evidence, and Lindsay (2015) argues that its difficulty is overstated for consequential operations. On the economic architecture of coercion, Farrell and Newman (2019) is the foundational statement of weaponised interdependence, with its panopticon and chokepoint effects. Wider datasets that include non-state actors, such as Zettl-Schabath et al. (2025), now allow the rival-dyad picture to be set against the full record of attributed incidents, and the firm’s experience of state operations is documented most vividly in Greenberg (2019).
crumbs: 8  Cyber Geopolitics: Restraint, Rivals and Weaponised Networks

title: 8  Cyber Geopolitics: Restraint, Rivals and Weaponised Networks
section: 8.12 What the matrix will not tell the firm
text:
8.12 What the matrix will not tell the firm
The practice round rebuilds the incident picture and the initiator × target matrix, and then sets them against a wider dataset. The dashboard that results is informative. It shows that cyber conflict between rivals concentrates in a few dyads, that most incidents are of low severity, and that the methods have shifted over two decades. It is tempting to read it as a map of where a multinational’s cyber risk lies. It is not, and the reasons are the arguments of this chapter.
The matrix does not license a firm to conclude that it is safe in a country whose cells are empty. An empty cell means no publicly attributed incident between rivals; it says nothing about operations that were never attributed, about operations between states that are not coded as rivals, or about criminal groups, which account for much of the cyber harm firms actually suffer. Nor does a dense cell tell a firm that it is a target. The incidents in that cell were aimed mostly at governments, and the firm’s exposure to them depends on whether it is technically in the path — whether it runs software, holds data or provides infrastructure that an operation against the government might traverse. NotPetya would have appeared in the data as one incident in one dyad; its cost fell on firms in dozens of countries.
Nor does the evidence for restraint license complacency. It is a pattern in state behaviour to 2020, measured on a scale of harm between states. It does not bound the commercial cost of a low-severity operation, and it does not tell a firm what has happened since a large-scale war began in Europe. The question to carry into the practice round is the one the dashboard cannot answer by itself: given where interstate cyber conflict concentrates, which of the firm’s networks, suppliers and hubs lie in its path — and what has the firm agreed with its insurer about the operations that its government will one day attribute to a state?

title: 9  Economic Diplomacy Redefined: Two-Level Games, Embassies and the Firm
text:
9.1 From serving firms to screening them
For most of the period covered by Session 02 — the decades in which the liberal economic order was built out and then globalised — economic diplomacy had a settled meaning and a settled direction. Diplomats negotiated trade agreements, opened markets, promoted exports and courted investors. Trade commissioners in embassies found distributors for small exporters; ministers led delegations of chief executives on state visits; export credit agencies insured contracts that private insurers would not touch. The state served the firm, and the firm’s success abroad was counted as the state’s success.
That meaning has not disappeared, but it has been joined by others, and the direction of travel has partly reversed. The same governments that promote their firms abroad now screen foreign firms at home, restrict what their own firms may sell and to whom, and draw companies into public quarrels conducted on social media. A multinational today is still the beneficiary of economic diplomacy. It is also, increasingly, its object and its instrument — and sometimes a diplomat in its own right.
Three shifts have redefined the field. The first is securitisation: trade, investment and technology are now treated as matters of national security, so that a firm faces screening, export controls and “trusted vendor” rules not only from rival states but from its own side. The second is the move from promotion to coercion: the networks that were built to promote exports — financial messaging, payment systems, technology supply chains — are the same networks that states now use to deny access, as Session 08’s chokepoints showed and Session 10’s sanctions will show in detail. Home- state support can become home-state constraint overnight. The third is digitalisation: diplomacy is increasingly conducted in public, on social media, addressed to domestic and foreign audiences at once, and firms are pulled into it — through boycotts, hashtags and official denunciations — without having chosen to be.
This chapter takes the redefinition in three steps. It begins with the theory that best captures how international bargaining is shaped by domestic politics, Robert Putnam’s two-level game, and with the argument of Corneliu Bjola and Ilan Manor that digital diplomacy has changed how that game is played. It then turns to the empirical question at the heart of the replication: whether the most traditional instrument of commercial diplomacy, the embassy, actually promotes exports, as Andrew Rose found. Finally it turns to the relationship between states and firms directly — bargaining, screening and the choice a firm faces about when to lean on its home state.

title: 9  Economic Diplomacy Redefined: Two-Level Games, Embassies and the Firm
text:
Economic diplomacy — the use of the instruments of foreign policy for economic ends, and of economic instruments for foreign-policy ends. The first covers trade negotiation, export and investment promotion; the second covers sanctions, export controls, aid and investment screening used to pursue security or political goals.


Commercial diplomacy — the part of economic diplomacy that serves particular firms and sectors: trade commissioners, market intelligence, introductions, advocacy in disputes, trade missions, export credit and investment promotion. Its unit of account is the firm, not the economy.

title: 9  Economic Diplomacy Redefined: Two-Level Games, Embassies and the Firm
text:
9.2 Two boards at once
Putnam’s article begins from a frustration with theories of international relations that treated the state as a unitary actor, and with theories of domestic politics that ignored the international environment (Putnam 1988). His alternative is to model an international negotiation as two games played simultaneously.
At Level I, negotiators representing their governments bargain with each other to reach a tentative agreement. At Level II, each negotiator’s domestic constituencies — legislatures, parties, interest groups, bureaucracies, public opinion — decide whether to ratify it. Ratification need not be formal; any domestic process that can kill an agreement counts. An agreement survives only if it is acceptable at both levels, on both sides.

Win-set — for a given Level II constituency, the set of possible Level I agreements that it would ratify. An agreement is possible only where the two sides’ win-sets overlap. The size of each win-set depends on the distribution of power and preferences at home, on the domestic institutions that govern ratification, and on the strategies of the negotiators themselves.

Three lessons follow, and each has a direct application to firms.
The first is that larger win-sets make agreement more likely. If many possible deals would be ratified at home, the negotiators have more room to find one that the other side can also accept. But a large win-set also leaves a negotiator open to being pushed: the other side knows that concessions can be extracted without endangering ratification.
The second, and the most counter-intuitive, is that a small win-set can be a bargaining asset. A negotiator who can say, credibly, “my parliament will never accept that” has a reason to refuse that the other side cannot argue away. Thomas Schelling had made a version of this point about the power of binding oneself; Putnam located the binding in domestic politics. The credibility matters. A constraint that is invented for bargaining purposes is a bluff, and bluffs can be called.
The third is that negotiators play both boards at once. A skilled negotiator does not simply report the constraints of Level II; he or she works to shape them — building support at home for a deal that is coming, and reaching across to the other side’s Level II to make its ratification easier. Putnam called the latter “reverberation”: a move at Level I that changes the balance of opinion in the other country’s domestic politics.
Putnam’s framework also explains two features of international agreements that otherwise look irrational. The first is involuntary defection: an agreement that a negotiator sincerely accepted fails at Level II because the domestic coalition behind it collapses. The second is the role of side-payments and issue linkage: a negotiator who cannot win ratification on the merits of a deal can enlarge the win-set by compensating the losers at home, or by linking the deal to a concession on another issue that brings a new constituency into the coalition. Both have a direct bearing on firms. The firms and sectors that stand to lose from an agreement are the ones a government must compensate or overrule; the firms that stand to gain are the ones it mobilises. And the domestic institutions that govern ratification — a legislature’s voting rules, the role of sub-national governments, the timing of elections — determine how large the win-set can be, which is why a firm’s analysis of a negotiation that affects it should begin with the other side’s ratification process rather than with the negotiators’ public statements.

9.2.1 Where the multinational sits
Draw the two-level game on a board — two negotiators facing each other at Level I, each standing on a circle of domestic constituencies at Level II — and ask where a multinational belongs. The answer is that it belongs in several circles at once. At home, an export-oriented firm or industry is one of the constituencies whose support enlarges the win-set for a trade agreement; firms lobby, testify and fund campaigns, and governments count their support before signing. Abroad, the same firm’s subsidiaries, plants and employees are part of the other country’s Level II, where they may be assets (a large employer can argue for an agreement locally) or hostages (a visible foreign firm is a convenient target for retaliation if negotiations go badly).
The double position changes what a firm should expect from negotiations that concern it. A firm whose home government is negotiating with a host government on its behalf is not a spectator. It is part of the domestic politics that determine what its own negotiator can accept, and part of the foreign domestic politics that determine what the other side can accept. The question it must ask is which of its positions — lobbyist at home, employer abroad, symbol of its home country — the negotiators will use, and whether it can control that use.
The renegotiation of the North American Free Trade Agreement between 2017 and 2018 shows the game at work, with firms on every board. The United States imposed tariffs on Canadian and Mexican steel and aluminium in June 2018, on national-security grounds, while the negotiation was under way — a Level I move aimed squarely at the other sides’ Level II, where steel and aluminium producers and their workers would press their governments to settle. Canada’s system of supply management in dairy was a constraint at its own Level II, defended by a well-organised domestic constituency, and the eventual agreement opened only a limited part of the dairy market. Automobile manufacturers, whose supply chains crossed all three borders many times, were Level II actors in all three countries at once, and the new rules of origin for vehicles were written with their production networks in view. For each firm involved, the question was not only what the agreement would say but which domestic coalition in which country would decide whether there was an agreement at all.

title: 9  Economic Diplomacy Redefined: Two-Level Games, Embassies and the Firm
text:
9.3 The two-level game goes digital
Putnam wrote in 1988, about a world in which Level II was reached mainly through legislatures, interest groups and the press. Bjola and Manor revisit his model three decades later through the negotiations over Iran’s nuclear programme, which culminated in the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action of July 2015 (Bjola and Manor 2018). Their argument is that digital diplomacy — ministries, embassies and leaders communicating directly with publics on social media — gives negotiators a new instrument for acting on Level II, both their own and the other side’s.
The mechanics are straightforward. Before social media, a negotiator who wanted to build domestic support for a deal worked through intermediaries: parliamentary allies, friendly editors, interest groups. A negotiator who wanted to reach the other side’s public had few channels at all. Digital platforms remove the intermediaries. Foreign ministers and their staff can address their own public directly, framing the negotiation as it happens, and can address the other side’s public in its own language, bypassing its government. In the Iran negotiations, Bjola and Manor show, governments used these channels to shape how the negotiation was perceived at home and abroad, attempting to widen the win-sets on which ratification depended while the bargaining was still going on.
Two implications matter for multinationals. The first is speed. Domestic opinion now moves within the negotiation rather than after it, so that the outcome a firm plans around can change faster, and for reasons visible to anyone who follows the right accounts. The second is exposure. A firm’s brand can be pulled into a digital campaign by either government — praised as a model of cooperation, denounced as a symbol of the other side, or made the subject of a boycott that a ministry amplifies. Neither role is chosen by the firm.
The Iran agreement also illustrates the fragility of win-sets over time, which is the deeper lesson for planning. The agreement was concluded and ratified in the sense Putnam meant; it then lost its domestic support in one of the countries that had made it. The United States withdrew in 2018 and reimposed sanctions, including sanctions aimed at foreign firms that continued to do business with Iran. European companies that had re-entered the Iranian market after 2015 found that the domestic politics of a third country — the United States — determined whether they could stay. The two-level game, for a multinational, is played on more boards than two.

title: 9  Economic Diplomacy Redefined: Two-Level Games, Embassies and the Firm
text:
9.4 Do embassies sell?
The most traditional instrument of commercial diplomacy is the diplomatic post itself: the embassy, high commission or consulate, with its commercial section, its trade commissioners and its network of contacts. Governments spend substantial sums maintaining these networks and justify part of the cost by their contribution to trade. Rose asked whether the justification holds (Rose 2007).
His design combined, in a single recent cross-section, data on the embassies and consulates that 22 large exporting countries maintain in some 200 destinations with their bilateral exports, using the framework that economists have used to explain bilateral trade since Jan Tinbergen first applied it in the 1960s (Tinbergen 1962).

Gravity model — the empirical relationship in which bilateral trade between two countries rises with their economic size and falls with the distance between them, by analogy with Newton’s law of gravitation. Modern versions add measures of trade costs — common language, shared borders, colonial ties, trade agreements — and controls for each country’s overall openness to trade with all partners.

The model’s empirical success is remarkable — few relationships in economics fit cross-country data as well — and its theoretical foundations were put on a firm footing by Anderson and van Wincoop, who showed that what matters is not only the trade cost between two partners but each partner’s trade costs with everyone else, which they called multilateral resistance (Anderson and Wincoop 2003). Head and Mayer’s survey is the practical guide to estimating it (Head and Mayer 2014). For Rose’s purposes the gravity model is a way of asking a precise question: holding constant the size of the partners and the distance between them, and the other standard determinants of trade, do countries export more to places where they keep more diplomatic posts?
His answer was yes. Exports are higher where a country keeps more posts, and the association survives the standard gravity controls. Bilateral exports rise by approximately six to ten per cent for each additional consulate abroad, and the effect varies by exporter and is non-linear: consulates have smaller effects than the creation of an embassy (Rose 2007). The size should be read off his tables, by exporter and type of post, rather than remembered from a summary.

title: 9  Economic Diplomacy Redefined: Two-Level Games, Embassies and the Firm
text:
9.5 Three objections
The replication tests the result against three objections. Each is a general problem in inferring the effect of a policy from a cross-section, and each will recur in the evaluation of sanctions in Session 10.

9.5.1 Reverse causality
Countries open posts where they already trade. A foreign ministry deciding where to open a new consulate looks, among other things, at where its exporters are active and where its nationals travel and invest. If posts follow trade, then a cross-section in which posts and trade go together tells us that ministries are sensible, not that embassies generate exports. The two explanations predict the same snapshot.
They predict different dynamics. If posts promote exports, then pairs of countries in which a post is opened should see faster subsequent growth in exports than comparable pairs in which it is not. If posts follow exports, then export growth should come first and the post should follow. Telling the two apart requires data over time, and even then requires that the timing of openings not be driven by anticipated growth — a ministry that opens a consulate because it expects a market to boom will produce a post that “precedes” growth without causing it. Rose took the objection seriously and argued that his evidence was consistent with posts having an effect, but a cross-section cannot settle the question. That is the catch of the replication, and its extension step is a first, rough attempt at the dynamic comparison.


9.5.2 Omitted variables
Large, rich and nearby partners receive more posts and more trade, for reasons that have nothing to do with each other. The gravity controls are designed to absorb exactly this, but a raw scatter of exports against posts does not include them. The replication’s simplest correction — dividing exports by the partner’s GDP — removes the most obvious confounder and shows how much of the raw relationship was simply size. Other confounders are harder: a shared language, a large diaspora, a history of colonial ties or a security alliance may raise both the number of posts and the volume of trade.


9.5.3 Measurement
A post is not a budget. A small consulate with two staff and a large embassy with a commercial section of fifty count the same in a tally of posts, and an honorary consulate run by a local businessman may count too. The type of post matters, which is why the replication separates embassies from consulates. The direction of the measurement problem is not obvious. Consulates are often placed in commercial cities precisely to serve trade; yet Rose found the creation of an embassy to matter more than an additional consulate, which may say as much about what an embassy signals as about what it does.


9.5.4 The zeros
There is a fourth problem, which the data file makes unavoidable. The Lowy Institute’s file lists posts that exist. A country with no post in a partner does not appear — the zero is missing, not zero — and must be constructed. Once constructed, the zeros create a second difficulty: the logarithm of zero is undefined, so on a chart with logarithmic axes the partners with no posts fall off the plot. Dropping them silently changes the sample in a way that is correlated with the outcome, because the partners with no posts are disproportionately the small and distant ones with little trade. The same problem in the trade variable — pairs of countries that do not trade at all — led Santos Silva and Tenreyro to argue that the standard practice of estimating gravity equations in logarithms is biased, and to propose an estimator that keeps the zeros in (Santos Silva and Tenreyro 2006). The lesson for a chart is simpler: say how many observations a log scale has removed, and show what the relationship looks like with and without them.

A trend line with a high R² and a tiny p-value does not show that embassies cause exports. It shows a strong association in a cross-section. The R² measures how closely the points cluster around the line; the p-value measures how surprising the slope would be if there were no association at all. Neither says anything about which way the causation runs, or whether a third variable drives both.

title: 9  Economic Diplomacy Redefined: Two-Level Games, Embassies and the Firm
section: 9.6 The rest of the toolbox, and what the evidence says
text:
9.6 The rest of the toolbox, and what the evidence says
Embassies are one instrument among several. The literature on the others is useful both for what it finds and for how it finds it, because each study faces the same objections as Rose.
State visits and trade missions. Nitsch examined the travel of the heads of state of France, Germany and the United States from 1948 to 2003 and found that state and official visits are associated with exports higher by about 8 to 10 per cent; when he turned to a difference-in-differences design to address reverse causality, the effect on export growth was strong but short-lived (Nitsch 2007). Head and Ries studied Canada’s trade missions, which during the 1990s took the prime minister abroad with large delegations of provincial premiers and business leaders. Their conclusion was sobering. Canada does trade more than normal with the countries to which it sent missions, but the missions do not seem to have caused the increase: in their preferred specification, with country-pair fixed effects, the effects are small, negative and mainly insignificant (Head and Ries 2010).

From the archive · Team Canada, 1994
In November 1994 the Canadian prime minister, Jean Chrétien, led a delegation to China that included most of the provincial premiers and hundreds of business representatives. The mission was branded “Team Canada”, and it became the model for a series of similar missions over the following years, to destinations in Asia, Latin America, Europe and elsewhere. Each mission announced a large total of contracts and agreements signed during the visit; according to the Canadian government, the missions generated tens of billions of dollars in new business deals (Head and Ries 2010).
The announced totals were the wrong evidence. Critics pointed out that many of the agreements were memoranda of understanding, that some were deals that had been negotiated before the trip and timed to be signed during it, and the missions were sent to markets that were already growing. Head and Ries’s later evaluation used the missions as a natural test of whether high-profile commercial diplomacy changes trade flows, and compared Canada’s trade with mission destinations before and after the missions against the trade it would otherwise have been expected to have. They found that the missions had small, negative and mainly insignificant effects.
The episode is a clean illustration of the reverse-causality objection to Rose. Governments direct their most visible commercial diplomacy at the markets they expect to matter — which are, very often, the markets that would have grown anyway. A ministry that evaluates its missions by the deals announced during them, or by the subsequent growth of trade with the destinations, will always conclude that the missions succeeded.

Export promotion agencies. Lederman, Olarreaga and Payton surveyed national export promotion agencies and found that, on average, their budgets are associated with higher exports, with diminishing returns as budgets grow and with considerable differences in effectiveness depending on how the agencies are organised (Lederman, Olarreaga, and Payton 2010). The body of evidence as a whole. Moons and van Bergeijk assembled 32 empirical studies published between 1986 and 2011 into a meta-analysis and found a positive and significant effect of economic diplomacy on trade and investment — with the exception of state visits — and reported effects that are sensitive to the design of the individual studies (Moons and Bergeijk 2017). The fair summary is that commercial diplomacy probably helps at the margin, that the size of its effect is hard to pin down, and that the most visible instruments are the most vulnerable to the selection problems that inflate naive estimates.

title: 9  Economic Diplomacy Redefined: Two-Level Games, Embassies and the Firm
text:
9.7 Triangular diplomacy
The two-level game puts firms inside the domestic politics of states. A second tradition puts them across the table. John Stopford and Susan Strange argued that the changing structure of the world economy had turned diplomacy into a triangle (Stopford, Strange, and Henley 1991; Strange 1992). Alongside the familiar state–state diplomacy of governments, there is state–firm diplomacy, in which governments bargain with multinationals over the terms of investment — where a plant will be built, what share of inputs will be sourced locally, what will be exported — and firm–firm diplomacy, in which companies form alliances, joint ventures and consortia that shape markets as surely as treaties do. Governments, on this account, compete for world market shares through the firms they attract, and firms compete partly by bargaining with governments.
The bargaining has a dynamic, and Raymond Vernon described it before Stopford and Strange formalised the triangle (Vernon 1971). Before an investment is made, the firm holds the cards: it can choose among countries, and each host must offer terms good enough to win. Once the investment is made — once the mine is dug, the plant built, the pipeline laid — the firm’s capital is sunk and cannot be moved. The host’s bargaining power rises and the firm’s falls. Terms that were agreed when the firm was mobile can be renegotiated when it is not.

Obsolescing bargain — the tendency for a multinational’s bargaining power over a host government to decline after its investment is sunk, so that the terms agreed at entry become vulnerable to renegotiation, higher taxation or, in the limit, expropriation. The bargain “obsolesces” because the conditions that made it acceptable to the host no longer hold.


From the archive · The nationalisation of Chilean copper, 1971
In the 1960s the large copper mines that dominated Chile’s exports were owned by two American companies, Anaconda and Kennecott. The terms on which they operated had been renegotiated more than once during the decade, in each case with the Chilean state taking a larger share — first through taxation, then through partial state ownership under the “Chileanisation” policy of President Eduardo Frei. In July 1971, under President Salvador Allende, the Chilean Congress unanimously approved a constitutional amendment nationalising the large copper mines. The compensation formula allowed the government to deduct “excess profits” earned in previous years, and the deductions largely eliminated what the companies would otherwise have been owed.
The episode is the textbook case of the obsolescing bargain, and it was a geopolitical event as much as a commercial one. The companies’ home government treated the nationalisation as a matter of foreign policy, and the dispute became entangled with the wider hostility of the United States to Allende’s government in the years before the coup of 1973. Kobrin’s study of expropriations across developing countries from 1960 to 1979 placed Chile’s in a wider wave, in which natural resources — where capital is most sunk — were prominent (Kobrin 1984). For a firm, the lesson has two halves: sunk capital weakens bargaining power over time, and a dispute over that capital can quickly stop being a dispute between a firm and a host and become one between two states.

title: 9  Economic Diplomacy Redefined: Two-Level Games, Embassies and the Firm
text:
9.8 Screening: diplomacy aimed at firms
The newest element of economic diplomacy reverses the direction of the oldest. Commercial diplomacy helps a state’s firms abroad; investment screening examines foreign firms at home, and blocks or conditions their acquisitions on grounds of national security.
The United States has had a screening body, the Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States (CFIUS), since the 1970s, but its reach and visibility have grown sharply. In 2006 the acquisition by Dubai Ports World of a British company that operated terminals at several American ports, approved under the existing procedures, provoked a political storm in Congress; the company agreed to divest the American operations, and the following year Congress tightened the law. A further reform in 2018 widened the committee’s jurisdiction to non-controlling investments in businesses involving critical technologies, critical infrastructure and sensitive personal data. The European Union adopted a framework regulation for the screening of foreign direct investment in 2019 (Regulation 2019/452), which created a mechanism for member states and the Commission to share information and comment on each other’s cases. Canada added a national-security review to the Investment Canada Act in 2009, and has since used it in a widening range of sectors.
The widening is the important part. Screening began as a defence matter — who may own a supplier of military equipment. It now reaches data, critical minerals, infrastructure, semiconductors and artificial intelligence, which is to say much of the modern economy. For a multinational this is geopolitical risk through the market access and assets channels at once: an acquisition can be blocked, a completed one unwound, and a firm’s ownership structure — who its shareholders are, where its parent is incorporated — becomes a determinant of what it may buy. It is also, in Putnam’s terms, a Level II phenomenon: screening decisions are made by bodies that answer to domestic politics, and they are subject to the same reverberation as any other part of a negotiation between states.

title: 9  Economic Diplomacy Redefined: Two-Level Games, Embassies and the Firm
section: 9.9 When to lean on the home state
text:
9.9 When to lean on the home state
Commercial diplomacy is not only promotion. When a firm’s investment is threatened by a host government — an expropriation, a cancelled licence, a discriminatory regulation — its home state’s embassy is one of the places it turns. Gertz, studying the commercial work of American embassies, showed that diplomats routinely intervene on behalf of their firms in disputes with host governments, and argued that commercial diplomacy is therefore in part an instrument of political-risk management: a way of raising the cost to a host of mistreating a foreign investor (Gertz 2018).
That protection has a price, and the price has risen with the redefinition this chapter describes. In a dispute that remains commercial, home-state backing helps: the host weighs the diplomatic cost of mistreatment against the gain. In a confrontation between states, being seen as an instrument of one of them can make the firm a target of the other. A firm that accepts its ambassador’s offer to raise its mining concession with a host president has gained an advocate and has also, in the host’s eyes, become part of its home state’s foreign policy. If relations between the two states deteriorate, that association will not be forgotten. Blackwill and Harris describe a world in which states use economic instruments systematically for geopolitical ends (Blackwill and Harris 2016); in such a world, the line between being protected by one’s home state and being used by it is thin.
Canada’s experience after December 2018 shows how quickly a firm can move from beneficiary to hostage. When Canadian authorities arrested a senior executive of Huawei in Vancouver at the request of the United States, China detained two Canadian citizens and, in March 2019, suspended the export permits of major Canadian canola exporters, citing quality concerns. The exporters had done nothing in the dispute; they were simply the most visible Canadian commercial interest in China that could be squeezed without large cost to China itself. Their home state could protest, and did, but it could not restore their market access without conceding on an issue that was not theirs. In Putnam’s terms, they had become instruments for acting on Canada’s Level II — a constituency whose losses were meant to raise the domestic cost of the government’s position.
The decision can be framed with the course’s five channels. Leaning on the home state may protect market access and assets in a dispute, but it may endanger market access in a rival’s market, inputs sourced from a rival, finance from banks that fear sanctions, and the safety of people posted in a country where the firm has become a symbol. And it may draw the firm into the data demands that come with being seen as part of a state’s infrastructure. The question is not whether a firm should ever accept help. It is whether the firm has thought about what the help will mean if relations between the two states change — and whether it is prepared to be, in the eyes of its host, its government’s instrument.

title: 9  Economic Diplomacy Redefined: Two-Level Games, Embassies and the Firm
text:
9.10 From concept to data
The replication asks whether a country’s exports to a partner rise with the number of diplomatic posts it keeps there, using the most comprehensive public record of diplomatic networks. The Lowy Institute’s Global Diplomacy Index records the networks of 66 countries and territories — G20, OECD and Asian states, with data collected up to November 2023 — at the level of the individual post. Each row of its 2023 sheet is one post, about 7,700 in all, with the sending country, the host country, the city and the type of post, which distinguishes embassies and high commissions from consulates, permanent missions and other offices. Earlier sheets allow the 2023 networks to be compared with those of 2017, which covers 60 senders.
Three features of the data carry the arguments of this chapter into the replication. The first is that the file is at the wrong level: the gravity question is about pairs of countries, and the file is about posts. Turning posts into a count per pair is a reduction in Krippendorff’s sense, and like every reduction it discards information — the city, the type of post — that the analysis may later need. The second is the missing zeros. The pairs in which a country keeps no post do not appear, and must be built from the list of partners in the trade data; without them, the analysis can only compare partners with one post against partners with several, which is not Rose’s question. The third is the exports themselves, taken from the IMF’s bilateral trade statistics as reported by the exporter, and scaled in one variant by the partner’s GDP — the simplest available correction for the most obvious omitted variable.
The type of post deserves a moment of its own. Embassies and high commissions are the standard bilateral posts; consulates and consulates-general are usually in commercial or populous cities other than the capital, and are the posts most directly concerned with trade and with citizens abroad. Permanent missions are a different thing altogether: a mission to the United Nations in New York or Geneva, or to an international organisation elsewhere, is located in the host country but is accredited to the organisation, not to the host. Counting it as a bilateral post would credit Switzerland or the United States with diplomatic attention that is really directed at multilateral bodies. Deciding which types to count is a measurement decision of exactly the kind Session 07 asked to be made explicitly.
Two further features are worth knowing before the first chart is drawn. The Lowy file identifies countries by name only, with inconsistent spellings, and the trade and GDP data use codes, so every join depends on a concordance built by hand. And a join done carelessly, on country fields that do not uniquely identify a pair, can multiply rows and inflate exports without any error message. Both are data problems; both, unnoticed, would change the slope of the trend line more than any of the substantive objections.

title: 9  Economic Diplomacy Redefined: Two-Level Games, Embassies and the Firm
section: 9.11 A short review of the literature
text:
9.11 A short review of the literature

The theory of how domestic politics shapes international bargaining is Putnam (1988), whose two-level game and win-set remain the standard vocabulary; Bjola and Manor (2018) extend it to digital diplomacy through the Iran nuclear negotiations. On the relationship between states and firms, Vernon (1971) introduced the dynamic later called the obsolescing bargain, Kobrin (1984) documented the wave of expropriations that gave it empirical content, and Stopford, Strange, and Henley (1991) and Strange (1992) recast diplomacy as a triangle of state–state, state–firm and firm–firm relations. Blackwill and Harris (2016) describe the return of geoeconomics — the systematic use of economic instruments for geopolitical ends — that has redefined the field.
The empirical evaluation of commercial diplomacy rests on the gravity model, introduced by Tinbergen (1962) and given its modern theoretical foundation by Anderson and Wincoop (2003); Head and Mayer (2014) is the practical guide and Santos Silva and Tenreyro (2006) the warning about logarithms and zeros. Rose (2007) is the central study of diplomatic posts and exports. Nitsch (2007) examines state visits, Head and Ries (2010) Canada’s trade missions, Lederman, Olarreaga, and Payton (2010) export promotion agencies, and Moons and Bergeijk (2017) synthesises the econometric evidence in a meta-analysis. Gertz (2018) shows commercial diplomacy at work in investment disputes, connecting the promotion of firms abroad to the management of political risk.

title: 9  Economic Diplomacy Redefined: Two-Level Games, Embassies and the Firm
section: 9.12 What the trend line will not tell the firm
text:
9.12 What the trend line will not tell the firm
The practice round produces a scatter of exports against diplomatic posts, on logarithmic axes, with a trend line and a model summary. It will almost certainly slope upwards, and the R² will be respectable. The temptation is to read it as Rose’s finding confirmed: posts promote exports.
The trend line does not license that conclusion, for a multinational or for a foreign ministry. It does not show that opening a post in a market will raise exports there, because posts are opened where exports are expected, and the snapshot cannot tell the two directions apart. It does not show that the relationship is about diplomacy at all until the size of the partner has been removed, and it may show something quite different once embassies and consulates are separated. And if the zeros have been dropped — silently, by a logarithmic axis — it does not show the relationship for the partners where the question is most interesting: the markets in which a country has no presence yet.
For a firm, the more useful reading is the reverse of the naive one. The density of a home state’s diplomatic network in a market is a measure of how much that state already cares about the market — a measure of the political attention a firm can expect when it needs help, and of the political attention it will attract when relations sour. The question to carry into the practice round is the one this chapter has framed: in the markets that matter to the team’s firm, is the firm the object of its home state’s diplomacy, its instrument, or its hostage — and what would change that answer?

title: 9  Economic Diplomacy Redefined: Two-Level Games, Embassies and the Firm
text:
9.13 In the practice

The target. Rose (2007)’s central relationship: for each exporter–partner pair, exports against the number of diplomatic posts the exporter keeps in the partner — on log scales, with a trend line — rebuilt with the Lowy Global Diplomacy Index (2023 data) and IMF trade.

Work in your project teams. Everyone builds their own workbook; the team hands in one slide.


9.13.1 1 · Collect — 15 min
In data/raw/ (see ../data/README.md):

DataDownload.xlsx — Lowy Global Diplomacy Index;
IMF IMTS — exports of goods, FOB, US$, 2023, for Canada and at least four other Lowy countries × all partners;
WDI NY.GDP.MKTP.CD — GDP, current US$.

Provenance log — one line per file, including which side of the trade flow you used (exporter- reported exports) and the IMF indicator name exactly as shown.



9.13.2 2 · Prepare — 25 min
This is the hard part today. Take your time.

Lowy. Connect to DataDownload.xlsx, sheet 2023. The columns for sending country, host country and post type are COUNTRY, POST COUNTRY and TYPE OF POST. Filter out posts that are not bilateral: TYPE OF POST = Permanent Mission (missions to the UN, EU, OECD…). Look at what Other holds (representative and trade offices, e.g. in Taipei) and log your choice.
IMF. Add the IMF file as a second table on the canvas. Keep only the five exporters and the year 2023; drop aggregate partners (“World”, regional totals — codes starting with G or TX). Rename OBS_VALUE → Exports.
Concordance. Lowy has country names only; the IMF file has ISO3 codes (COUNTRY, COUNTERPART_COUNTRY). Make a small sheet name → ISO3 for the Lowy COUNTRY and POST COUNTRY names (watch the typos listed in the data README) and add ISO3 to Lowy.
Relate, don’t join. Drag the IMF table first, then the Lowy table, and create a relationship on exporter ISO3 = sending ISO3 and partner ISO3 = host ISO3. A relationship keeps the export totals at their own grain; a plain join would repeat each export value once per post and inflate it.
Build the zeros. Calculated field Posts:
ZN(COUNT([POST CITY]))
(POST CITY is never empty in the 2023 sheet). Partners with exports but no post now get 0.
Make logging possible. Calculated field Posts + 1 = [Posts] + 1. Write this decision in the log: it is the same compromise most gravity papers make, and it has consequences.
Exports per partner GDP. Add WDI GDP (relationship on partner ISO3, year 2023) and create Exports / partner GDP (‰) = SUM([Exports]) / SUM([GDP]) * 1000.




9.13.3 3 · Replicate — 20 min

9.13.3.1 Sheet 1 · “More posts, more exports”

Posts + 1 → Columns (as a measure; aggregation SUM at the dyad level).
Exports → Rows.
Exporter ISO3 and partner ISO3 → Detail — one mark per pair.
Exporter → Colour.
Right-click each axis → Edit Axis → Logarithmic.
Analytics → Trend Line → Linear. Right-click the line → Describe Trend Model. Note the slope, R² and p-value (one line per exporter if colour splits them — try both ways).
Title states the finding; caption cites Lowy (2024 edition, 2023 data) and IMF IMTS, with access dates.





9.13.4 4 · Compare and break — 20 min

Differ. Rose used an earlier period and a different set of exporters. Is your slope steeper or flatter than the relationship he reports? Name one reason.
Break: size. Replace Exports by Exports / partner GDP (‰). What happens to the slope and the R²? What did the raw chart owe to the sheer size of partners?
Break: type of post. Filter TYPE OF POST to Embassy / High Commission only, then to Consulate / Consulate-General only. Which carries the relationship? Does that match Rose?
Break: the zeros. Exclude partners with Posts = 0. How much does the trend line move? Why should a careful analyst never drop them silently?
Extend — reverse causality (fast teams). Add the Lowy 2017 sheet and IMF exports for

For each pair, compute the change in posts and the growth of exports 2017→2023. Do pairs that gained posts show faster export growth — or did posts open where exports had already grown? What would you need to tell the two apart?





9.13.5 5 · The catch — 10 min








Original
Ours
The catch




Rose’s posts–exports relationship
Your Sheet 1
One sentence: what this trend line does not license a multinational — or a foreign ministry — to conclude



A member drawn at random presents in two minutes.



9.13.6 Hand in
On ZoneCours before leaving: .twbx and provenance log, including your concordance fixes. Formative; counts towards participation.
The one rule: your log records at least one place where the data disagreed with the paper.



9.13.7 What loses credit

A join that inflated exports, unnoticed (check one pair’s total against the IMF file)
Zeros dropped without saying so
“R² = 0.6, so embassies explain 60% of exports” — they explain nothing; they co-vary
Unmatched countries silently missing from the chart

title: 10  Economic Sanctions: Do They Work, and Whom Do They Hit?
text:
10.1 The instrument of first resort
When a government wants to do something about a foreign state’s behaviour and is not prepared to go to war over it, the menu is short. It can protest, which costs nothing and changes nothing. It can withdraw an ambassador, which is visible and mostly symbolic. Or it can impose economic sanctions: restrict what its firms and banks may sell to, buy from, lend to or invest in the offending state, its government, its companies or its leading citizens. Over the last three decades the third option has moved from the end of the menu to the top. Sanctions are now what governments reach for first, in response to invasions and coups, nuclear programmes and election interference, human-rights abuses and cyberattacks. The Global Sanctions Data Base, whose descriptive picture the practice round rebuilds, documents both the rise in the number of active cases since the end of the Cold War and the change in what those cases are made of (Felbermayr et al. 2020).
The session’s question is whether this instrument is an efficient mechanism for regulating geopolitical risk — a way of raising the cost of aggression without the cost of war — or a source of it. The two are not mutually exclusive, and the chapter argues that, for a multinational, the second matters more than the first. A firm does not need to know whether the sanctions on a given state will achieve their political goal. It needs to know whether they will cut it off from a customer, a supplier, a bank or an asset; how far the effective perimeter of the measures extends beyond their legal text; and what the target can do to it in return.
That definition contains the whole debate in compressed form. Its last clause lists four objectives, and the answer to “do sanctions work?” depends on which of them you hold the instrument to. A measure that fails to change a regime’s policy may still succeed in making its weapons programme slower and more expensive, or in telling allies and voters at home that something has been done. A large part of the disagreement in the literature, as we shall see, comes from asking the same question of cases that were never trying to do the same thing.
crumbs: 10  Economic Sanctions: Do They Work, and Whom Do They Hit?

title: 10  Economic Sanctions: Do They Work, and Whom Do They Hit?
text: Economic sanctions — restrictions on economic relations imposed by one or more senders on a target — a state, a government, a firm or an individual — in order to change its behaviour, weaken it, constrain what it can do, or signal disapproval. The instrument is the restriction; the objective is political.
crumbs: 10  Economic Sanctions: Do They Work, and Whom Do They Hit?

title: 10  Economic Sanctions: Do They Work, and Whom Do They Hit?
text:
10.2 A very old weapon
Economic coercion is older than the states that now practise it. Thucydides records the Megarian decree, by which Athens barred the merchants of Megara from the harbours of its empire, among the grievances that preceded the Peloponnesian War; Napoleon’s Continental System tried to defeat Britain by closing the continent to British trade, and was undone by smuggling and by the costs it imposed on France’s own allies. Both episodes contain, in miniature, the problems this chapter returns to: sanctions hurt the sender’s own merchants, they invite evasion through third parties, and their effect on the target’s political decisions is uncertain at best.
The modern idea — sanctions as an organised, collective alternative to war — dates from the League of Nations. Article 16 of its Covenant obliged members to sever trade and financial relations with any member that resorted to war in breach of its commitments. The idea was tested once, and the test is the founding case of the literature.

From the archive · The League of Nations and Italy, 1935
Italy invaded Ethiopia in October 1935. Within days the League’s Council found that Italy had resorted to war in breach of the Covenant, and the members agreed a package of measures that came into force in November: an arms embargo, a ban on loans and credits to the Italian government, a ban on imports of Italian goods, and an embargo on the export to Italy of a list of raw materials.
What was left off the list mattered more than what was on it. Oil was not embargoed; nor were coal and steel, and the Suez Canal, through which Italy supplied its army in East Africa, stayed open. The great powers that would have had to enforce a wider embargo feared driving Italy into Germany’s arms, and the United States, not a member, was outside the system. Italian forces took Addis Ababa in May 1936, and the League lifted the sanctions in July.
The lesson drawn at the time was that collective sanctions had failed. The lesson worth drawing now is subtler. The measures were designed by senders who wanted to be seen to act while protecting their own interests, and the gap between the announced objective — to stop a war — and the instrument actually deployed was visible to everyone, including the target. Every later debate about whether sanctions “work” is, in part, a debate about whether the measures studied were ever designed to.

The United Nations Charter, drafted a decade later, put the idea on a firmer legal footing: Article 41 allows the Security Council to decide on “measures not involving the use of armed force”, including the “complete or partial interruption of economic relations”, and makes them binding on all members. For most of the Cold War the veto kept the provision almost idle. The Council imposed mandatory sanctions on Southern Rhodesia after its unilateral declaration of independence in 1965 and an arms embargo on South Africa in 1977, and little else. Sanctions in this period were overwhelmingly unilateral, and overwhelmingly American. The end of the Cold War unblocked the Council, and the 1990s were later called the “sanctions decade”. The instrument has not looked back.
