title: 10  Economic Sanctions: Do They Work, and Whom Do They Hit?
section: 10.3 Four ways to describe a sanction
text:
10.3 Four ways to describe a sanction
Before anything can be counted it must be classified, and the classification already embeds a theory of what sanctions are for. The lecture uses four dimensions, and the GSDB codes three of them directly.
The sender may be one state acting alone, a group of states acting together — the European Union is the most important plurilateral sender, its measures adopted by unanimity in the Council — or the United Nations Security Council, whose decisions bind every member. The distinction matters to a firm because it determines how many jurisdictions it must satisfy and how much room there is for a competitor from a non-sending state to take its place.
The type describes the instrument: restrictions on trade (exports, imports, or both, partial or complete), on finance (loans, investment, payments, asset freezes), on travel, on arms, on military assistance, and a residual category. The GSDB records each as a separate indicator, so a single case can be of several types at once — which is why, in the practice round, the stacked count of cases by type exceeds the number of cases.
The scope distinguishes measures aimed at a whole economy from measures aimed at named persons, entities or sectors.

Comprehensive versus targeted sanctions — comprehensive sanctions restrict all, or nearly all, economic relations with a target country; targeted or “smart” sanctions restrict relations only with named individuals and entities (asset freezes, travel bans), with specific sectors (energy, finance, defence), or in specific goods (arms, dual-use items, luxury goods). The distinction is about who is meant to bear the cost.

The objective is what the sender says it wants. The GSDB distinguishes changing a policy, destabilising a regime, resolving a territorial conflict, preventing a war, ending one, fighting terrorism, protecting human rights and restoring or defending democracy. Many cases have more than one, and the stated objective is not always the real one. A sender that announces “policy change” may be content with “punishment”, and one that announces “democracy” may care more about signalling to its own electorate. Coders work from the public record, so the objective variable is a record of what senders said, not of what they wanted.
crumbs: 10  Economic Sanctions: Do They Work, and Whom Do They Hit?

title: 10  Economic Sanctions: Do They Work, and Whom Do They Hit?
text:
10.4 Do they work? Coding success
The modern empirical literature begins with one book in three editions. Gary Clyde Hufbauer and Jeffrey Schott, later joined by Kimberly Ann Elliott and Barbara Oegg, assembled every sanctions episode of the twentieth century they could document and asked of each a question that sounds simple: did it succeed (Hufbauer et al. 2007)?
Their answer to the problem of defining success has become the field’s reference point, so it is worth stating precisely. Each episode is scored on two components. The first is the policy result: how far the outcome the sender sought was actually achieved, on a scale from failure to success. The second is the contribution of sanctions: how far the sanctions, as opposed to other factors — military force, a change of government for unrelated reasons, a negotiation that would have happened anyway — contributed to that outcome. Each component is scored from 1 to 4, and the two are multiplied into a success score. A case counts as a success when the product reaches 9 or more: that is, when the outcome was at least partly achieved and sanctions made at least a modest contribution to it.

Sanctions success (Hufbauer et al.) — an episode in which the sender’s policy goal was at least partly achieved and sanctions made at least a modest contribution to that achievement, operationalised as a product of the two scores, each from 1 to 4, of 9 or more. Success is a joint judgement about an outcome and a cause.

On this definition, roughly a third of the episodes in the study count as at least partial successes. The rate varies systematically with the circumstances. Sanctions succeed more often when the goal is modest — the release of a prisoner rather than the overthrow of a regime — when the target is economically small and weak relative to the sender, when target and sender were previously on friendly terms and trade heavily, and when the measures are imposed quickly and decisively rather than ratcheted up slowly, giving the target time to adapt. They succeed less often when the goal is major, when the target is an adversary, and when the target can turn to other suppliers and buyers.
That last condition was formalised by Bryan Early as sanctions busting: third countries whose firms step into the trade the sanctions forbid, for profit or for strategic reasons, and so supply the target with the alternatives that make resistance affordable (Early 2015). It is the reason multilateral sanctions are not straightforwardly more effective than unilateral ones. The more senders there are, the fewer alternatives remain for the target, but the harder it is to agree on anything strong, and the more likely the package resembles the League’s of 1935.
The “about a third” figure has had a long public life. It appears in policy debates as a fact about the world: sanctions work a third of the time. It is nothing of the kind. It is a fact about one coding of one set of cases, produced by one team’s judgements on two four-point scales, and changing any of those three elements changes the number.
crumbs: 10  Economic Sanctions: Do They Work, and Whom Do They Hit?

title: 10  Economic Sanctions: Do They Work, and Whom Do They Hit?
section: 10.5 Pape’s audit, and why the debate never closed
text:
10.5 Pape’s audit, and why the debate never closed
The most consequential demonstration of this came from Robert Pape, who in 1997 went back through the cases Hufbauer and his colleagues had counted as successes in their second edition and asked whether each one survived scrutiny (Pape 1997). His conclusion was that most did not. In many of the claimed successes, he argued, the outcome had been achieved by the use or threat of military force rather than by economic pressure; in others the target had made no real concession, or the concession could not be attributed to sanctions at all. By his reckoning only five of the forty claimed successes held up, and he concluded that economic sanctions rarely achieve major political goals and should not be expected to.
Elliott replied that the glass was half full rather than empty (Elliott 1998). Sanctions, she argued, had never been claimed to be a substitute for force in pursuit of major goals, and judged against the modest goals for which they are typically used they did better than Pape allowed; moreover, their record had improved as they were used more often in concert, after the Cold War. Pape answered that sanctions still did not work (Pape 1998). The exchange has been taught ever since as a debate about effectiveness. It is better understood as a debate about coding: about what counts as a concession, how much a contribution must be, and what the counterfactual is.
The counterfactual problem is the deep one, and David Baldwin had set it out a decade earlier (Baldwin 1985). To say that sanctions failed is to say that some other instrument would have done better. If the alternative was war, a sanction that achieved nothing at little cost may still have been the better choice; if the alternative was diplomacy, a sanction that achieved a little at great cost may have been the worse one. Effectiveness, on Baldwin’s account, is always comparative and always relative to cost, and a success rate computed without reference to the alternatives answers a question no policymaker faces.
A second line of argument asks how sanctions are supposed to work, and finds the naive answer wanting. Johan Galtung, studying the sanctions on Rhodesia, described what he called the naive theory: economic pain causes political disintegration, which forces the government to comply (Galtung 1967). The Rhodesian evidence suggested the opposite. Pressure from outside produced a rally around the government, a reorganisation of the economy towards self-sufficiency, and a set of domestic winners — smugglers, import substitutes, those who controlled scarce foreign exchange — with an interest in the sanctions continuing. Jonathan Kirshner later generalised the point: sanctions work, when they work, by changing the relative power of groups within the target, and their effect therefore depends on who inside the target bears the cost and who profits from it (Kirshner 1997).

The lesson for an analyst. “Do sanctions work?” has no answer independent of how a case, an objective and a success are coded, and of what the comparison is. Every number in this debate is a coding decision. The practice round makes several of them — which objective counts when a case has several, whether ongoing cases enter the denominator — and each one moves the share judged successful.
crumbs: 10  Economic Sanctions: Do They Work, and Whom Do They Hit?

title: 10  Economic Sanctions: Do They Work, and Whom Do They Hit?
text:
10.6 The cases we never see
There is a deeper problem with any success rate computed from imposed sanctions, and it was put most clearly by Daniel Drezner. His first book began from a puzzle: states impose sanctions most often on their adversaries, yet adversaries are the targets least likely to concede, because they expect future conflict and fear that any concession will be exploited; allies concede more readily, but are sanctioned less often (Drezner 1999). The second step of the argument concerns the threat (Drezner 2003). If a target that would concede does so as soon as sanctions are threatened, the episode ends before any measure is imposed. The cases that reach imposition are disproportionately those in which the target had decided to resist.

Selection effect of threats — the bias that arises when sanctions most likely to succeed do so at the threat stage and are therefore never imposed. Samples of imposed sanctions over-represent hard cases, so imposed sanctions look less effective than the instrument is. The most significant effects of economic coercion may be the ones that never appear in a list of sanctions.

The implication for measurement is direct. A dataset that records only impositions cannot estimate the effectiveness of the instrument, because it has selected its cases on a variable correlated with the outcome. This is the reason the Threat and Imposition of Economic Sanctions dataset exists. T. Clifton Morgan, Navin Bapat and their colleagues recorded threats as well as impositions, first for 1971–2000 (Morgan, Bapat, and Krustev 2009) and then, in the version used in the practice round, for 1945–2005 (Morgan, Bapat, and Kobayashi 2014). In TIES a case begins with a threat or an imposition, whichever comes first, and the dataset records whether sanctions were in fact imposed. A substantial share of its cases never were.
The selection argument also cuts the other way, and an honest analyst should say so. Imposition is a costly signal of the sender’s seriousness, and some of its effects may come from the signal rather than from the economic pain. None of this can be read off a count of cases. It can only be argued, with evidence about each episode.

title: 10  Economic Sanctions: Do They Work, and Whom Do They Hit?
text:
10.7 From comprehensive to smart
The sanctions decade of the 1990s produced the instrument’s most damaging case, and that case changed how sanctions are designed.

From the archive · Iraq, 1990–2003
Four days after Iraq invaded Kuwait in August 1990, the Security Council adopted Resolution 661, imposing comprehensive sanctions: a ban on all trade with Iraq except medical supplies and, in humanitarian circumstances, foodstuffs. The war of 1991 expelled Iraq from Kuwait; the sanctions stayed, tied now to the disarmament of Iraq’s weapons programmes.
They stayed for more than a decade, and their humanitarian consequences became the central fact of the debate about them. Malnutrition, the collapse of water and health services, and a sharp rise in mortality were documented by UN agencies and independent researchers, although the size of the excess mortality and how much of it to attribute to sanctions rather than to war damage and the regime’s own choices were — and remain — contested. In 1995 the Council created the Oil-for-Food Programme (Resolution 986), allowing Iraq to sell oil under UN supervision to pay for food and medicine. The programme relieved the shortages and was in turn corrupted: the regime used surcharges and kickbacks from the firms that bought its oil and sold it goods, and the subsequent inquiry named companies from many countries.
The regime survived the sanctions intact. Those who bore their cost were the population and, through the programme’s scandals, the firms that had traded with the regime under UN licence.

The Iraqi experience made it difficult for senders to defend comprehensive sanctions on a whole population, and the response was the turn to targeted measures. In a series of intergovernmental processes around the turn of the century — at Interlaken on financial sanctions, at Bonn and Berlin on arms embargoes and travel bans, at Stockholm on implementation — governments, the UN Secretariat and experts worked out how to aim sanctions at those responsible: freeze the assets and ban the travel of named leaders and their financiers, embargo arms and the specific goods that sustain a war or a weapons programme, restrict specific sectors.
Targeted sanctions created problems of their own. Listing a person under UN or EU measures is an executive act with severe consequences for the person listed, and in the Kadi judgment of 2008 the European Court of Justice annulled the EU’s implementation of a UN listing because it did not respect the listed person’s rights of defence. Listing procedures, review mechanisms and an Ombudsperson for one of the UN regimes followed. For firms the lesson was that lists change, are litigated, and may be annulled — and that a listing in one jurisdiction may not exist in another.
Whether targeting works better is an empirical question with a mixed answer. The most comprehensive study of UN targeted sanctions distinguishes three purposes — to coerce a change in behaviour, to constrain the target’s ability to act, and to signal a norm — and finds that the measures do better at constraining and signalling than at coercing (Biersteker, Eckert, and Tourinho 2016). On humanitarian cost the evidence is clearer for the comprehensive kind: Dursun Peksen finds that sanctions are associated with a deterioration of the target government’s respect for physical-integrity rights, and that the effect is stronger for comprehensive measures (Peksen 2009). The targets of sanctions, in other words, tend to pass the cost down.

title: 10  Economic Sanctions: Do They Work, and Whom Do They Hit?
text:
10.8 The financial turn
The second change in the design of sanctions since 2000 has been the rise of financial measures, and it is the change that matters most to a multinational.
Henry Farrell and Abraham Newman explained it in a framework the course met in Session 08 (Farrell and Newman 2019). Global economic networks — payment systems, financial messaging, correspondent banking, the internet’s infrastructure — are not flat. They have hubs, and the hubs are disproportionately under the jurisdiction of a few states, above all the United States. A state with jurisdiction over a hub can exploit it in two ways: as a panopticon, using the information flowing through the hub to see what others are doing, and as a chokepoint, denying others access to the hub and therefore to the network. International dollar payments clear, in the end, through banks with access to the US financial system; banks around the world communicate payment instructions through SWIFT, a Belgian cooperative subject to European law. Cutting a bank off from either is a sanction of a different order from an embargo on its country’s exports.
This is why targeted does not mean contained. A financial sanction is aimed at named banks, but every firm that pays or is paid through those banks is affected, and the banks of third countries — which need access to the dollar system more than they need any single customer — will cut off a sanctioned client long before the law requires them to. Sanctions on banks, insurers and shippers propagate down every supply chain that depends on them. The measures of 2022 against Russia showed the reach of the instrument: the freezing of a large part of the Russian central bank’s foreign reserves, the disconnection of major Russian banks from SWIFT, and a price cap on Russian oil enforced not by blockade but through the Western insurers and shipping services the oil trade relied on.
crumbs: 10  Economic Sanctions: Do They Work, and Whom Do They Hit?

title: 10  Economic Sanctions: Do They Work, and Whom Do They Hit?
text:
10.9 The firm in the middle
Sanctions are aimed at states, governments and the people who run them. They are implemented by firms. Governments write the rules; banks, exporters, shippers and insurers decide, transaction by transaction, whether a given payment, shipment or contract falls within them, and bear severe penalties if they decide wrongly. The firm is therefore not a bystander to sanctions policy. It is its executor, and its executor of last resort.

10.9.1 Lists, ownership and the perimeter
Each sending jurisdiction maintains its own legal architecture. In the United States, sanctions programmes rest mostly on the International Emergency Economic Powers Act of 1977 and are administered by the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control, whose Specially Designated Nationals list is the most consulted list in global commerce. In the European Union, restrictive measures are adopted by Council decision under the Common Foreign and Security Policy and given effect by Council regulations that bind every person and firm in the Union. In Canada, they rest on the Special Economic Measures Act, the United Nations Act and the Justice for Victims of Corrupt Foreign Officials Act. The lists overlap but do not coincide, and a firm operating across jurisdictions must satisfy all of them.
The list is only the beginning of the perimeter. Under the US “50 percent rule”, an entity owned, directly or indirectly, 50 percent or more in aggregate by listed persons is itself treated as blocked, whether or not it appears on any list; EU guidance extends the restrictions to entities owned or controlled by listed persons, with control judged on a range of indicators. A firm must therefore screen not only its counterparties but their owners, and their owners’ owners, through chains of holding companies that may be designed to obscure them.

Compliance perimeter — the set of counterparties, transactions, goods and jurisdictions a firm must treat as restricted in order to comply with every sanctions regime that applies to it. It is wider than any list: it includes entities owned or controlled by listed persons, goods restricted by end use, and the jurisdictions whose rules reach the firm through its nationality, its currency, its banks or its inputs.



10.9.2 Secondary sanctions and blocking statutes
Primary sanctions bind the sender’s own nationals and transactions on its territory. Secondary sanctions go further: they threaten third-country firms with penalties — exclusion from the sender’s market, its financial system, or its government contracts — if they deal with the target, even where no person or transaction of the sender is involved.

Secondary sanctions — measures that penalise third-country persons for dealing with a sanctioned target, by restricting their own access to the sender’s market or financial system. They make a sender’s foreign policy binding on firms that are not its nationals, by forcing them to choose between the sender and the target.

The tension this creates between allies is old. When the United States legislated against foreign firms investing in Cuba, Iran and Libya in 1996, the European Union adopted a Blocking Statute forbidding EU firms to comply with the US measures. When the United States withdrew from the Iran nuclear agreement in 2018 and reimposed secondary sanctions, the EU updated the Statute. European firms nevertheless left Iran in large numbers. The choice a secondary sanction forces is not a legal one but a commercial one: the US market and the dollar are worth more to almost any multinational than the target’s market is, and no blocking statute changes that arithmetic. The case of BNP Paribas, which pleaded guilty in the United States in 2014 to processing transactions for sanctioned parties and paid a penalty without precedent at the time, settled the question for many compliance departments: dollar transactions with sanctioned parties anywhere in the world fall within US reach.


10.9.3 Overcompliance and de-risking
Penalties are severe, rules are complex, lists change without notice, and the cost of a mistake is asymmetric: a bank that refuses a lawful payment loses a fee, a bank that processes an unlawful one may lose its licence. The rational response is to go further than the law.

Overcompliance and de-risking — the withdrawal of firms, and above all banks, from whole countries, sectors or categories of client that the law does not close, because the expected cost of an error exceeds the revenue at stake. The effective scope of sanctions is set by compliance departments as much as by governments.

The evidence that this matters is now substantial. Matthieu Crozet and Julian Hinz, studying the sanctions on Russia after 2014 and the Russian counter-sanctions, find that the trade losses borne by the sending countries fell largely on products that were not embargoed at all — “friendly fire” that they attribute mainly to the financial measures and the uncertainty they created (Crozet and Hinz 2020). A firm selling unrestricted goods to an unrestricted customer may still be unable to get paid, insured or shipped. The question the lecture puts to the room captures it: if your compliance team tells you the new measures do not legally require you to exit, and your bank tells you it will no longer process your payments to that country, who has just set your sanctions policy?
crumbs: 10  Economic Sanctions: Do They Work, and Whom Do They Hit?

title: 10  Economic Sanctions: Do They Work, and Whom Do They Hit?
text:
10.10 Russia 2022: the exit decision
The full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 produced the largest and fastest expansion of sanctions against a major economy since the Second World War, and it confronted hundreds of Western multinationals with a decision most had never modelled: whether to leave a large market that the law, for many of them, did not require them to leave. Public pressure, employee pressure, the practical impossibility of making payments and moving goods, and the expectation of further measures pushed many to suspend, scale back or exit.
Exit turned out to be harder than announcing it. Russia’s countermeasures made the sale of a foreign-owned business subject to approval by a government commission, required sellers to accept a steep discount on the valuation, and added a payment to the state budget; buyers were frequently local managers or firms close to the state. In 2023 a presidential decree allowed the temporary state management of foreign-owned assets, and the Russian subsidiaries of Danone and Carlsberg were placed under it within weeks. The firms that waited lost the option of selling on their own terms.
The four options — stay, suspend, sell, walk away — each have a cost and a residual risk. McDonald’s sold its Russian restaurants to a local licensee, which reopened them under a new name. Renault sold its controlling stake in AvtoVAZ to a state entity for a symbolic rouble, keeping an option to buy it back within six years — a sale designed to preserve an option on a return. Others suspended operations and paid for idle assets while hoping the situation would change. Others stayed, citing obligations to employees and customers or the essential nature of their products, and accepted the reputational cost and the risk of further sanctions or of seizure.

The right answer depends on the firm, not on the country. Ask the room to choose for a consumer-goods firm and then for an energy firm, and the answers diverge: the first has brands, local staff and a domestic supply chain that a buyer can run; the second has assets that cannot be moved, partners that may be sanctioned, and a product the target state regards as strategic. Country-level exposure tells you that a decision must be taken. It does not tell you which one.
crumbs: 10  Economic Sanctions: Do They Work, and Whom Do They Hit?

title: 10  Economic Sanctions: Do They Work, and Whom Do They Hit?
section: 10.11 Through which channels sanctions reach the firm
text:
10.11 Through which channels sanctions reach the firm
The course organises the ways geopolitical risk reaches a multinational’s profit and loss account into five channels, and sanctions run through all of them.
Market access. Export bans and import bans close markets, either directly — the goods may not be sold — or indirectly, when customers are listed or owned by listed persons. Dual-use export controls, which increasingly operate alongside sanctions, close specific product lines to specific end users.
Inputs. A supplier that is sanctioned, or that sits in a sanctioned jurisdiction, can no longer be paid. Counter-sanctions and export restrictions imposed by the target close supply from the other side. The firm’s exposure here is often deeper in the supply chain than it can see.
Finance and payments. This is where financial sanctions bite first: the correspondent bank that will not process a payment, the letter of credit that cannot be confirmed, the insurer that will not cover a cargo. It is also the channel through which overcompliance operates.
Assets and people. Assets in a target country can be frozen by the sender if they are linked to listed persons, or seized, placed under temporary management, or sold only at a forced discount by the target in retaliation. Employees in the target country, and the firm’s obligations to them, are part of the exit calculation and part of its cost.
Data and operations. Software licences, cloud services, maintenance contracts and technical support may be restricted services in themselves; screening a customer base against changing lists is an operational burden; and a sanctioned partner on a shared platform can force the firm to cut off its access.
The lecture’s list of what a risk dashboard should track maps onto these channels. The firm’s own exposure — revenues, assets and suppliers in sanctioned or at-risk jurisdictions — is the starting point. The pipeline of threats and announced measures is the TIES lesson applied: the cases that matter most to a firm are the ones that have not yet been imposed. The propagation risk sits in the banks, insurers and logistics providers whose own exposure could cut the firm off. And the counter-measures the target can take against foreign firms on its soil are, as Russia showed, the risk that determines what an exit costs.

title: 10  Economic Sanctions: Do They Work, and Whom Do They Hit?
text:
10.12 From episodes to a dataset
The Global Sanctions Data Base was built to answer, at scale, questions that case studies cannot: how the use of sanctions has changed over time, what types and objectives dominate, and — joined to trade data — what sanctions do to trade flows (Felbermayr et al. 2020). Its unit is the case: a sanctions episode defined by its senders, its target, its start and end, its types and its objectives, with an outcome coded for each objective. Its producers have released it repeatedly, extending the period and revising earlier cases; the third release added the measures following the pandemic and the escalating sanctions on Russia (Syropoulos et al. 2024), and the practice round works with the fifth.
Turning episodes into a time series of “active cases” requires a decision about what being active means. An episode with a start year and an end year is active in every year in between, so the practice round expands each case into one row per active year, with a year scaffold and a range join. Three decisions are buried in that construction. Cases that have not ended must be given an end — and the distributed file gives ongoing cases an end year that is the last year of the data, which is not what its codebook says. A case of several types appears once in each type, so a stacked chart of types overstates the number of cases. And a case is a case whether it consists of a single listing or of a comprehensive embargo, so the number of active cases measures the frequency of the instrument’s use, not its intensity.
The outcome coding carries the success debate into the data. Each objective of each case receives an outcome — total success, partial success, a negotiated settlement, failure, or ongoing — and the share judged successful depends on which objective a multi-objective case is counted under and on whether the ongoing cases, which by definition have not succeeded yet, enter the denominator. These are not technical details. They are Hufbauer’s and Pape’s disagreement reproduced in two calculated fields.
TIES, set beside the GSDB, supplies what the GSDB cannot: the threats that were never imposed. The two datasets differ in their unit of observation, their period, their coding of senders and targets and their definition of an outcome, so they cannot be merged case by case. What they can do is be compared, year by year, to give an order of magnitude to the selection effect: how much of economic coercion happens before any measure is imposed.

title: 10  Economic Sanctions: Do They Work, and Whom Do They Hit?
section: 10.13 A short review of the literature
text:
10.13 A short review of the literature

The empirical study of sanctions begins with Hufbauer et al. (2007), whose three editions established the case list, the two-component coding of success and the “about a third” finding; Pape (1997) audited the claimed successes and found few that survived, Elliott (1998) replied, and Pape (1998) rejoined. Baldwin (1985) had already argued that effectiveness must be judged relative to the alternatives and their costs, which reframes the whole exchange. The mechanism literature runs from Galtung (1967), whose study of Rhodesia dismantled the “naive theory” that pain produces compliance, to Kirshner (1997), who located the effect of sanctions in the redistribution of power among groups within the target.
The strategic turn came with Drezner (1999), who explained why sanctions are imposed most on the adversaries least likely to concede, and Drezner (2003), who identified the selection effect of threats. The data response was TIES, which records threats as well as impositions (Morgan, Bapat, and Krustev 2009; Morgan, Bapat, and Kobayashi 2014). Early (2015) showed how third-country sanctions busters sustain targets, which helps explain why multilateral sanctions do not always outperform unilateral ones.
On design, Biersteker, Eckert, and Tourinho (2016) evaluate UN targeted sanctions against the purposes of coercing, constraining and signalling, and Peksen (2009) documents the human-rights cost of sanctions to the populations of target states. Farrell and Newman (2019) explain the rise of financial sanctions through the chokepoints of global networks. The GSDB (Felbermayr et al. 2020) and its later releases (Syropoulos et al. 2024) made it possible to study sanctions at the scale of trade data, and Crozet and Hinz (2020) used that kind of data to show that much of the trade cost of the Russia sanctions after 2014 fell on products that were not sanctioned at all — the quantitative trace of overcompliance.

title: 10  Economic Sanctions: Do They Work, and Whom Do They Hit?
section: 10.14 What the figure will not tell the firm
text:
10.14 What the figure will not tell the firm
The practice round rebuilds the GSDB’s descriptive picture: the number of active sanctions cases per year by type, and the distribution of outcomes by objective. It will show the rise of the instrument since the end of the Cold War and the changing mix of its types. It will also show the decisions underneath: the end year given to ongoing cases, the double counting of multi-type cases, the first-objective rule, the denominator of the success share.
The question to carry into the round is the one every round ends on: what does this figure not license a multinational to conclude? It does not license a conclusion about the firm’s exposure. A count of cases naming a country says how often senders have used the instrument against it, not how much of the firm’s revenue, supply or payments the measures touch; a single financial sanction on a country’s largest banks can matter more to a firm than a dozen travel bans. It does not license a conclusion about the perimeter, which is drawn by ownership rules, secondary sanctions and the firm’s own banks rather than by the list of cases. It does not license a conclusion about the pipeline, because the cases that would matter most next year are threats today, and the GSDB does not record threats. And the share of cases judged successful says nothing about whether a sanction will be lifted soon enough to make waiting the cheaper option.
The figure is the right place to start a sanctions view on a team dashboard, because it shows where the instrument has been used and how its use has changed. It is the wrong place to stop. The firm’s own sanctions risk lives in its footprint, its counterparties’ owners, its banks, and the countermeasures of the states it operates in — and none of those is in the case list.

10.15 In the practice

The target. The Global Sanctions Data Base’s descriptive picture (Felbermayr et al., 2020): active sanctions cases per year, by type, from 1950 to today, and the distribution of outcomes by objective — rebuilt from Release 5, then confronted with the threats in TIES.

Work in your project teams. The last 20 minutes are the team dashboard skeleton review.

10.15.1 1 · Collect — 5 min
Everything should already be in data/raw/: the GSDB files as e-mailed, TIES v4.0, both codebooks, and years.csv (see ../data/README.md). Fill the provenance log — for the GSDB, the release number and the date of the e-mail.



10.15.2 2 · Prepare — 20 min

Connect → Text file / Excel → the GSDB case-level file. Confirm in the codebook, and log, the names used below: case_id, sanctioned_state, sanctioning_state, begin_year, end_year, the six type columns, objective, success.
Pivot the types. The six types are separate 0/1 columns (trade, financial, travel, arms, military, other): select them in the grid → right-click → Pivot. Rename Pivot Field Names → Type, Pivot Field Values → Type flag. Filter later on Type flag = 1.
Build the years. Add years.csv to the canvas and join it to the GSDB table with two clauses:

Year >= begin_year
Year <= join calculation IFNULL([end_year], 2025) (click the right-hand field of a clause → Create Join Calculation). Each case now has one row per active year — and, after the pivot, one per type. (In the R5 file ongoing cases already carry end_year = 2025; the IFNULL is a guard for releases that leave it empty.)

Check the grain. Note the row count before and after. Write in the log what one row now is.
Outcomes. Outcomes are not indicator columns: success is one text field holding one code per objective, in the order of objective (e.g. objective = human_rights,democracy, success = failed,ongoing). Take the first objective and its outcome:
Objective  =  TRIM(SPLIT([objective], ",", 1))
Outcome    =  CASE TRIM(SPLIT([success], ",", 1))
              WHEN "success_total"   THEN "Success"
              WHEN "success_part"    THEN "Partial success"
              WHEN "nego_settlement" THEN "Negotiated settlement"
              WHEN "failed"          THEN "Failure"
              WHEN "ongoing"         THEN "Ongoing"
              ELSE "Not coded" END
Log the decision: cases with several objectives count here under their first one only.




10.15.3 3 · Replicate — 25 min

10.15.3.1 Sheet 1 · “Active sanctions cases per year, by type”

Year → Columns (continuous).
COUNTD([case_id]) → Rows — count distinct, never SUM, because the pivot and the scaffold multiply rows.
Filter Type flag = 1; Type → Colour; mark type Area or Bar.
Note in a caption: a case with several types is counted once in each type, so the stacked total exceeds the number of cases. Then build a version with no colour to show the true total.
Annotate 1990–91, 2014 and 2022. What explains the shape?



10.15.3.2 Sheet 2 · “How do cases end, by objective?”

Use the case-level grain: duplicate the data source without the year scaffold, or use {FIXED [case_id] : MIN([Outcome])}.
Objective → Rows, COUNTD([case_id]) → Columns, Outcome → Colour.
Quick Table Calculation → Percent of Total; Edit Table Calculation → Compute using Outcome so each objective sums to 100%.
Exclude ongoing cases from the denominator in a second version. How much does the success share move? (That is a coding decision too.)



10.15.3.3 Sheet 3 · “One target’s history” — a Gantt chart

Filter sanctioned_state to one target (Iran, Russia, Cuba, North Korea…) — with a calculated filter CONTAINS([sanctioned_state], "Iran"), because some cases list several targets.
begin_year → Columns (continuous); case_id (or sanctioning_state + case_id) → Rows.
Mark type Gantt Bar; calculated field Duration = IFNULL([end_year], 2025) - [begin_year] → Size.
Type → Colour. What does the target’s history look like — layers added, never removed?

Differ. Put Sheet 1 beside the GSDB paper’s figure. Release 5 runs years further and has added and recoded cases: write one difference.
Threats vs impositions. Open TIES. Using the manual, separate threatened-only cases (imposition = 0) from imposed cases (imposition = 1) and count each per startyear (1945–2005). Put the counts beside GSDB impositions for the same years. What does the gap say about Drezner’s selection effect?

title: 11  Space Geopolitics: The Orbital Commons and the New Space Race
text:
11.1 Infrastructure overhead
Few multinationals own a satellite. Almost all of them depend on one, and most do not know which. A container line tracks its ships by satellite and talks to their crews by satellite when they are out of range of land. A mining company runs its remote sites over satellite links. An agribusiness forecasts harvests from imagery, an insurer settles flood claims from it, and a buyer of commodities checks the stockpiles of its suppliers with it. Above all, almost every firm depends on satellites for time. Telecommunications networks, electricity grids, data centres and trading venues synchronise their clocks to the signals of global navigation satellite systems, because those signals carry time from atomic clocks in orbit to any receiver on the ground, cheaply and everywhere.
Three services carry most of this dependence. Positioning, navigation and timing comes from four global systems, each run by a state: GPS by the United States, Galileo by the European Union, BeiDou by China and GLONASS by Russia. Connectivity comes from operators in geostationary orbit, 36,000 kilometres up, and since 2019 from constellations of thousands of satellites in low Earth orbit, a few hundred kilometres up. Earth observation comes from state agencies and from a growing number of commercial imaging firms.
Sessions 08 and 10 showed how networks become instruments of power: a network’s hubs are under someone’s jurisdiction, and whoever has jurisdiction can watch the traffic or cut it off. This session’s network is physically above the firm. Its hubs are a handful of states and, increasingly, a handful of companies, and its environment is degrading in a way no terrestrial network’s does — through debris that stays where it was created for years or centuries. The scale of the change is recent. The European Space Agency’s 2026 environment report notes that the exponential growth in the number of new payloads continued in 2025, driven by a higher launch frequency, rideshare launches and the deployment of large constellations by commercial operators (ESA Space Debris Office 2026).
The session’s question is who holds the risk when orbit is crowded, contested and dominated by one operator — and what the firm can do about it. The answer the chapter builds is that the firm holds more of it than it thinks, that most of it arrives through the reversible and unspectacular threats rather than the destructive ones, and that dependence on a satellite service is, by the construction of space law, dependence on a state.

title: 11  Space Geopolitics: The Orbital Commons and the New Space Race
section: 11.2 A domain written for two superpowers
text:
11.2 A domain written for two superpowers
The law of outer space was written at speed, during the Cold War, by and for two states that were then the only ones able to get there. Sputnik’s launch in October 1957 settled one question before anyone had negotiated it: the Soviet satellite passed over every country on Earth, and no state protested that its airspace had been violated. The principle that satellites may overfly territory — which the United States, planning reconnaissance satellites of its own, had every interest in establishing — became the foundation of the domain.
The rest of the foundation was laid in the Outer Space Treaty, opened for signature in January 1967 and in force by October of that year (United Nations 1967). It remains the constitution of the domain, and the articles that matter to a firm can be read in two pages. Article II declares that outer space “is not subject to national appropriation by claim of sovereignty, by means of use or occupation, or by any other means”: no one can own an orbit. Article IV forbids placing nuclear weapons or other weapons of mass destruction in orbit, and reserves the Moon and other celestial bodies for peaceful purposes — but it says nothing to prohibit conventional weapons in orbit, or the testing of weapons that destroy satellites from the ground. Article VI makes states internationally responsible for national activities in space “whether such activities are carried on by governmental agencies or by non-governmental entities”, and requires those activities to be authorised and continually supervised by “the appropriate State”. Article VII makes the launching state liable for damage caused by its objects. Article IX requires states to act with “due regard” to the interests of others and to consult before activities that could cause harmful interference — the closest the Treaty comes to traffic rules, without anyone to enforce them.

Orbital commons — Earth orbit treated as a resource that no one may appropriate (Outer Space Treaty, Article II) and from whose use no one can easily be excluded, but whose use by one actor degrades it for others — through congestion of orbits and spectrum and through debris. The commons is legal in origin and physical in its consequences.

Article IV’s silence on conventional weapons was not an accident; neither superpower wanted to give up the option. Its prohibition on nuclear weapons in orbit, by contrast, had been learned the hard way.

From the archive · Starfish Prime, 1962
On 9 July 1962 the United States detonated a thermonuclear warhead of about 1.4 megatons some 400 kilometres above Johnston Island in the Pacific. The test, Starfish Prime, was intended to study the effects of a nuclear explosion at high altitude. Its most lasting effect was one its planners had underestimated: electrons from the explosion were trapped in the Earth’s magnetic field, creating an artificial radiation belt that persisted for years.
The satellites then in low orbit were few, and several were damaged. Telstar 1, the first commercial communications satellite — built by AT&T’s Bell Laboratories and launched the day after the test — suffered radiation damage to its electronics and failed within months; Britain’s first satellite, Ariel 1, was also damaged. A single test by one state had degraded an orbital environment shared by everyone, and the first commercial satellite was among the casualties.
The Partial Test Ban Treaty of 1963 prohibited nuclear tests in outer space, and the Outer Space Treaty four years later prohibited nuclear weapons in orbit. Neither prohibited the next form of the same problem: a conventional weapon that destroys a satellite and fills its orbit with fragments.

title: 11  Space Geopolitics: The Orbital Commons and the New Space Race
section: 11.3 Liability, registration and the right to transmit
text:
11.3 Liability, registration and the right to transmit
The Outer Space Treaty is the constitution; three further layers turn it into rules a firm encounters.
The first is liability and registration. The Liability Convention of 1972 elaborated Article VII: a launching state is absolutely liable for damage its space objects cause on the surface of the Earth or to aircraft in flight, and liable for fault for damage elsewhere in space. The Registration Convention of 1975 requires launching states to register their objects with the United Nations. The two together mean that every object in orbit has, in law, a state that answers for it — long after it has stopped working.

From the archive · Cosmos 954, 1978
On 24 January 1978 a Soviet ocean-surveillance satellite, Cosmos 954, re-entered the atmosphere over the Northwest Territories of Canada. It was powered by a small nuclear reactor, and its re-entry scattered radioactive debris over a wide stretch of the Canadian north. Canada and the United States mounted a search and clean-up operation, Operation Morning Light, that lasted for months.
Canada presented a claim to the Soviet Union under the Liability Convention and general principles of international law, for the cost of locating, recovering and cleaning up the debris. The claim was settled in 1981, by protocol, for three million Canadian dollars — about half the amount claimed. It remains the only claim ever brought under the Convention.
The case shows both the strength and the limits of the regime. Liability attaches to a state, and a state paid. But it took three years, the settlement was negotiated rather than adjudicated, and the claimant was a state. A firm whose satellite is destroyed by a fragment from another state’s anti-satellite test has no standing under the Convention: it must persuade its own state to claim, against a launching state that may deny responsibility, for damage whose cause it may be unable to prove.

The second layer is spectrum. A satellite is useless without radio frequencies to command it and to carry its service, and frequencies and orbital positions are coordinated by the International Telecommunication Union through its Radio Regulations. An operator’s state files a satellite network with the ITU and must coordinate it with networks filed earlier, so priority goes, broadly, to the first to file. The incentive is to file early and large — sometimes for “paper satellites” that may never fly — and the result is that orbital slots and frequencies are a scarce asset allocated by a procedure most firms never see.
The third layer is national licensing. Article VI’s “authorization and continuing supervision” becomes, in practice, a set of permits: to launch, to use spectrum, to operate a remote-sensing system, to export a satellite or its components, to land a service in a national market. This is where a firm meets space law directly, and where the balance of power enters most visibly — through the export-control lists discussed below and through decisions about which foreign constellations may sell service in which countries.

title: 11  Space Geopolitics: The Orbital Commons and the New Space Race
text:
11.4 The physics of a commons
Law makes orbit a commons in one sense: no one may own it. Physics makes it a commons in the stricter sense economists use. A common-pool resource is one from which exclusion is difficult and whose use by one actor subtracts from what is left for others. Garrett Hardin’s parable of the herdsmen on a common pasture, each adding animals because he captures the whole gain while bearing only a share of the cost, is the classic statement of why such resources tend to be overused (Hardin 1968). Elinor Ostrom showed that real communities often escape the tragedy through rules they design and enforce themselves — but under conditions of clear boundaries, monitoring and graduated sanctions that Earth orbit does not meet (Ostrom 1990). Brian Weeden and Tiffany Chow applied her framework to space and found most of its design principles missing (Weeden and Chow 2012).
What turns congestion into a tragedy in orbit is a mechanism identified by Donald Kessler and Burton Cour-Palais in 1978 (Kessler and Cour-Palais 1978). Objects in the same orbital shell occasionally collide; each collision produces fragments; the fragments raise the density of objects in the shell and therefore the rate of further collisions. Below a critical density, the atmosphere drags enough debris down to keep the population in check. Above it, collisions generate fragments faster than drag removes them, and the debris population grows on its own.

Kessler syndrome — the self-sustaining growth of the debris population in an orbital shell once the density of objects passes a threshold at which collisions create fragments faster than atmospheric drag removes them. Past the threshold, the population grows even if nobody launches again.

Altitude matters enormously, because the drag that cleans orbits weakens with height. Debris a few hundred kilometres up re-enters within years; debris above about 800 kilometres can remain for decades or centuries. A fragmentation in a high, busy shell is therefore a long-lived degradation of an asset shared by every operator in it. Two decades ago, simulations by NASA’s debris specialists already suggested that the low-orbit debris population would keep growing through collisions even if all launches stopped (Liou and Johnson 2006).
Economists have since modelled the incentives. Nodir Adilov, Peter Alexander and Brendan Cunningham show that, because each operator ignores the collision risk its satellites and debris impose on others, open access leads to more launches and more debris than would be efficient (Adilov, Alexander, and Cunningham 2015). Akhil Rao, Matthew Burgess and Daniel Kaffine estimate that an internationally harmonised fee on each satellite in orbit — making operators pay for the risk they impose — would greatly increase the long-run value of the space industry (Rao, Burgess, and Kaffine 2020). No such fee exists. Mitigation guidelines adopted through the UN and by space agencies ask operators to limit debris and to remove satellites from busy orbits at the end of their lives; compliance is voluntary and uneven.

For the firm: an orbit is a shared infrastructure whose quality is set by its least careful user. A destructive test by one state, or a rocket stage that explodes years after launch, raises the collision risk — and the insurance price — for every operator in that shell, and therefore for every customer of those operators.

title: 11  Space Geopolitics: The Orbital Commons and the New Space Race
section: 11.5 Three readings of the new space race
text:
11.5 Three readings of the new space race
Who will govern this commons, and in whose interest? International relations offers three readings of what has come to be called the new space race, and they do not exclude one another.
The first is classical geopolitics carried upwards. Everett Dolman’s Astropolitik takes Mackinder’s logic — whoever controls the pivot controls the world — and applies it to orbit: whoever controls low Earth orbit controls access to the rest of space, and through it can dominate the Earth below (Dolman 2002). On this realist reading the United States should seize and hold that control while it can, and space is a territory to dominate, its orbits and transfer routes the chokepoints of a new strategic geography. It is Session 03’s anarchy, with orbits in place of straits.
The second reading is institutional and commercial. Saadia Pekkanen describes the new space race as driven by three intertwined trends (Pekkanen 2019). Democratisation: many more states, and many non-state actors, now operate in space. Commercialisation: firms no longer only supply governments but strike out on their own, with their own capital and customers. Militarisation: states increasingly treat space as a domain of warfare. Binding them together is the fact that about 95 percent of space technologies, on her account, are dual-use. With treaty-making in decline, the domain is governed less by new international law than by national legislation, contracts, and a few old principles. On this reading space is a market, and the firms in it are part of the security problem.
The third reading puts the Earth back at the centre. Bleddyn Bowen argues that spacepower matters for its effects on Earth: orbit is a “cosmic coastline” from which states support — and threaten — what happens on land, at sea and in the air (Bowen 2020). Satellites are valuable because they make terrestrial forces see, communicate and navigate; that is also why they are targets when terrestrial power is contested.
Read together, the three explain why the same constellation can be a consumer broadband business, a military communications network and an instrument of foreign policy all at once. Pekkanen supplies the dual use; Dolman and Bowen supply the strategic stakes. For a multinational the practical conclusion is the same under all three: a commercial satellite service is never only commercial.
crumbs: 11  Space Geopolitics: The Orbital Commons and the New Space Race

title: 11  Space Geopolitics: The Orbital Commons and the New Space Race
section: 11.6 Counterspace: what states can do to satellites
text:
11.6 Counterspace: what states can do to satellites
If satellites are targets, the question is what can be done to them, by whom, and with what consequences for the firms that use them. The Secure World Foundation’s annual open-source assessment tracks the capabilities of thirteen countries to deceive, disrupt, deny, degrade or destroy space systems, in five categories (Samson and Brett 2026).

Counterspace capabilities — the means of deceiving, disrupting, denying, degrading or destroying space systems: direct-ascent missiles, co-orbital systems, electronic warfare, directed energy and cyber operations. They differ in whether their effects are reversible and in who bears them first — the satellite’s owner, every operator in the orbit, or the users on the ground.

Direct-ascent weapons are missiles launched from the Earth to destroy a satellite. Their effects are irreversible and, at most altitudes, create debris that threatens every operator in the shell. Co-orbital systems are satellites that approach another to inspect it, interfere with it or attack it. Electronic warfare jams or spoofs signals — the uplink to a satellite, its downlink to users, or navigation signals on the ground — and its effects end when the jamming stops. Directed-energy weapons use lasers or microwaves to dazzle or damage sensors. Cyber operations attack satellites, ground stations or user terminals, and can disable a service without touching a satellite.
The assessment’s central finding is the one that matters most for business: many states have researched and tested destructive capabilities, but only non-destructive ones are actively used against satellites in current military operations. Four states have destroyed one of their own satellites with a missile launched from the ground: the United States in 1985 — and, in 2008, by intercepting a failing satellite at low altitude — China in 2007, India in 2019 and Russia in 2021. In April 2022 the United States declared that it would not conduct destructive direct-ascent tests, and in December 2022 the UN General Assembly called on all states to make the same commitment.
What firms have actually suffered is the reversible kind. On 24 February 2022, the day Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine began, a cyberattack on the ground segment of Viasat’s KA-SAT network disabled thousands of user modems in Ukraine and across Europe, including those used for the remote monitoring of thousands of wind turbines in Germany. The European Union, the United Kingdom and the United States attributed the attack to Russia. The satellite was untouched; the service failed for its customers, many of them nowhere near the war. Since then, the jamming and spoofing of navigation signals around conflict zones has become routine. In 2024 Finnair suspended its flights to Tartu, in Estonia, for several weeks because interference made the airport’s satellite-based approach procedures unusable.

The lesson for an analyst. Destructive tests make headlines and debris. Jamming, spoofing and cyberattacks on ground segments make losses — and the losses fall on the customers, not on the satellite. A firm’s counterspace exposure is measured on the ground, in the regions where its ships, aircraft and sites depend on signals from orbit.

title: 11  Space Geopolitics: The Orbital Commons and the New Space Race
section: 11.7 The debris record, and how it is counted
text:
11.7 The debris record, and how it is counted
The evidence on the state of the orbital environment comes, for this session, from ESA’s Space Debris Office, which has published an annual Space Environment Report since 2017. The 2026 edition, with data to the end of 2025, is the session’s big work (ESA Space Debris Office 2026), and its method deserves reading before its figures.
ESA counts two kinds of objects. Catalogued objects are those tracked and published in catalogues: the US public catalogue, the Russian Vimpel catalogue and, for the early decades, the United Kingdom’s historical RAE tables. Asserted objects are known to exist by design — a satellite released from a dispenser, a component separated as planned — even if not yet catalogued. The two are cross-correlated in ESA’s DISCOS database and classified into object classes. Objects too small or too erratic to be tracked are outside the report’s scope.
On that basis, the report counts 44,964 objects in Earth orbit at the end of 2025, of which 16,946 are payloads, and 25,060 objects in low Earth orbit (ESA Space Debris Office 2026). It observes that, ever since the start of the space age, there has been more debris in orbit than operational satellites. And its most important finding for anyone who thinks the debris problem is the weapons tests is this: fragmentations other than collisions — explosions, mostly of old rocket stages and batteries — are the dominant source of debris. Non-deliberate fragmentations have averaged 9.8 a year over the last two decades, and 2024 alone added more than 3,000 catalogued fragments, mostly from propulsion-related break-ups.
The report’s Figure 2.1, the number of objects in geocentric orbit by object class since 1957, is the practice round’s target. It shows the cumulative result of seven decades of launches, explosions, collisions and re-entries, and three events stand out on it. On 11 January 2007 China destroyed its Fengyun-1C weather satellite with a ground-launched missile, at about 850 kilometres; the test remains the largest single source of catalogued debris in the public catalogue, and most of its thousands of fragments are still in orbit. On 10 February 2009 the active Iridium 33 and the defunct Cosmos 2251 collided at about 780 kilometres — the first accidental collision between two intact satellites, Kessler’s mechanism observed. And on 15 November 2021 Russia destroyed Cosmos 1408 at roughly 470 to 490 kilometres, producing some 1,800 catalogued fragments; at that altitude almost all re-entered within three years, and ESA attributes the 2022 spike in re-entering debris to the test.
The contrast between the first and third events is a lesson in altitude. Both were deliberate destructions of a satellite by its own state; one polluted a high orbit for decades, the other a low orbit for a few years. A count of objects treats them alike.

What the figure does not measure. It counts objects, not risk: a ten-centimetre fragment and a five-tonne rocket stage each count once, and the objects too small to catalogue — the majority of the fragments able to disable a satellite — do not appear at all. It is drawn from catalogues that themselves improve: when sensors get better, the count rises with nothing new having happened in orbit. And it shows the environment, not the exposure of any operator or customer, which depends on which shells their satellites use.

title: 11  Space Geopolitics: The Orbital Commons and the New Space Race
text:
11.8 One operator
The new space race has a feature the Cold War one did not. In the first years of the space age, concentration was extreme because only two states could launch anything; it fell for decades as Europe, Japan, China, India and many others acquired the capability, and as commercial operators multiplied. It has risen again — not because states have dropped out, but because one company has launched more satellites than everyone else together. SpaceX’s Starlink, first launched in May 2019, grew in six years into the majority of the world’s operating satellites. The practice round measures how large a majority, and finds that the concentration of who launches payloads has returned to Cold War levels, with a firm rather than a superpower at the top.
Concentration needs a measure, and the course uses the one antitrust authorities use. Its origins are in geopolitics: Albert Hirschman devised an index of the concentration of a country’s trade in 1945, to show how Nazi Germany had used the structure of trade to make its smaller partners dependent on it (Hirschman 1945). Orris Herfindahl reinvented it a few years later for industrial concentration, and it carries both their names.

Herfindahl–Hirschman index (HHI) — the sum of the squared market shares of all participants, with shares in percent, so that it runs from near 0 (many small participants) to 10,000 (one participant with everything). It weights large shares heavily: one participant with 75 percent contributes 5,625 on its own. US merger guidelines treat markets above 2,500 (U.S. Department of Justice and Federal Trade Commission 2010) or, in the 2023 revision, above 1,800 (U.S. Department of Justice and Federal Trade Commission 2023) as highly concentrated.

Concentration matters to a firm because of what it implies about dependence, and Starlink in Ukraine shows what that dependence means. Within days of the 2022 invasion, Starlink terminals became a backbone of Ukraine’s military and civil communications. The company’s decisions about where its service would work — including, by its owner’s account, a refusal to enable it for an attack near Crimea in 2022 — became questions of war policy, and governments moved to contract for the service directly.
Farrell and Newman’s framework, met in Session 08, applies without modification (Farrell and Newman 2019). A constellation is a hub. Its operator sees who connects and from where — a panopticon — and can switch off a user, a region or a country — a chokepoint. Weaponisation requires two conditions: that the network be concentrated, and that a state can direct the firm that runs the hub. Article VI of the Outer Space Treaty guarantees the second, because every operator has a licensing state that is internationally responsible for its activities and must supervise them. A firm that depends on one operator depends on that operator’s state as well.
States are responding as Session 03 would predict: by building their own. The European Union’s IRIS² secure-connectivity programme, established by Regulation (EU) 2023/588, China’s Qianfan and Guowang constellations, and the many national launch programmes are all, in part, answers to dependence on one American firm. Export controls draw the same line from the other side. Spacecraft and their components sit either on the US Munitions List, under Category XV of the International Traffic in Arms Regulations, or — for most commercial satellites since 2014 — under the Export Administration Regulations, in the “9x515” entries; a non-US manufacturer whose satellite contains a controlled US component needs US permission to sell it to some customers. The balance of power reaches into the bill of materials.
Navigation is the older case of the same pattern, and the one on which almost every firm already depends. GPS was built by the US military. Its opening to the world followed a tragedy: after the Soviet Union shot down Korean Air Lines Flight 007, which had strayed into Soviet airspace, in September 1983, the United States announced that GPS would be made available for civilian use once it was operational. For years the civilian signal was deliberately degraded — “Selective Availability” — until the degradation was switched off in May 2000. The service on which the world’s networks and logistics came to rely was, and remains, a gift that one state chose to give and could in principle withdraw or degrade, regionally or globally. Europe’s decision to build Galileo, and China’s to build BeiDou, were in large part refusals to accept that dependence. For a firm, the existence of four global systems is a genuine diversification — but only if its receivers use more than one, and only against the failure or withdrawal of a system, not against a jammer in the next port.

title: 11  Space Geopolitics: The Orbital Commons and the New Space Race
section: 11.9 Through which channels, and what the firm can do
text:
11.9 Through which channels, and what the firm can do
Space risk reaches the profit and loss account through the same five channels as every other risk in the course, and naming the channel is the first step towards a decision.
Through market access, export controls and licensing decide whether a satellite, a terminal or a service can be sold or switched on in a given market, and spectrum and landing rights decide whether a constellation may serve a country at all. Through inputs, a firm that buys connectivity for its ships or mines from one constellation, or that times its networks from one state’s navigation system, has a single point of failure with a sovereign behind it. Through finance and payments, trading venues and payment systems time-stamp transactions from navigation signals, and the insurance capacity for space assets — a thin market — shrinks after large losses, so that a fragmentation event can double a premium. Through assets and people, ships and aircraft operating in jammed or spoofed regions are rerouted, delayed, or misreport their positions, with consequences for safety and for sanctions compliance alike. Through data and operations, a cyberattack on a ground segment cuts the firm’s links, as the KA-SAT modems showed, and the loss of an imagery feed leaves a crop forecast or a supply-chain monitor blind.
A dashboard view of space risk should therefore track four things, each with a threshold that triggers a named decision. Dependence: the share of a critical service — connectivity, imagery, timing — supplied by one operator or one state’s system; above a set share, say half from one operator, the decision is to contract a second. Interference: official warnings of navigation-signal interference, which aviation authorities publish, in the regions where the firm’s ships, aircraft or sites operate. Environment: destructive tests and fragmentation events in the orbital shells used by the firm’s providers, and the yearly indicators in ESA’s report. Rules: changes in export-control lists, licensing conditions and ITU filings that affect the firm’s suppliers or markets.
The strategies available each have a cost and a limit. A firm can buy multi-orbit, multi-operator connectivity — geostationary and low-orbit links from two providers — at the price of integration, but the second operator may share the first one’s licensing state. It can use multi-constellation receivers that combine GPS, Galileo and others, which is cheap and protects against the failure of one system, but a local jammer can still blind them all. It can invest in terrestrial back-ups — holdover clocks and time delivered by fibre, cellular and fibre links — which requires capital and is unavailable at sea or at remote sites. It can buy insurance, in a thin market whose capacity shrinks after large losses. And it can practise compliance by design, classifying every space-related component it buys or sells under the relevant export-control regimes, at the cost of staff and delay, knowing that the rules change with the balance of power.
The question the lecture puts to the room ties these together. A shipping subsidiary’s only broadband at sea is one low-orbit constellation; the operator’s government has been asked by an ally to switch the service off over a strait the firm’s ships use. What does the firm do this quarter? The answer turns on the distinction between dependence on a service and dependence on a state. A second operator under the same licensing state diversifies the first and not the second.

title: 11  Space Geopolitics: The Orbital Commons and the New Space Race
section: 11.10 From a catalogue to a stock
text:
11.10 From a catalogue to a stock
The practice round rebuilds ESA’s figure from the public catalogue maintained by CelesTrak from US Space Force data, and the construction is a lesson in how a concept — the number of objects in orbit — becomes data.
The catalogue does not record a stock. It records objects: one row for each catalogued object over its whole life, with a launch date and, if it has re-entered, a decay date. There is no “year” in the file. An object is in orbit in a given year if it was launched by then and had not decayed by then, so the stock in each year is the running sum of launches minus the running sum of decays — a stock rebuilt from two flows. The construction is general: much of what a risk analyst needs to know is a stock that no one publishes, and has to be rebuilt from the events that change it.
The construction exposes the catalogue’s decisions. Debris carries the launch date of its parent object, not the date of the event that created it: the fragments of China’s 2007 test are dated to the launch of Fengyun-1C in 1999, so a debris line built on launch dates moves in the wrong year. “Not decayed” is not the same as “in Earth orbit”, because some objects orbit the Sun, the Moon or a Lagrange point. The owner field records a country, organisation or company code, not the operator: every Starlink satellite is simply American, and the former Soviet Union and Russia share one code. Operational status describes today only, so the file cannot say how many satellites were active in any past year. And the public catalogue is not the environment: it omits classified objects and everything too small to track, which is one reason ESA’s totals, drawn from more catalogues and asserted objects, are higher.
Concentration is built from the same file by computing each owner’s share of the payloads launched in a year and summing the squares. Here the owner-code problem bites twice: concentration by state hides the fact that one company dominates the American share, and concentration by operator must be reconstructed from object names. Each choice yields a different index, and each answers a different question — about the balance of power among states, or about the dependence of customers on firms.

title: 11  Space Geopolitics: The Orbital Commons and the New Space Race
section: 11.11 A short review of the literature
text:
11.11 A short review of the literature

The legal foundation is the Outer Space Treaty (United Nations 1967), whose Articles II, VI and VII make orbit unappropriable, place every private operator under a responsible state, and attach liability to the launching state. The governance problem it leaves open is that of a commons. Hardin (1968) states why open-access resources are overused and Ostrom (1990) the conditions under which communities escape the tragedy; Weeden and Chow (2012) apply Ostrom’s design principles to orbit and find most of them absent. The physical mechanism is Kessler and Cour-Palais (1978), with Liou and Johnson (2006) showing by simulation that the low-orbit debris population would grow even without new launches. The economics of the externality is set out by Adilov, Alexander, and Cunningham (2015), and Rao, Burgess, and Kaffine (2020) estimate the gains from orbital-use fees.
The strategic literature divides along the lines of the session’s three readings. Dolman (2002) carries classical geopolitics into orbit; Bowen (2020) argues that spacepower matters for its terrestrial effects; Pekkanen (2019) describes the democratisation, commercialisation and militarisation of a domain in which most technology is dual-use and treaty-making has stalled. The empirical record of threats is the Secure World Foundation’s annual assessment (Samson and Brett 2026), and that of the environment ESA’s annual report (ESA Space Debris Office 2026).
For the firm, the bridge is Farrell and Newman (2019): a concentrated constellation under a state’s jurisdiction meets both conditions for weaponised interdependence. The measure of concentration is Hirschman (1945)’s index, conceived to analyse how trade structures create political dependence, and its antitrust thresholds are those of the US merger guidelines (U.S. Department of Justice and Federal Trade Commission 2010, 2023).

title: 11  Space Geopolitics: The Orbital Commons and the New Space Race
section: 11.12 What the figure will not tell the firm
text:
11.12 What the figure will not tell the firm
The practice round rebuilds ESA’s count of objects in orbit by class, annotated with the 2007 test, the 2009 collision and the 2021 test, and adds the concentration of who launches payloads, from Sputnik to today. It will show the steady accumulation of debris, the steps that the three events cut into the record, the explosion of payloads since the large constellations began, and a concentration index that falls for decades and then climbs back. It will also show the decisions: the dating of debris, the filtering of objects that do not orbit the Earth, the reading of owner codes, the definition of an active satellite.
The question to carry into the round is what this figure does not license a multinational to conclude. A rising count of objects does not tell a firm that its services are at greater risk, because risk depends on the size of objects, the shells its providers use, and the manoeuvring capability of their satellites — none of which the count contains. The absence of a spike does not mean the absence of a threat: the counterspace effects firms have actually suffered — jamming, spoofing, cyberattacks on ground segments — leave no trace in a catalogue of objects. And concentration by owner code is not the firm’s dependence. A firm may buy its connectivity from a small operator in an unconcentrated market and still depend on one state’s navigation system for its time, or buy from the dominant operator through a reseller and not know it.
The figure is the right place to begin a space-infrastructure view on a team dashboard, because it shows the condition of the commons and the shape of the new space race. The firm’s own exposure begins elsewhere: with the list of satellite services it buys, the operators and states behind each, and the regions where its ships, aircraft and sites depend on signals that someone else can switch off.

title: 11  Space Geopolitics: The Orbital Commons and the New Space Race
text:
11.13 In the practice

The target. ESA’s Space Environment Report 2026, Figure 2.1: the number of objects in geocentric orbit by object class, from 1957 to the end of 2025, with the 2007 Chinese ASAT test, the 2009 Iridium–Cosmos collision and the 2021 Russian ASAT test annotated — rebuilt from the public catalogue. You add the concentration of who puts payloads into orbit, year by year, and who operates the active satellites today — and wire the views into one dashboard with an action.

The last practice round of the term. The last twenty minutes of Session 10 reviewed your team dashboard’s skeleton. Most skeletons still lack a space-infrastructure channel and any interaction between views. Leave today with both: the dependence view you build is designed to be dropped into your team dashboard, for the satellite services your own firm relies on.
Work in your project teams. Everyone builds the workbook; the team hands in one.


11.13.1 1 · Collect — 15 min
You arrive with satcat.csv (one download per team, pre-session). Use these fifteen minutes to check, not to download again:

The snapshot. What is the latest LAUNCH_DATE in the file? Log it with your download date: the catalogue changes every day.
The codes. Open the format documentation and the status codes. Which OBJECT_TYPE values are present? Which OPS_STATUS_CODE values count as active? What does a blank status mean?
The trap you found before class. Filter OBJECT_NAME = FENGYUN 1C DEB. How many rows? Which LAUNCH_DATE? Write the gap to 11 January 2007 in your log.

Provenance log — one line per file, as always:
