11.13.2 2 · Prepare — 15 min
You build two data sources from the same file: one reshaped into events (for the stock of objects in orbit), one left as it is (for concentration).

11.13.2.1 Data source A · “SATCAT events”

Connect → Text file → satcat.csv. Check the types: LAUNCH_DATE and DECAY_DATE must be dates (click the type icon above the column if they arrive as strings), NORAD_CAT_ID a number.
Data source filter (top right of the data source page → Filters → Add): ORBIT_CENTER = EA. Objects around the Sun or the Moon never decay and would stay “in orbit” for ever.
Pivot the two dates. Select LAUNCH_DATE and DECAY_DATE in the grid → right-click → Pivot. Rename Pivot Field Names → Event and Pivot Field Values → Event date. Each object now has two rows: its launch and its decay (empty if it is still in space).
Calculated fields:
Change  =  IF [Event] = "LAUNCH_DATE" THEN 1 ELSE -1 END
Year    =  YEAR([Event date])
Check the grain. Note the row count before and after the pivot, then exclude the null Event date rows (decays that have not happened). What is one row now? Write it in the log.



11.13.2.2 Data source B · “SATCAT objects”

Data → New Data Source → the same satcat.csv, not pivoted. Data source filter OBJECT_TYPE = PAY — a data source filter, not a sheet filter (step 3 explains why).
Calculated fields:
Launch year  =  YEAR([LAUNCH_DATE])
Power        =  CASE [OWNER] WHEN "US" THEN "United States"
                             WHEN "PRC" THEN "China"
                             WHEN "CIS" THEN "USSR / Russia"
                             ELSE "Rest of the world" END
Active       =  [OPS_STATUS_CODE] = "+" OR [OPS_STATUS_CODE] = "P" OR [OPS_STATUS_CODE] = "B"
                OR [OPS_STATUS_CODE] = "S" OR [OPS_STATUS_CODE] = "X"
Operator     =  IF STARTSWITH([OBJECT_NAME], "STARLINK") THEN "Starlink (SpaceX)"
                ELSEIF STARTSWITH([OBJECT_NAME], "ONEWEB") THEN "OneWeb"
                ELSEIF STARTSWITH([OBJECT_NAME], "KUIPER") THEN "Kuiper (Amazon)"
                ELSEIF STARTSWITH([OBJECT_NAME], "QIANFAN") THEN "Qianfan"
                ELSEIF STARTSWITH([OBJECT_NAME], "HULIANWANG") THEN "Guowang"
                ELSE "Other: " + [OWNER] END
CIS is CelesTrak’s code for the USSR and Russia; OWNER is a registry-style code, not the operator — log both decisions.





11.13.3 3 · Replicate — 35 min

11.13.3.1 Sheet 1 · “Objects in Earth orbit, by type” — the target figure (data source A)

Year → Columns: right-click → Convert to Dimension, keep it continuous (green).
SUM([Change]) → Rows. You see net additions per year — a jagged line.
Right-click the pill → Quick Table Calculation → Running Total. Now you see the stock.
OBJECT_TYPE → Colour. Edit Table Calculation → Compute using → Specific Dimensions → tick Year only, so the running total restarts for each type. Mark type Area (stacked).
Filter Year ≤ 2025 to match ESA’s end point. Never filter out early years with a normal filter: it runs before the table calculation and the running total would restart from zero. (To hide early years, use a table-calculation filter such as LOOKUP(MIN([Year]), 0).)
Annotate 2007, 2009 and 2021 (right-click → Annotate → Point). Look at the debris band. Where are the steps?
Title stating the finding; caption with source, snapshot date and “objects dated by launch date”.



11.13.3.2 Sheet 2 · “Payloads launched per year, by power” (data source B)

Launch year → Columns (continuous dimension), CNT([NORAD_CAT_ID]) → Rows, Power → Colour, mark type Bar. Where does the Cold War end, and where does the new race begin?



11.13.3.3 Sheet 3 · “How concentrated is the new space race?” — the HHI (data source B)

Create:
Owner share  =  {FIXED [Launch year], [OWNER] : COUNT([NORAD_CAT_ID])}
              / {FIXED [Launch year] : COUNT([NORAD_CAT_ID])}
HHI piece    =  10000 * [Owner share] / {FIXED [Launch year] : COUNT([NORAD_CAT_ID])}
Why the second line: each owner’s squared share must be counted once, but the owner appears on as many rows as it has payloads. Spreading share × 10,000 over the year’s rows means that summing an owner’s rows gives exactly share² × 10,000.
Launch year → Columns, SUM([HHI piece]) → Rows, mark type Line. That sum is the HHI. Check: 1957 must give 10,000 (two Soviet payloads). Reference lines at 2,500 and 1,800, labelled.
Why the data source filter in step 6: a FIXED expression is computed before ordinary filters. Had you filtered OBJECT_TYPE on the sheet, the shares would still include debris and rocket bodies. (Adding the filter to context also works.)



11.13.3.4 Sheet 4 · “Who launched that year?” (data source B)

OWNER → Rows, CNT([NORAD_CAT_ID]) → Columns, sorted descending, Operator → Colour; a Top 10 by count filter on OWNER. This is the target of the action.



11.13.3.5 Sheet 5 · “Who operates the active satellites today?” (data source B)

Filter Active = True and ORBIT_CENTER = EA. Operator → Rows, CNT([NORAD_CAT_ID]) → Columns, sorted; Quick Table Calculation → Percent of Total. Caption: “status as of the snapshot date; blank status excluded”.



11.13.3.6 Dashboard · “Space infrastructure exposure”

New Dashboard. Sheet 1 top left, Sheet 3 top right, Sheet 4 bottom left, Sheet 5 bottom right.
Action 1. Dashboard → Actions → Add Action → Filter. Source: Sheet 1. Target: Sheet 4. Run on: Select. Clearing the selection: Show all values. Filter: Selected fields → source field Year → target data source SATCAT objects, target field Launch year. Because the two sheets use different data sources, map the fields explicitly.
Action 2. The same, with Sheet 3 as source (same data source as Sheet 4: field Launch year → Launch year).
Click 1965 on Sheet 3, then 2025. Sheet 4 should show who launched that year. If it shows nothing, the field mapping is wrong: fix it, and log it.





11.13.4 4 · Compare and break — 15 min

Differ. Put Sheet 1 beside ESA’s Figure 2.1 and Table 3.1 (end of 2025: 44,964 objects, of which 16,946 payloads). Give your totals by type and one reason for each gap — which catalogues ESA adds, what it calls “unidentified”, what the public catalogue leaves out.
Break: when does debris appear? Your debris band does not step up in 2007, 2009 or 2021. Re-date the four big events’ debris to the date the event happened. In data source A:
Appearance year  =  IF [Event] = "LAUNCH_DATE" AND CONTAINS([OBJECT_NAME], "FENGYUN 1C DEB") THEN 2007
                    ELSEIF [Event] = "LAUNCH_DATE" AND (CONTAINS([OBJECT_NAME], "COSMOS 2251 DEB")
                         OR CONTAINS([OBJECT_NAME], "IRIDIUM 33 DEB")) THEN 2009
                    ELSEIF [Event] = "LAUNCH_DATE" AND CONTAINS([OBJECT_NAME], "COSMOS 1408 DEB") THEN 2021
                    ELSE [Year] END
Duplicate Sheet 1 and replace Year by Appearance year. How big is each step now? What about the thousands of other fragments whose event you did not re-date?
Break: flag or firm? On Sheet 5, replace Operator by OWNER, and compute the HHI of active satellites both ways. Which number describes your firm’s dependence better?
Extend. For your team’s firm, name the satellite services it relies on (GNSS timing, connectivity at sea or in remote sites, imagery). Find their operators in the file — NAVSTAR (GPS), GSAT0… (Galileo, coded ESA), BEIDOU, [GLONASS-M] — and add the one that matters to Sheet 5. Optional, with GCAT: orbital launch attempts per year (LaunchCode starting O or D) by launch-provider state.




11.13.5 5 · The catch — 10 min
One slide, three panels:








Original
Ours
The catch




ESA’s Figure 2.1
Your dashboard
What it does not license your firm to conclude



The model catch, if you need one to beat: a count of objects is not a count of risk — the fragments able to disable a satellite are mostly too small to catalogue, and the public catalogue dates debris by its parent’s launch, so the ASAT tests vanish from a chart built naively on it; and concentration by flag hides dependence on one firm. Beat it — say something specific to your firm.
A member drawn at random presents in two minutes.



11.13.6 Hand in
Upload to ZoneCours before leaving: the .twbx, the provenance log, and the slide. Formative: commented, not marked; counts towards participation. (The SATCAT is freely available, so the workbook may also go to Tableau Public — credit CelesTrak in the caption.)
The one rule: the log records at least one place where the data disagreed with the paper — a total that does not reach ESA’s, debris dated to the wrong year, an owner code that is not the operator.



11.13.7 Into the team dashboard
Before Session 12, re-point Sheet 5 at your firm’s satellite services, keep the action, and add the dependence view to your channel views with a threshold — for example more than half of a critical service from one operator → contract a second one. A board member should be able to click a year and see who controlled access to orbit then, and see in one screen who the firm depends on now.



11.13.8 What loses credit

A running total that restarts because early years were filtered out
Objects around the Sun or the Moon counted as “in orbit”
An HHI that is not 10,000 in 1957 — shares computed after a sheet filter, or squared on every row
OWNER presented as the operator, or blank status counted as inactive
A dashboard action that silently filters to nothing
A catch about ESA rather than about your firm

title: 12  From Indicators to Decisions
text:
12.1 The question the course began with
The course opened with a question: how does a multinational firm know how much geopolitical risk it faces — and what should it do about it? Eleven sessions later the honest answer to the first half is that it never knows, in the sense of holding a number that settles the matter, and that the course’s work has been to show why. The answer to the second half is more encouraging. A firm can organise what it does not know so that someone acts on it, at the right moment, for reasons that can be stated in advance and checked afterwards. That is what a risk function is for, and it is what the team dashboards presented in the final session try to do for one real multinational each.
This closing chapter draws the threads together. It does not introduce a new big work or a new dataset. It takes the two closing readings — Stephen Kobrin’s review of political risk, published in 1979, and Witold Henisz’s measure of political constraint, published in 2000 — and uses them to frame what the eleven sessions established: that geopolitical risk is a contingency rather than an event; that it is measured through families of indicators that disagree; that every famous figure is a stack of decisions; that the system a firm operates in moves slowly and then suddenly; that the risk reaches the firm through identifiable channels; and that indicators do not decide anything until someone attaches a threshold, a decision and an owner to them. It ends with the question every team was asked in its defence, which is also the question with which any analyst should end: what would change your mind?

title: 12  From Indicators to Decisions
section: 12.2 The event is not the risk
text:
12.2 The event is not the risk
Frank Knight drew the distinction that every risk analyst still uses, even when they do not name it (Knight 1921). Risk, in his sense, is uncertainty that can be measured: the outcomes are known and their probabilities can be estimated from experience, so the uncertainty can be priced, insured or diversified. Uncertainty proper is the rest: situations unique enough, or new enough, that no frequency distribution exists. Most of what the course has called geopolitical risk is Knightian uncertainty in that sense. There is no actuarial table of invasions, no frequency distribution of secondary sanctions on a given country, no base rate for a constellation operator’s government ordering it to switch off a region. The indices the course rebuilt are attempts to make the second kind of uncertainty behave a little more like the first — to give it a scale, a history and a comparison — and it is important to remember that they do not succeed entirely.
Kobrin’s contribution, in a review written as the field of political risk assessment was taking shape, was to insist on a second distinction (Kobrin 1979). The literature he surveyed used “political risk” in two ways: some writers meant political events — instability, violence, changes of government — and others meant the effects of politics on business — expropriation, restrictions, changes in the rules. Kobrin argued that the first is not the risk. Political instability in a country is a property of that country; whether it affects a particular firm’s operations depends on the firm’s industry, its assets, its partners and its relationship with the government. A coup may leave a consumer-goods importer untouched and ruin a mining concession; a peaceful election may produce a government that rewrites the tax code for one sector. Risk lies in the contingency between the event and the firm.

Political risk (Kobrin) — not the political event itself, but the contingency that political events or conditions will affect a particular firm’s operations — its revenues, costs, assets and freedom to act. The same event carries different risks for different firms; a measure of the event is not a measure of the risk.

The course widened Kobrin’s frame in one direction. His concern was largely with host-country risk: what the government of the country in which a firm invests might do to it. Geopolitical risk, as the course defined it in Session 01, includes the risk that originates outside the host country — in Washington, Beijing, Brussels or Moscow — and reaches the firm through its suppliers, customers, banks and networks. A sanction imposed by the firm’s home state on the country where it has a subsidiary, an export control on a component it buys, a jammer operating in a strait its ships use: none of these is a decision of the host government, and all of them reach the firm through the contingencies Kobrin described.

From the archive · Iran, 1979
Kobrin’s review appeared in the spring of 1979, in the first months of the revolution that ended the Shah’s rule in Iran. Few events have taught multinationals more about the gap between country analysis and firm risk. Iran had been a favoured destination for Western investment and contracting through the 1970s, rich with oil revenue and governed by a regime regarded as a firm ally of the United States. Its collapse cancelled contracts, stranded assets and exposed staff to danger within months.
The year ended with a second lesson. After the seizure of the US embassy in Tehran in November 1979, President Carter used the International Emergency Economic Powers Act — the statute on which most of the sanctions programmes of Session 10 still rest — to freeze Iranian government assets under US jurisdiction. Many American firms had claims against Iran. Their recourse came only through the Algiers Accords of January 1981, which ended the hostage crisis and created the Iran–United States Claims Tribunal in The Hague to arbitrate them. The firms were paid, eventually, out of the frozen assets: their risk had been settled by a negotiation between states in which they had no seat.
The episode is commonly cited as a reason so many firms built or expanded formal political risk units in the years that followed. Kobrin’s own study of how American firms organised political assessment appeared three years later (Kobrin 1982). The lesson both drew was the one this course has tried to teach: the analysis of a country is the beginning of the assessment of a firm’s risk, not the end.

Every dashboard presented in the final session is a claim about Kobrin’s contingency. The footprint — where the firm’s revenue, assets, suppliers and people are — is where that claim starts. A dashboard that begins with a map of the world coloured by a country index has not yet begun to assess the firm’s risk; one that begins with the firm’s own disclosures, and asks which of its countries, suppliers and channels the index bears on, has.

title: 12  From Indicators to Decisions
text:
12.3 Six families that disagree
Session 01 sorted the indicators of geopolitical risk into six families, and the sorting has carried the course. Event-based indicators count things that happened, coded from reports: conflicts, cyber incidents, sanctions episodes. Text-based indicators measure how much the press or firms talk about a risk. Expert-based indicators are scores assigned by analysts or by surveys. Structural indicators describe slow-moving features of the system: the distribution of material capabilities, the pattern of trade dependence. Market-based indicators are prices that embed risk, such as sovereign credit-default swap spreads. Firm-level indicators capture risk as firms themselves perceive and disclose it.

Family of indicators — a class of measures of geopolitical risk that share a source of information and therefore a characteristic strength and blind spot: event-based (concrete, but only what was reported and coded), text-based (timely, but measures attention rather than exposure), expert-based (covers latent concepts, but opaque and sticky), structural (explains why, rarely when), market-based (forward-looking, but mixes risk with risk appetite), firm-level (speaks to the decision, but self-reported).

The most cited text-based measure is the one Session 01 rebuilt. Dario Caldara and Matteo Iacoviello count the share of articles in leading newspapers that mention geopolitical tensions, wars and terrorism, and show that their index rises with the events that history books record and that high values are followed by lower investment and employment (Caldara and Iacoviello 2022). Its sibling, the economic policy uncertainty index of Scott Baker, Nicholas Bloom and Steven Davis, applies the same logic to economic policy (Baker, Bloom, and Davis 2016). Session 07 went down to the level of the firm with the measure of Tarek Hassan and his colleagues, built from the share of conversation in firms’ earnings calls devoted to political topics and risk, which shows that political risk is largely firm-specific rather than aggregate (Hassan et al. 2019). Each of these is ingenious, carefully validated and limited by its source: newspapers in a few countries, in one language, attending to what their readers care about; earnings calls of listed firms, speaking to investors.
The families disagree, and the disagreement is information. When the text-based indices are calm and the market-based ones signal danger, someone with money at stake knows or fears something the press has not yet written about. When an expert rating stays unchanged through a crisis that the event data record in detail, the rating is sticky or the raters see a resilience the events do not. When a structural indicator shows a power transition under way and every short-run indicator is quiet, the structural one is telling you why something may happen and the others are telling you, correctly, that it has not happened yet. A risk assessment that relies on one family inherits that family’s blind spot. This is why the team brief required at least four datasets from at least three families: not because more is better, but because triangulation is the only defence against a blind spot one cannot see from inside one family.

title: 12  From Indicators to Decisions
section: 12.4 Every figure is a stack of decisions
text:
12.4 Every figure is a stack of decisions
The design of the course rested on a claim: that a chart in a famous work is a set of decisions, and that one sees the decisions only by remaking them. Eleven practice rounds put the claim to the test, and each one found the decisions where the claim said they would be.
A share of world GDP depends on whether output is valued at market exchange rates or at purchasing-power parity, and on which deflator and base year are used. A share of world capabilities depends on which components enter the index and how they are weighted. Trade “within” and “between” blocs depends on where the line between blocs is drawn, which is itself an estimate from voting data. A count of sanctions cases per year depends on how a case with no end is ended and how a case of several types is counted. A count of objects in orbit depends on whether debris is dated by the event that created it or by the launch of its parent. None of these decisions is wrong. Each is defensible, and each is a choice someone made, usually for reasons stated in a codebook that few readers open.
The one rule of every practice round — that each deliverable must document at least one place where the data disagreed with the paper — was a way of making the decisions visible. Series are revised; countries are recoded; a release adds cases the paper did not have; a variable’s meaning changes between the codebook and the distributed file. A replication that matches the original perfectly is less informative than one that does not, if the difference is understood and explained. The analyst who notices and records the disagreement has learned something about the instrument that the analyst who reproduces the chart has not.
The same holds for the dashboards themselves. A dashboard is not a window onto the firm’s risk; it is an argument about it, assembled from decisions of exactly the kind the practice rounds exposed. Which countries enter the footprint, and on what measure of exposure — revenue, assets, employees, suppliers? Which indicator stands for which risk, and from which release? How are missing values treated, and how are countries named so that the joins work? A board shown a dashboard sees none of this unless the analyst shows it. The appendices the memo required — a provenance log for every dataset, a list of data decisions — are where the dashboard’s argument is made inspectable, and an analyst who cannot produce them is asking the board to trust the picture rather than the reasoning behind it.

The catch slides, read together. Each practice round ended with one slide: original, ours, and the catch — what the figure does not license a multinational to conclude. Read in sequence, the eleven catches form the course’s list of what each indicator cannot tell a firm: that attention is not exposure, that shares are not levels, that capabilities are not intentions, that votes are not trade, that counts are not intensity, that a catalogue is not the environment. That list is the most useful thing to take from the course into the take-home examination, and into a risk function.

title: 12  From Indicators to Decisions
section: 12.5 Structure as well as events: Henisz on constraint
text:
12.5 Structure as well as events: Henisz on constraint
Most of the indicators the course rebuilt measure what is happening: events, attention, prices, perceptions. Henisz’s measure of political constraint, the second closing reading, measures something different: how easily what is happening could change (Henisz 2000).
The idea comes from the theory of veto players, which George Tsebelis later developed into a general account of policy stability (Tsebelis 2002). A government that wants to change a policy — a tax, a regulation, a contract with a foreign investor — must secure the agreement of every actor with the power to block it: the executive, each chamber of the legislature, the courts, sub-national governments. The more such actors there are, and the more their preferences differ, the harder it is to change anything. Henisz built from this an index, POLCON, that combines the number of independent branches of government with veto power and the alignment of their partisan composition into a measure, between zero and one, of the feasibility of policy change. He found, across a large panel of countries, that greater political constraint was associated with higher economic growth (Henisz 2000), and in later work with more investment in infrastructure — the kind of long-lived, immobile asset most exposed to a government changing its mind (Henisz 2002).

Political constraint (POLCON) — a measure of the feasibility of policy change, built from the number of independent veto players in a political system and the alignment of their preferences. Low constraint means a government can change policy quickly, in either direction; high constraint means change is slow, which protects existing commitments and delays new ones.

The measure matters for the closing argument in three ways. First, it is the structural complement to every event- and text-based indicator of the course. An index of attention tells a firm that tension is rising; a measure of constraint tells it how fast that tension could become a change in the rules. Second, constraint cuts both ways, and a firm must ask which way it cuts for it. Low constraint means a government can expropriate quickly, but also that it can grant a licence, settle a dispute or lift a restriction quickly; high constraint protects an existing investment and slows the policy change a new entrant needs. Third, constraint connects the closing readings to Session 08’s account of weaponised interdependence. The second condition for a network hub to become a chokepoint is that a state can direct the firms that run it (Farrell and Newman 2019). Whether a government can in practice order a bank, a cloud provider or a satellite operator to cut off a customer — quickly, without a court or a legislature stopping it — is a question about political constraint. The same measure that tells an investor how exposed it is to its host government tells a customer how exposed it is to its supplier’s.
Henisz’s work also carries a lesson Kobrin would recognise. Constraint is a property of a country; its effect on a firm depends on the firm’s position. A firm whose contract was negotiated with the current coalition is protected by constraint; a firm that needs the next coalition to change the law is obstructed by it. The indicator is structural, but the risk it measures is still a contingency.
The bargain between a firm and its host government also changes over time, and in a direction that Raymond Vernon identified half a century ago (Vernon 1971). Before a multinational invests, the host government needs its capital, technology and market access, and the firm can extract favourable terms. Once the plant is built or the mine is sunk, the balance shifts: the firm’s assets are hostage, its technology has been transferred or copied, and the government can revise the terms with less to lose. Vernon called this the obsolescing bargain, and the wave of expropriations of the 1960s and 1970s that Kobrin documented (Kobrin 1980) gave it its evidence. Constraint slows the obsolescence; it does not stop it. For a risk function the implication is that the assets-and-people channel is not a fixed exposure measured once at the time of investment. It grows as the firm’s bargaining power declines, and the analysis that justified the investment must be redone as the bargain ages — which is one more reason a watchlist must be revisited rather than filed.

title: 12  From Indicators to Decisions
section: 12.6 The system moves slowly, then suddenly
text:
12.6 The system moves slowly, then suddenly
Sessions 02 to 06 built the system in which multinationals operate: an international economic order resting on a distribution of power among states that has no government above them, partly governed by public institutions and by private authority. The structural indicators of those sessions — shares of world output, shares of material capabilities, the alignment of states in UN votes, the diffusion of standards — share a characteristic. They move slowly. A power transition takes decades; the reorganisation of trade into blocs shows up in data over years; the authority of an institution erodes before anyone announces its collapse.
The danger for a risk function is that slow-moving indicators are easy to ignore, because nothing in them demands a decision this quarter. The history of the twentieth century and of the last decade suggests that slow structural change is released in sudden events: the system bends for years and then breaks in a week. The interwar order of the League, examined in Session 10’s archive, looked intact until it was tested; the integration of Russia into European energy and financial markets looked like interdependence until February 2022 revealed it as exposure. The structural indicator does not tell the firm when. It tells the firm where the break, when it comes, will be most costly — where interdependence has become dependence, where a bloc boundary runs through its supply chain, where an institution it relies on has lost the support of the states that made it.
This is why the team dashboards combine families. The structural indicators locate the fault lines; the event-based and text-based ones signal movement along them; the market-based ones show whether anyone with money at stake has noticed. None of them alone is a warning system. Together, with thresholds, they can be.

title: 12  From Indicators to Decisions
section: 12.7 Channels: where the risk meets the profit and loss account
text:
12.7 Channels: where the risk meets the profit and loss account
Sessions 08 to 11 took four instruments through which geopolitical risk now reaches the firm most directly: cyber operations, economic diplomacy, sanctions and space. Across them the course used five channels to trace how a risk becomes a cost.
Market access is the firm’s ability to sell: closed by sanctions, export controls, licensing decisions, boycotts and the loss of a diplomatic relationship, opened by commercial diplomacy and trade agreements. Inputs are what the firm buys: components and raw materials whose supply is concentrated in one country, services — connectivity, timing, cloud computing — supplied by one operator under one state’s jurisdiction. Finance and payments are the plumbing: correspondent banks, payment networks, insurance, the currency of settlement — the channel through which financial sanctions and overcompliance operate. Assets and people are what the firm has in place: plants, mines, ships, inventories and employees exposed to expropriation, temporary management, conflict or interference. Data and operations are the systems the firm runs on: networks open to cyberattack, software and services that can be withdrawn, imagery and signals that can be denied.

Risk channel — the route by which a geopolitical development reaches a firm’s revenues, costs, assets or ability to operate: market access, inputs, finance and payments, assets and people, data and operations. Naming the channel converts a statement about the world into a statement about the firm, and points to the decision that could reduce the exposure.

The channels matter because they turn Kobrin’s contingency into something a firm can analyse. A statement that “tension between the United States and China is rising” is about the world. A statement that “forty percent of our revenue is in a market exposed to bloc realignment, our key component comes from a single supplier in a country subject to export controls, and our payments in that market clear through banks that would be cut off by a financial sanction” is about the firm — and each clause points to a decision.

12.7.1 When risks compound
The most demanding element of the team brief was the analysis of interactions: how two risks compound or offset for this firm. It is demanding because indicators are built one at a time, and dashboards display them side by side, which invites the reader to add them up. Risks do not add. They interact.
They compound when one risk removes the remedy for another. A firm that depends on a single supplier in a country that is drifting out of its home state’s bloc faces an input risk and an alignment risk; if the same country is a plausible target of sanctions, the sanction would cut the input at the moment the alignment drift made a replacement supplier in a friendly country most expensive. A firm whose ships depend on one satellite constellation faces a dependence risk; if the operator’s state is a sender of sanctions against a country whose waters the ships cross, the dependence becomes an exposure to a foreign-policy decision. They offset when one exposure hedges another: a firm with plants on both sides of a bloc boundary loses one market in a rupture but may keep the other, and a firm whose suppliers are spread across states with different alignments can shift sourcing as the boundary moves.
Interactions are where the analyst’s knowledge of the firm, rather than of the world, does the work. No index can be built for them in advance, because they depend on the particular combination of the firm’s footprint and the system’s fault lines. That is why the presentations reserved two of their twelve minutes for them, and why the defence returned to them most often.

title: 12  From Indicators to Decisions
section: 12.8 The composite index, and who chooses the weights
text:
12.8 The composite index, and who chooses the weights
Every team built a composite exposure index for its firm’s main countries, with the method of Session 07: select indicators, normalise them to a common scale, weight them, and aggregate. The handbook the session relied on sets out each step and the choices it involves (OECD and European Commission Joint Research Centre 2008).

Composite index — a single measure built by combining several indicators after normalisation and weighting. Its ranking of units depends on which indicators are chosen, how they are normalised and how they are weighted — and the weights are not technical parameters but statements of what matters, and how much.

The lesson of building one is that the composite is the least neutral number on the dashboard. Normalisation decides whether a country’s score is relative to the best and worst in the sample or to a fixed benchmark, and therefore whether adding a country changes everyone else’s score. Weighting decides how much a conflict risk counts against a sanctions risk or a dependence risk, and no data can settle that, because the answer depends on the firm’s exposure through each channel and on how much loss of each kind it can bear. Equal weights are a choice too: the choice to treat every indicator as equally important, which is rarely what anyone believes.
This is why the team dashboards exposed the weights as parameters the board could move, and why the presentations required one live move of a weight. A ranking that does not change when the weights move within a plausible range is robust, and the board can rely on it. A ranking that reverses when the weight on one indicator moves from a third to a half is telling the board that the decision depends on a judgement about priorities, not on the data — and that judgement belongs to the board, not to the analyst. Showing the sensitivity is not a confession of weakness. It is the analyst handing the decision to the person who must own it.
crumbs: 12  From Indicators to Decisions

title: 12  From Indicators to Decisions
text:
12.9 Indicators do not decide
The third point of the closing address was the bluntest. An indicator without a threshold and an owner is decoration. A dashboard can display every indicator the course built, beautifully, and change nothing in the firm, because nothing on it tells anyone what to do or when.

Watchlist — a short list of indicators, each paired with a threshold that triggers a named decision and with the person who owns that decision. It converts monitoring into commitment: the decision is made in advance, conditionally, so that when the threshold is crossed the question is no longer whether to act but whether the threshold was right.

The format the teams were asked to use has four columns: the indicator one watches, the number that triggers, the decision that follows — what happens on Monday — and the person who signs. Each column does work. The indicator must be one the firm can actually observe, at the frequency it needs, from a source it has logged. The threshold must be a number, set before the event, so that it cannot be rationalised away when the moment comes; it may be revised, but revising it should be a decision with a record. The decision must be specific — contract a second operator, cap new commitments in a market, pre-position inventory, start the approval process for a sale — not “monitor the situation” or “review our exposure”. And the owner must be a person with the authority to take the decision, because a threshold crossed without an owner is crossed in silence.

From the archive · Shell’s scenarios, 1972–1973
The most famous case for deciding in advance comes from the oil industry. In the early 1970s the planning group of Royal Dutch Shell, led by Pierre Wack, concluded that the forecasting methods on which the company based its investment decisions assumed a continuation of the conditions of the previous two decades — cheap oil, controlled by the companies — that the politics of the producing countries no longer guaranteed. Instead of a single forecast, the group produced scenarios, among them one in which producing governments took control of supply and prices rose sharply.
Wack’s later account emphasised that the scenarios at first changed little: managers read them as forecasts to accept or reject, not as alternative worlds whose signposts they should watch. The group’s work became effective only when it was recast to change how managers thought about their business, and to make them identify in advance what they would do in each world. When the producers’ embargo and the price rises of 1973 arrived, Shell’s managers had, in Wack’s telling, already thought through what such a world would require of them (Wack 1985).
The lesson the course takes from the episode is not that scenarios predict. It is that a risk analysis changes behaviour only when it is tied, in advance, to the signals that would reveal which world is arriving and to the decisions each world calls for. A scenario without signposts and a dashboard without thresholds fail in the same way.

The best dashboards in the final session were the ones that would make someone do something on a given Monday. They did not have the most indicators or the most elaborate composite. They had three indicators the firm could observe, three thresholds set in advance, and three decisions with names attached.

12.9.1 Why firms wait, and when they should not
There is a rational reason firms delay decisions in the face of geopolitical risk, and it deserves to be stated, because a watchlist must be designed against it. Nicholas Bloom showed that a rise in uncertainty leads firms to pause investment and hiring: when the future is less predictable, the option to wait and see becomes more valuable, and the economy slows as many firms exercise it at once (Bloom 2009). Waiting is often right. But the sanctions and space sessions both showed cases where waiting destroyed options rather than preserving them — the firms that delayed their exit from Russia until the target’s countermeasures had closed the door on a sale at their own terms; the firm with one connectivity provider that waits until the service is switched off to contract a second. The value of waiting depends on whether the options remain open while one waits. A good threshold is set at the point where they begin to close.

title: 12  From Indicators to Decisions
text:
12.10 Where the risk function sits
A dashboard is an instrument; a risk function is an organisation that uses one. The course has said little about organisation, but the closing argument implies three things about it.
The first is that geopolitical risk assessment cannot live only in a central team. Kobrin’s contingency is discovered in the firm’s operations — in procurement, which knows where the inputs come from; in treasury, which knows which banks clear the payments; in the country managers, who know what the host government is likely to do. A central function can build the indicators and the method; the exposure must be mapped with the people who run the business. The footprint slide of every presentation was, in effect, an argument that the team had done this mapping, from the firm’s own disclosures, before reaching for any index.
The second is that the function must report to people who can decide. Ian Bremmer and Preston Keat argued that the most damaging political risks are in the “fat tail” — rare, high-impact events that standard models underweight — and that firms need political knowledge integrated into strategic decisions, not appended to them (Bremmer and Keat 2009). The memo to the board, with its three risks and what to do about them, was the course’s version of that integration: a document addressed to the people who own the decisions, written so that they can act on it.
The third is that the function must keep a record. The provenance log, which every practice round required, is not an academic formality. It is what allows a firm, a year later, to know which version of which dataset produced the number on which it acted, and therefore to learn whether the number, the threshold or the decision was wrong. A risk function that cannot reconstruct its own past judgements cannot improve them.
crumbs: 12  From Indicators to Decisions

title: 12  From Indicators to Decisions
text:
12.11 What would change your mind?
The defence that followed each presentation asked questions of many kinds, but the one that mattered most was the last: what would change your recommendation? It is the question that separates an assessment from an opinion.
An assessment that nothing could change is not an assessment. A team that recommends reducing exposure to a market should be able to say which indicator, moving by how much, would make it recommend the opposite — and should be able to say it before the indicator moves. This is the same discipline as the threshold, applied to the analyst rather than to the firm. It protects against the most common failure of risk analysis, which is not ignorance but commitment: the analyst who has argued for a view reads every new piece of evidence as confirmation, and the firm that has invested on a view finds reasons to stay.
It also returns the course to its method. Every practice round asked what a famous figure did not license a multinational to conclude. The defence asked the same question of the team’s own work. The rubric rewarded answers that conceded what the data could not show and said what would change the recommendation, because those are the answers that tell a board how much weight to put on the recommendation in the first place.
crumbs: 12  From Indicators to Decisions

title: 12  From Indicators to Decisions
section: 12.12 A short review of the literature
text:
12.12 A short review of the literature

The study of political risk in international business took shape in the 1970s, in the shadow of the wave of expropriations that Kobrin (1980) documented. Kobrin (1979) reviewed the early literature and argued that risk lies in the contingency between political events and a firm’s operations, not in the events themselves; Fitzpatrick (1983) surveyed the same field and found its definitions of risk equally unsettled; and Kobrin (1982) studied how firms actually organised the assessment. The distinction between measurable risk and unmeasurable uncertainty on which the field rests is Knight (1921)’s.
The institutional strand begins from veto players (Tsebelis 2002). Henisz (2000) turned the idea into the POLCON index of political constraint and related it to growth, and Henisz (2002) to investment in infrastructure, the asset class most exposed to policy reversal. The measurement strand is more recent and largely text-based: Baker, Bloom, and Davis (2016) on economic policy uncertainty, Caldara and Iacoviello (2022) on geopolitical risk, and Hassan et al. (2019) on political risk as firms themselves discuss it. Bloom (2009) established the mechanism by which uncertainty, once measured, depresses investment, and OECD and European Commission Joint Research Centre (2008) codified the construction of composite indicators that most practical risk scores rely on.
The geopolitical turn of the last decade reframed the field around networks and dependence: Farrell and Newman (2019) explain how states weaponise the hubs of global networks, which turns a firm’s suppliers and service providers into channels of state power. On the practice of deciding under such uncertainty, Wack (1985) remains the classic account of scenarios tied to decisions, and Bremmer and Keat (2009) the practitioner’s case for integrating political knowledge into strategy.
crumbs: 12  From Indicators to Decisions

title: 12  From Indicators to Decisions
text:
12.13 After the last session
The course ends where a risk function begins. Each team leaves with a dashboard for one multinational, a memo to its board, and a method it has defended in public. Each student leaves with eleven replications behind them, each documenting at least one place where the data disagreed with the paper, and eleven catch slides that together list what each indicator cannot tell a firm.
The take-home examination tests the whole of this under the conditions in which the work is actually done: an unseen scenario, a source from which to collect the data, a firm, a time limit, and one’s own notes. It will ask for the same moves the course has practised. Find the data at source and record where it came from. Notice where it disagrees with what one expected. Build the view that answers the question. Say which family of indicators it belongs to, and what that family cannot see. Name the channel through which the risk reaches the firm. And end, as every practice round ended, with what the figure does not license the firm to conclude, and what the firm should do anyway.
That last clause is the course in miniature. Geopolitical risk will never be known with the confidence of a price or the regularity of an actuarial table. The analyst’s job is not to remove that uncertainty but to make the decisions inside it visible — the decisions in the data, the decisions in the method, and the decisions the firm will take when a threshold is crossed — to the person who must act. A dashboard that does that is finished. One that does not is a picture of the world.

12.14.4 The closing address — from indicators to decisions
Ten minutes, after the last team. Its content is in the deck; in summary:

Kobrin (1979) was right about the hard part. Political risk is not the event — it is the contingency that the event affects this firm’s operations. Every dashboard presented today is a claim about that contingency.
Henisz (2000) on constraint. The POLCON index measures how many independent veto players constrain a government. Low constraint means policy can change fast — in either direction. It is the structural complement to every event- and text-based indicator of the course.
Indicators do not decide. A watchlist is useful only if each indicator has a threshold and an owner. The best dashboards today were the ones that would make someone do something on a given Monday.
What the twelve weeks established. Geopolitical risk is measured through families of indicators that disagree; each figure in a famous work is a stack of decisions; and the analyst’s job is to make those decisions visible to the person who must act.

section: A.2 Why replicate figures, not regressions
text:
A.2 Why replicate figures, not regressions
This is not an econometrics course. The figure at the heart of a big work is where its argument meets the reader — the image that ends up in board presentations and ministerial speeches. Rebuilding it forces every decision the authors made into the open: which countries, which years, which deflator, which coding rule, which normalisation. A multinational’s risk team makes the same decisions every time it builds a dashboard. Learning to see them is the point.

Uses COW country codes, not ISO; states enter and exit the system (GMY absent 1946–1990, when GFR/GDR cover 1955/1954–1990). Missing components are coded -9. Yearly CINC sums run 1.000–1.075, not exactly 1. Ends in 2022.


SIPRI
Several sheets (Constant (2024) US$, Current US$, Share of GDP, Per capita, Share of Govt. spending, local-currency and Regional totals); ... = data unavailable, xxx = the state did not exist — notes atop each sheet, plus a Footnotes sheet. Country strings: United States of America; Russia from 1992, USSR before.


UNGA ideal points
Carries both COW ccode and ISO iso3c; estimated by calendar year since the July 2025 releases (v36/37; current v39, 30 July 2026) — earlier versions by session, so the variable meaning changed between versions. Higher = closer to the US.


IMF IMTS
Exports reported by A ≠ imports reported by B (“mirror” asymmetry). Choose one side and say which.


UNSC members
Two-year terms starting 1 January; election happens the October before — the paper’s “election year” matters.


US aid
Obligations vs disbursements; current vs constant dollars; the official site moved in 2025.


ISO Survey
Coverage of certification bodies changed over time: jumps in a country’s count can be reporting, not adoption.


Firm-level risk
Listed firms holding earnings calls in English — mostly US. Stops in 2021.


DCID
State-to-state rivals only; StateA/StateB are the dyad as names, not initiator and target — derive the target from initiator (COW code) and Dyadpair; coded from open sources — attribution is by definition uncertain.


EuRepoC
Much wider than DCID (includes criminal and non-state); filter on initiator_category (State / State affiliated actor) before comparing.


Lowy GDI
66 countries or territories only (including Taiwan and the EU’s EEAS); names, not codes, with typos (Portual, Nigaragua); counts posts, not staff or budget.


GSDB
Licence forbids redistribution: workbooks go to ZoneCours, never Tableau Public with the raw data. “Success” is the coders’ judgement of objectives met.


TIES
Includes threats of sanctions — a case may never have been imposed.


POLCON / WGI
WGI’s 2025 edition changed scale and recalculated history: never mix editions.


SATCAT
Debris carries its parent’s LAUNCH_DATE (Fengyun-1C debris is dated 1999, not 2007); OWNER is not the operator (Starlink US, Galileo ESA, Russia CIS); filter ORBIT_CENTER = EA; a blank status is not “inactive”; one download per team.


GCAT
The state is the launch provider’s, not the customer’s (Rocket Lab = New Zealand); vague-date text, padded values.


UCS Satellite Database
Frozen: data current through 1 May 2023. Use SATCAT for anything later.

Join on ISO 3166 alpha-3 codes, never on names. NMC and DCID (in initiator and Dyadpair) use Correlates of War codes (official list): keep a concordance sheet (COW ccode ↔︎ ISO3) in your workbook. The countrycode concordance tables published by Arel-Bundock et al. are the standard reference. The UNGA ideal points carry iso3c too. title: Appendix C — The Tableau toolkit
text:
C.3 3. Conventions every chart follows

A title that states the finding, not the variable. “The G7’s share of world GDP fell by a third after 1990”, not “GDP share”.
A source caption: dataset, producer, version, access date. No caption, no credit.
Units on every axis. Current US dollars or constant? Index base year? Share or count?
Direct labels in place of legends wherever there are fewer than six series.
One accent colour for the series the argument is about; greys for the rest.
Annotate the events that explain the shape of the line.
Name your decisions in a footnote: countries dropped, years rebased, codes changed.

title: Appendix C — The Tableau toolkit
section: C.4 4. The traps that cost marks
text:
C.4 4. The traps that cost marks








Trap
Symptom
Fix




Joining on country names
Côte d’Ivoire, Türkiye, Korea, Rep. silently drop out
Always join on ISO 3166 alpha-3 codes. Keep a concordance sheet for datasets that use COW or UN codes


Wide years
66 columns called 1960 … 2025
Pivot them in the data source pane (select columns → right-click → Pivot)


SUM of an index
A line ten times too high
An index is averaged, not summed. Check the aggregation on every pill


Discrete vs continuous dates
A bar for “May” across all years
Use the continuous date (green pill) for time series


Duplicated rows after a join
Totals inflate
Check the row count before and after; use a relationship instead of a join when the grain differs


Revised data
Your numbers do not match last year’s paper
That is a finding, not an error: log the release you used


Aggregates in country lists
“World”, “High income” and “Euro area” counted as countries
Filter on a country list, not on “everything that is not blank”


Percent of total computed the wrong way
Shares that sum to 100% across years instead of within each year
Edit Table Calculation → Compute using the country dimension, restart every year

E.4.2 Specimen — Quiz 1
A · Concepts (4 points, 1 each)

Distinguish risk from uncertainty in Knight’s sense, and give one geopolitical example of each.
What is the difference between Kobrin’s macro and micro political risk?
In the GPR index, why are counts of geopolitical articles divided by the total number of articles?
What does “anarchy” mean in the realist tradition — and what does it not mean?

B · The big work (3 points)
Caldara and Iacoviello (2022) distinguish GPR Threats from GPR Acts. (a) Which categories enter each? (b) Why does the distinction matter for a firm’s investment decision? (c) Name one limitation of the index for a firm whose operations are mainly in sub-Saharan Africa.
C · Read the chart (3 points)
[A stacked area chart: shares of world GDP, current US dollars, 1970–2023, for the G7, China, and the rest of the world.]

State the finding in one sentence. (b) The chart uses current US dollars. How would it change at purchasing-power parity, and why? (c) What does the chart not tell a Canadian manufacturer deciding where to build its next plant?




E.4.3 Specimen answers (Part A)

Risk: probabilities estimable from experience (piracy losses on a shipping route). Uncertainty: probabilities not estimable (whether a given strait will be blockaded within five years).
Macro risk affects all foreign firms in a country (a general expropriation, currency inconvertibility); micro risk affects one sector or firm (a mining-code change, a contract cancellation).
Because newspapers’ total output changes over time; the share removes the effect of size, so the index measures relative attention to geopolitical tension.
The absence of a government above states — no authority to enforce agreements. It does not mean chaos or constant war.

E.5 The Risk Brief

Four minutes. One development. One view. One firm. One recommendation.

Each student delivers one Risk Brief, at the start of one of Sessions 02–11. Sign-up opens at the end of Session 01; four briefs per session.


E.5.1 The brief
You are the geopolitical risk analyst of a named multinational. Something happened in the last four weeks. Brief your chief risk officer.







Minute
What you say




0:00–0:30
The development. What happened, where, who decided it. One sentence of context, no history lecture.


0:30–2:00
The view. One Tableau chart, built from data you collected at source, that puts the development in perspective — is it large, new, accelerating, concentrated?


2:00–3:00
The exposure. Through which channel does it reach your firm — market access, inputs, finance, assets and people, data and operations? How much of the firm sits in the path?


3:00–4:00
The recommendation. One decision, and the indicator and threshold that would make you change it.



One question follows (one minute), from the room or the instructor. Four briefs fill the first twenty minutes of the session.
The firm. Any real multinational with public information on its footprint (annual report, 10-K, sustainability report). It may — but need not — be your team’s firm.
The data. Any source in DATA-SOURCES.md or any other public source, cited with version and access date. Ideally the concept or dataset of a session you have already had.



E.5.2 What you hand in
Before class on the day: the .twbx (or a Tableau Public link) and your provenance log, on ZoneCours.



E.5.3 Rubric (15 points)








Criterion
Points
Full marks look like




The development
2
Precisely dated, sourced, and genuinely geopolitical (between states or political actors)


The view
4
Data collected at source; correct aggregation; title states the finding; source caption; the chart does work in the argument


The exposure
4
A specific channel; evidence from the firm’s own disclosures; an order of magnitude


The recommendation
3
One decision, an indicator and a threshold that would reverse it


Time and question
2
Four minutes, not six; answers the question asked



Automatic deductions: no source caption (−2); over five minutes (stopped at five); a development older than four weeks (−2).

E.6.1.1 The dashboard
At least four datasets collected in the practice rounds, from at least three of the six families of indicators (Session 01): event-based, text-based, expert-based, structural, market-based, firm-level. It must contain:

The firm’s footprint — where its revenue, assets, suppliers and people are (from its own disclosures), as a map or a table.
A composite exposure index for the firm’s main countries, built with the method of Session 07: indicators chosen and justified, normalised, weighted by parameters the board can move.
At least two channel views — e.g. sanctions exposure (S10), dependence on satellite services (S11), bloc alignment of key markets (S04), cyber-incident exposure of its sector (S08).
A watchlist — three indicators, each with a threshold that triggers a named decision.

E.7 Take-home examination

Three hours of work, within a 48-hour window, during the final examination period. Individual. Open book, open notes, open internet. No collaboration of any kind.



E.7.1 The format
At the opening of the window you receive, on ZoneCours:

a scenario — a geopolitical development, real or plausible, dated;
a firm — a real multinational, with an extract from its disclosures;
a data instruction — one or two sources from DATA-SOURCES.md to collect from, with the variables to use.

You hand in, before the window closes:








Part
Points
What




A · Concepts in context
12
Three short essays (≈ 300 words each) applying the course’s concepts to the scenario: e.g. what realism and liberal institutionalism each predict; whether sanctions in this case are likely to work; how the firm’s standards exposure changes


B · The evidence
14
One packaged Tableau workbook (.twbx) built from data you collected, with its provenance log, and a 400-word reading of it


C · The assessment
14
A 900-word memo to the firm’s chief risk officer: the exposure, the interactions between risks, the decision, the watchlist with thresholds



Length limits are strict. Words beyond the limit are not read.



E.7.2 Marking criteria







Criterion
Weight




Correct and precise use of the course’s concepts
30%


Data collected at source, correctly prepared, honestly logged
25%


Analysis of interactions between risks and their implications for the firm
25%


A decision with triggers, defensible from the evidence
20%






E.7.3 On language models and integrity
You may use a language model to check syntax or to help you read a codebook. You may not use it to produce any text you submit. Every submission includes a one-paragraph statement of the tools you used and how. Undeclared use, or collaboration with another person, is a violation of HEC Montréal’s academic integrity regulations.



E.7.4 Specimen scenario
Dated 15 March. The European Union and the United States announce coordinated export controls on advanced battery-manufacturing equipment to a major Asian economy; that economy responds within a week with an export licensing regime on refined graphite.
Firm: a European automotive manufacturer with an EV assembly plant in Central Europe and a joint venture in the affected Asian economy.
Data instruction: IMF International Trade in Goods by partner country (XG_FOB_USD); the Global Sanctions Data Base; UN General Assembly ideal points (Bailey, Strezhnev & Voeten); the firm’s last annual report.
Part A (example): Using Farrell and Newman’s concept of weaponised interdependence, explain which side holds the stronger chokepoint and why. Part B: Build a view of goods trade between the EU, the United States and the affected economy since 2000, set against the sanctions cases in force between them and the distance between their UN voting positions. Part C: Advise the chief risk officer on the joint venture and on sourcing for the European plant.
